title: In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse
abstract: Tech AI Meta In Meta’s version of the future, I’ll have my Muse call your Muse “Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call. “Everyone is just going to have to adapt,” CFO Susan Li said during Meta’s third quarter earnings call. by Ellen Thomas Oct 22, 2026, 6:15 PM UTC Image: The Verge, Getty Images, Meta Mark Zuckerberg is barrelling toward a future in which an autonomous network of AI agents will run our lives — shopping for us, working for us, talking to other people’s AI agents for us. Are humans ready for this very specific and unrelenting vision of a life in which we communicate primarily through bot proxies? Actually, don’t answer that. The more urgent question coming off Meta’s quarterly earnings call Wednesday night is more likely to be: “Is he?” Zuckerberg is staking Meta’s future on Muse, the personal AI agent it released to the general public last month. It’s early days, but Zuckerberg told investors during Wednesday’s call that he sees a future where “billions” of people are using Muse, and those people’s Muses are talking to and transacting with other people’s Muses in a “large-scale Muse network.” The Muses will be “extremely capable” personal agents that will help us achieve our goals and improve our lives in “whatever ways you want,” Zuckerberg said during the call, “whether that’s improving your relationships, helping you save time, save money, build a business, create new things, or anything else that you can dream of.” By this logic, Zuckerberg says, we’ll all be so hooked on Muse that it will eventually generate more revenue per user for Meta than Instagram and Facebook, which, as of today, bring in pretty much all the money Meta makes. This ecosystem of personal AI agents “can work with your friends and your families, and if you want to buy something, it’s not just navigating to that business’s website; it’s talking to their agent,” Zuckerberg said. “I think that getting that all to work well together is going to unlock tremendous value at scale.” Zuckerberg predicts that Muse will be “highly profitable” in just a few years. All of this should sound great — if not a little freaky — to investors, who probably tuned in to Meta’s call hoping Zuckerberg would have some justification for the hundreds of billions of dollars his company is currently spending on AI data centers. But if anyone was hoping for more than a concept of a plan, they didn’t get one. To be fair to Muse, Zuckerberg shared a few promising data points. To date, the app has been downloaded and set up by more than 10 million users in the US and Canada, making it one of Meta’s “most successful launches ever,” according to Zuckerberg. He did not share specific retention numbers but said that a quarter of people who downloaded Muse initially are using it daily. He sees the biggest opportunity in commerce: A quarter of Muse users are shopping through the platform, Zuckerberg said, and are spending, on average, more than $200 per purchase. Meta earns a fee for every commercial transaction that takes place on Muse. Zuckerberg’s thinking seems to be that if AI agents are doing the shopping, the potential number of transactions that could take place on the platform is, essentially, unlimited. Unlike the average consumer, AI agents don’t sleep. In theory, they’re available 24/7 to scrape the Internet, generate product recommendations, and buy things, constantly, in real time. Meta didn’t offer any details as to how all of this will actually work in practice, which makes sense given the very legitimate concerns about how the company handles data privacy. In September, a YouTuber said his Muse agent sent a stranger to his home in the middle of the night while arranging a Facebook Marketplace transaction on his behalf. When Muse launched last month, Zuckerberg claimed it was “built for privacy and security from the ground up,” but there have been reports of agents leaking content from users’ private conversations. A Canadian bank executive told Bloomberg earlier this week that it would consider blocking Muse from accessing its customers’ financial data. Zuckerberg seems to think if people get on board with Muse, enterprise will have to follow. But, what if people don’t want to? What if they can’t afford to? Someone has to pay for all the stuff the bots are buying in this fever dream of a never-ending, Supermarket Sweep episode taking place inside our phones — or Muse Charms, if you’d rather. New research from the University of Michigan shows that consumer sentiment in the US is at an all-time low as gas prices and inflation continue to creep up. If Meta knows that all of this sounds dystopian and a little bizarre, it does not care. “Agents are going to be an important part of how reality evolves, and everyone is just going to have to adapt,” Meta’s CFO Susan Li said when one investor on the call asked about potential “friction points” in getting businesses on board with the Muse plan. After all, Meta says Muse will likely remain free for consumers, while businesses will be expected to cover the transaction fees. Meta really does need Muse to work. The company’s capex is through the roof, and other financial obligations are piling up. It plans to spend between $135 billion and $145 billion in 2026, double what it spent last year. As of yesterday, it owes New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found it had violated the state’s consumer protection laws. Meta, and the rest of Big Tech for that matter, is under increasing pressure to show that its AI investments will be worth it. Forget consumers — it’s not clear if Meta itself can afford its plans. Zuckerberg stated clearly on the call that the reason it hasn’t launched Muse internationally is because of compute efficiency. It’s incredibly expensive and energy-intensive to run GPUs at the level that a network of Muses would require, and Meta seems to have reached the limit of what it can achieve with its current data center operations. Zuckerberg told investors the plan is to “10x” the cost-efficiency of its compute next year. He didn’t explain how the company plans to do this. Luckily for him — and possibly the rest of us — there is already research on how data centers can maximize compute capacity with energy-use strategies that also reduce strain on the electric grid. Maybe he’ll read it. Ultimately, Muse won’t be profitable and won’t succeed if Meta can’t figure out how to get its compute costs down. Zuckerberg said it himself. “One of the biggest constraints so far is that because this is a compute-intensive service to run, we haven’t launched it globally,” Zuckerberg told an investor who asked about the “limiting factors” he sees in growing Muse’s user base. Muse’s 10 million downloads since launch are even more impressive considering they came only from the US and Canada, Zuckerberg said, adding, “If we actually did roll it out more broadly, then you would expect that number to be significantly larger than what we’re seeing today.” Zuckerberg at least seems to understand that some people — and, probably more importantly for him, some businesses — won’t immediately “get” Muse. That’s okay, he said. “We’ll work with folks on the terms that make sense for them,” he said. “I do think that over time, this is going to be quite valuable for everyone.” Then again, this is the same guy who brought you the Metaverse. We’ll see what happens. Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. Ellen Thomas AI Meta Tech

title: Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions
abstract: AI Science Tech Microsoft says its AI tool is better than doctors at diagnosing conditions ‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge. ‘We’re going to build something that is indistinguishable from human performance … in the next couple of years,’ Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge. by Robert Hart Oct 22, 2026, 6:00 PM UTC Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman. Getty Images Robert Hart is a London-based reporter at The Verge covering all things AI and a Senior Tarbell Fellow. Previously, he wrote about health, science and tech for Forbes . For years, AI leaders have touted healthcare as one of the clearest examples of where their technology will improve lives. Now “it is finally here,” Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman tells The Verge . The company claims to have developed an AI-powered tool it says can diagnose conditions up to four times more accurately than human doctors. The findings, published Thursday in one of the world’s most prestigious journals, Science , are based on tests pitting Microsoft’s AI system against human physicians on a series of scenarios drawn from medical case reports and emergency department data. Microsoft compiled the cases into its own benchmark, SDBench, which it plans to open-source. Designed to function like a panel of medical experts, Microsoft’s Diagnostic Orchestrator uses multiple AI agents to reason through symptoms and medical histories, decide what tests to order, and arrive at a diagnosis, mimicking the process doctors use to investigate cases. On cases taken from hundreds of reports published in The New England Journal of Medicine , Microsoft’s system achieved a diagnostic accuracy of around 83 percent, compared with roughly 36 percent for generalist physicians using references and 22 percent for those working without them. The Diagnostic Orchestrator also outperformed doctors on emergency department cases drawn from a large database of patient admissions at the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, scoring 80 percent accuracy compared with an average of 47 percent for human physicians. The AI system also tended to reach its diagnoses at a lower estimated cost than human counterparts. The researchers say that the system, which is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-5, also outperformed frontier AI models operating on their own, though the peer-reviewed paper does not include newer models like GPT-6 Astra , Meta’s Muse Wonder Full , Google’s Gemini 4 Argon , or Anthropic’s Opus 5.5 . The Diagnostic Orchestrator was first developed when GPT-4.1 was the most advanced model available, but the researchers say subsequent testing suggests that “improvements in model capability do not necessarily diminish the benefits” of having multiple agents work together. Microsoft acknowledges there’s a long road ahead before the technology can be widely deployed. While the tests more closely mirror the way doctors diagnose conditions — asking questions, weighing possible explanations, and ordering tests before reaching a diagnosis — the system has only been tested on past medical cases and it remains unclear how well it would perform in real clinical settings. “It needs clinical validation,” Suleyman says. “That is a leap, but this is a major milestone along that journey.” The research is part of a broader ambition at Microsoft to develop what the company calls “medical superintelligence” — AI that can outperform the best human-led healthcare systems. Microsoft has used the term “superintelligence” since before Donald Trump and his administration co-opted it as a catch-all replacement for “AI.” Diagnosis is just part of Microsoft’s health vision, says the company’s AI health lead, Dr. Dominic King, a coauthor of the study. In a blog post published Thursday and a forthcoming article in the BMJ Digital Health & AI medical journal, the company outlines five other areas it believes AI will need to master, including coordinating clinical care, making treatment decisions, and handling the human side of medicine. King tells The Verge that Microsoft plans to begin testing the system in hospital settings with the Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center to see how it performs in real-world clinical environments. Neither King nor Suleyman would commit to a firm timeline, though King says it will likely “get underway in the next couple of months.” Commercialization could also be on the horizon, though Microsoft has yet to say when or how the technology might become available. The company already has a significant presence in US healthcare through its digital tools, and health is one of the most popular uses for its consumer-facing chatbot Copilot . King emphasizes the need for a responsible rollout, noting the high regulatory and compliance requirements in medicine that would need to be followed. “Next year we’re going to see extremely impressive deployments of intelligent systems in production,” Suleyman says. “I think that this is just going to change the way care is delivered in a big way.” Suleyman has spoken previously about his “human-centered” vision for AI, and said medicine is no exception. Even as he predicts the arrival of “something that is indistinguishable from human performance on medical superintelligence in the next couple of years,” he insists that human clinicians should and will always have a central role in patient care. While he acknowledges AI could end up with doctors being handed more work, he says his hope is that it will take some of “the drudgery” out of medicine, freeing up clinicians to spend more time with patients. “I’m very optimistic about what’s coming next,” he says. “I think this is why we build technology.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Someone hacked the Switch 2 by using an old game and AI
abstract: Gaming AI Entertainment Someone hacked the Switch 2 by using an old game and AI Thanks to a new jailbreak, a modder showed off a custom Mario Kart World featuring Peter Griffin and the red Angry Bird. Thanks to a new jailbreak, a modder showed off a custom Mario Kart World featuring Peter Griffin and the red Angry Bird. by Jay Peters Oct 22, 2026, 5:21 PM UTC Image: pepsipu on X Part Of Reverse-engineered games: All the news on video game decomps, recomps, VR and web and 3D ports see all updates Jay Peters is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme. The Nintendo Switch 2 has apparently been jailbroken, and a modder has already shown the console running a custom version of Mario Kart World featuring new playable characters like Cinnamoroll, the red Angry Bird, Peter Griffin, and Steve from Minecraft . OpenAI’s Codex helped make this “ ns2jb ” jailbreak, according to Sammy Hajhamid , aka “pepsipu.” It’s a software-only, tethered jailbreak, which, in this case, means that you’ll have to run it from a game every time you turn the console on for it to work. This exploit requires the game SmileBASIC 4 , which lets users program and play games (though another modder claims that the title is “not strictly needed”). This jailbreak still seems extremely complex for most people, and its full impact isn’t clear yet; users on the Switch 2 hacks subreddit are debating how big of a deal it actually is. Still, this could mark the beginning of a string of exploits for the Switch 2, especially if modders use AI to help . title: Wildwood’s director says AI is ‘antithetical to everything that we are at this studio’
abstract: Entertainment AI Report Wildwood’s director says AI is ‘antithetical to everything that we are at this studio’ Laika CEO Travis Knight explains why he remains hopeful despite the potential for AI to be ‘devastating.’ by Andrew Webster Oct 22, 2026, 4:16 PM UTC Image: Laika Andrew Webster is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories. Wildwood is the most ambitious film yet from Laika, the stop-motion studio best known for the likes of Coraline and ParaNorman . It’s a sprawling fantasy adventure that took five years to complete. The process involved more 230 puppets — including 36 of the main character Prue alone — which were brought to life by a team of 49 animators. All told, more than 1,000 artists worked on the film in some form. The painstaking process that goes into making a Laika film offers a distinct counterpoint to the instant progress promised by generative AI tools. Recently Wildwood director and Laika CEO Travis Knight joined a chorus of influencer filmmakers in denouncing the technology. So when I had a chance to speak to Knight ahead of Wildwood ’s premiere on October 23rd, I asked him what it’s like releasing a film like this at a time when AI tools seem inescapable. “In so many ways generative AI is antithetical to everything that we are at this studio,” Knight told me. “It’s not that we don’t believe in technology. We do. We use technology, we use computers. We’re not just making films entirely with tools that we’ve inherited from a watchmaker’s widow. A pencil is technology, a paintbrush is technology, a 3D printer is technology, a computer workstation is technology. But all of these things have meaning and value when you put them in the hands of an artist.” “There is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that” In fact, Wildwood is full of technical advances for Laika, many of which iterate on the studio’s previous work. Many puppets are now equipped with diaphragms, for instance, that animators can use to make it appear as if characters are breathing. There is more advanced musculature on the puppets’ limbs, as well as more robust and flexible materials for clothing, hair, and fur. All of these elements together create a film that is decidedly more lifelike than its predecessors. (For a more detailed look at how Laika works, check out this good rundown from Tested .) For Knight, these tools and their continued advancement are an important part of the filmmaking process, but generative AI is something very different. “When the technology is doing the work of the artist, that’s a different proposition,” he explains. “And that’s something that I am steadfastly against, because there is no humanity in what comes out of the other side of that. When you’ve ingested the material that an artist has actually created, and then regurgitate it in a different way, there’s no soul, there’s no spirit, there’s no humanity behind it. That’s theft. I really do believe that when you’re telling a human story, when you’re telling a story about loss and grief and something that means something to someone, that has to come from a person. A computer has never fallen in love. A computer has never lost someone. They’ve never made a terrible choice and lost a brother. They’ve never had their heart broken. Only a person has done that. And so only a person can speak to what that experience is and what that feels like.” Even though AI-generated films still leave a lot to be desired , the technology is infiltrating Hollywood in various ways, whether it’s the prospect of digital replicas of movie stars , studios training AI models on their films and shows , or some of the biggest players in the field investing heavily in the technology . This can make a studio like Laika, which is firmly entrenched in its handmade approach to filmmaking, stand out all the more. Ultimately Knight says he isn’t entirely against AI in fields outside of the arts, but rather wary of how it’s being used, both now and in the future. “I think AI is extraordinary technology,” he says. “On the one hand you have to marvel at the advancement of it. And I do think that it’s going to be disruptive to our society and our world. I think there are a great many benefits that can come from it when you look at medicine and science. There’s a world in which these things can benefit humanity tremendously. And then there’s a world where they can be devastating. I fear for the latter, I hope for the former, but it requires people to be good stewards of this technology. As a group of humans we have not shown generally that we’re good at that. But I’m ever an optimist, and I hope that collectively we can see the value in the technology and use it responsibly, and see the danger in the technology and push back against it.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters
abstract: Policy AI Tech OpenAI, Anthropic, and Nvidia had record lobbying quarters Collectively, they spent nearly $6 million around cybersecurity, child safety, and more. Collectively, they spent nearly $6 million around cybersecurity, child safety, and more. by Lauren Feiner Oct 22, 2026, 3:50 PM UTC Image: The Verge, Getty Images Lauren Feiner is a senior policy reporter at The Verge, covering the intersection of Silicon Valley and Capitol Hill. She spent 5 years covering tech policy at CNBC, writing about antitrust, privacy, and content moderation reform. It was a busy summer for AI lobbyists. Anthropic, OpenAI, and Nvidia each had their highest-spending lobbying quarter between July and September, federal disclosures show. Nvidia spent the most of the group at $2.2 million, followed by Anthropic’s $2.1 million and OpenAI’s $1.5 million. Compared to other Big Tech companies with long-established presences in Washington, the sums aren’t out of the ordinary. Microsoft, for example, has spent at least $2 million a quarter going back to 2021, and Google regularly spends over $3 million, including this quarter. But it’s a clear signal that the three AI firms recognize how important shaping policy has become. Tech CEOs were already visible fixtures in Washington during this period, with many of them attending a White House lunch with President Donald Trump in late September, which resulted in a “morally binding” AI safety accord that they agreed to. The lobbying disclosures show that even more discussions were happening frequently behind the scenes, during a time just before Trump named his AI czar and task force . With Democrats expected to win back at least some control in Congress after this year’s midterm elections, AI companies may only find it more important to engage with lawmakers who see cracking down on the industry as a winning issue . Anthropic included a detailed list of bills, executive orders, and other topics it lobbied Congress and the White House about in the third quarter. Among them were AI-related provisions in the Kids Online Safety Act, export control provisions in the AI Overwatch Act, Trump’s executive order renaming AI “Super Intelligence,” and the Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to put energy costs for data centers on their developers. AI companies are becoming increasingly active in policymaking OpenAI’s lobbying looks like a response to some of the fallout from the Hugging Face attack , though the disclosures only list high-level topics. In addition to engaging on issues like copyright, OpenAI lobbied Congress, the White House, the Small Business Administration, and the Commerce and State Departments over cybersecurity evaluations for frontier models, AI safety oversight frameworks, and antitrust protections for information sharing. Nvidia lobbied Congress, as well as several different federal agencies and White House offices, on issues including 6G networks, “responsible AI design,” competition policy, quantum computing, and export control policy. Apple also had a record-breaking quarter, spending $3.1 million and engaging on issues including intellectual property, tariffs, kids online safety, competition, and domestic semiconductor manufacturing. It engaged on bills that seek to put the onus on app stores to verify users’ ages, for example. It’s the first quarter in which Apple has reported spending more than $3 million on lobbying. The disclosures show that leading AI companies are becoming increasingly active in policymaking, in a quarter that marks a lead-up to the midterm elections. OpenAI didn’t even spend $1 million on lobbying in a single quarter until this year, and it didn’t spend more than half a million until the end of 2024. The most Anthropic spent in a single quarter last year was just over $1 million. And this quarter is the first in which Nvidia has spent more than $2 million. With issues like data center development and AI safety on many voters’ minds, AI lobbyists’ work will likely only increase no matter whichever party has control next year. title: PHP: The three little letters wreaking havoc across the web
abstract: Tech Updated Today, Oct 22, 2026, 4:49 PM UTC PHP: The three little letters wreaking havoc across the web by Terrence O'Brien Two vulnerabilities found in the programming language PHP put enormous swaths of the internet in danger . By some accounts, up to 70 percent of websites use PHP in some capacity. It powers Wikipedia, WordPress, Drupal, and a host of other popular sites and platforms, including DeviantArt and 4Chan, which were temporarily shut down after the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Even governments weren’t immune. But it’s not as simple as updating a few servers. The vulnerability exists in every version of PHP dating back roughly 20 years, many of which are no longer supported. That means some older sites and services that are no longer actively maintained are at risk, leaving them with little option but to permanently shut down. Here’s all the latest developments in what security firm Wiz has called “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered … in software history.” Today, 4:49 PM UTC Emma Roth The disastrous PHP vulnerabilities were exploited days before the patch Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge Hackers attempted to exploit the PHP flaws impacting sites across the web days before they were patched, according to a report from Amazon Threat Intelligence . CJ Moses, Amazon chief information security officer, writes that the company’s security team found a PHP2Shell exploit attempt on October 17th through a monitoring system designed to bait hackers, as reported earlier by Wired and Bleeping Computer . On Wednesday, websites scrambled to apply a patch for two critical security vulnerabilities affecting PHP , a programming language used by a large portion of the internet, including WordPress sites. The flaws — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — could allow hackers to execute malicious code remotely on vulnerable devices. Elizabeth Barron, the PHP Foundation’s executive director, tells The Verge that “to our knowledge, there has been no successful attempt at remote code execution” but stresses that updating affected systems is “imperative.” Read Article > Today, 3:27 PM UTC Terrence O'Brien The Internet Archive was briefly forced offline because of PHP. The list of sites that had to go down , at least temporarily, because of the recently disclosed PHP vulnerability keeps growing. Thankfully, the Internet Archive’s ops team quickly got things patched, secured, and back online. Digital librarian Brewster Kahle posted his thanks on Mastodon last night: “Given the severity, there are heroes in many many orgs from last night. Could have been no lights, no traffic signals, real problems.“ Today, 1:42 PM UTC Terrence O'Brien Two old-school Japanese mobile games are shutting down over the PHP exploit. World Quest and Save My Demonic World have run for over a decade, but they’re built on older tech that the developers say can’t be updated to patch the apocalyptic PHP exploit disclosed this week . Because the vulnerability affects almost 20 years of PHP, big chunks of internet history are in danger of being lost. Per Kotaku : Many old websites and services that are no longer being actively updated (or may simply be too old to receive the update, as was the case for these two games) are now at risk of permanently going offline. Such an event would lock swathes of the old internet from public view, including bits that were already beginning to break down and become inaccessible. Today, 10:01 AM UTC Jess Weatherbed The PHP2Shell exploit hit Cloudflare hard. CEO Matthew Prince says the company saw thousands of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerability across the Cloudflare network in the 10 hours before the issue was publicly announced . That jumped to “hundreds of thousands” of attacks in the 2 hours after the disclosure, and “millions” by last night. Yikes. Matthew Prince 🌥 (@eastdakota) on X [ X (formerly Twitter) ] Oct 21 Terrence O'Brien and Jay Peters PHP: The three letters that shut down sites all over the internet today Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge Two bugs found with AI are behind major issues today for 4chan, DeviantArt, Wikipedia , and the blog where the bar around the corner posts pictures of people’s dogs. The “critical vulnerabilities” were discovered in the PHP programming language, which underpins much of the internet, including any site built on WordPress. But it’s far bigger than that. Some Dutch and Finnish government agencies took their sites down as a precaution. The NSA Cybersecurity account on X recommended that organizations take their systems offline if “an immediate update is not feasible,” as did the UK’s National Cyber Security Center . Even Pokémon Home and Pokémon Champions were taken offline, Kotaku reports . The vulnerability isn’t exactly new. It’s been present in PHP for roughly 20 years, but exploiting it “required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” according to security firm Wiz . However, powerful AI models have made it much easier to turn that kind of obscure bug into dangerous vulnerabilities. Read Article > Oct 21 Jess Weatherbed GPT‑5.6 Sol was used to identify critical PHP flaw. OpenAI says a security researcher at Calif used GPT-5.6 Sol to identify PHP exploits before attackers did, and has shared a tool that lets developers check if they’re using a potentially vulnerable version of PHP that needs patching. Ami Luttwak, co-founder of Google’s Wiz security team that also helped to identidy the PHP2Shell exploit, told the Wall Street Journal that its “the most severe AI vulnerability that was ever found.” Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities [ OpenAI ] Oct 21 Jess Weatherbed A critical PHP vulnerability may take websites down today This PHP issue sounds like a pretty huge problem. Illustration by Carlo Cadenas / The Verge Security patches for the PHP programming language, widely used to build websites and web apps, have rolled out today, with the goal of fixing two critical vulnerabilities that could wreak havoc on the internet if left unchecked. In an advisory published on Tuesday , PHP developers said the vulnerabilities have a severity rating of 9.2 out of a possible 10, with some cybersecurity agencies encouraging websites to temporarily take their systems offline if they’re unable to apply the fix immediately. The security patch was released today at 10AM ET, and PHP users are being urged to “upgrade ​as soon as the release is available.” According to cybersecurity firm watchTowr , the vulnerabilities are Remote Code Execution exploits that reportedly impact every PHP version from PHP 5 onward, and could enable attackers to run their own code on affected servers, allowing them to maliciously alter websites, steal data, and more. title: Bill Gates says to prepare for 20 years of ‘tumultuous’ AI disruption
abstract: Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation. You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late August titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical.” In his piece, Gates ratcheted up his rhetoric around AI safety, writing that “even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history.” In interviews since , Gates has called AI “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near,” and that AI “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing.” It is clear he does not think the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated efforts from the AI industry itself, is sufficient to combat this threat. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . So I wanted to know: Is Bill Gates an AI doomer? I also had a series of questions downstream from what he’s been arguing about AI. How can we ever hope to control AI, and align it to humanity, if we can’t even agree on what it is and whether it’s conscious ? How would you even technically construct a solution to alignment that could be enforced, not just for closed-source models but open-source ones, too? Bill gave us a big chunk of his time to dig into these issues with him, and the resulting conversation is a really illuminating one. He thinks we need to prepare for roughly two decades of AI disruption, and he says this period could be so painful it might split society in two — between people comfortable living near the technological frontier, and those who reject it. We also talked about the labor considerations, the nihilism of younger generations toward technological progress, and what should make us hopeful about the future. This is a deep one. Okay: Bill Gates, the cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Bill Gates, you are the co-founder and former CEO of Microsoft. You’re also the chairman of the Gates Foundation. Welcome to Decoder . It’s good to talk to you again. You and I have spoken many times over the years. I would say that the circumstances of this conversation feel very different. Previously, when you and I would talk, you were always very hopeful about technology and what it could bring. You had a Netflix series a few years ago. You talked to The Verge , and I want to just read you this quote. You said, “I believe AI is a beneficial thing, we just need to shape it in the right way.” I would say you still agree with that, you just think the time to shape it is now. Yeah, I agree with that. I’d say the response broadly hasn’t been adequate to the speed that the challenge is arising. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way I want to have this conversation with you in three parts. I want to understand how you feel about AI as a technology today and why it’s advancing so quickly. I’m very curious about the technology, and the technical solutions to potentially control it. There are policy solutions as well, but it seems like we have to build an awful lot of technology. I’m also very curious to talk about who might impose those solutions and controls, because that seems very much up for debate right now as well. So let’s just start at the start. What has made you feel the urgency that AI is arriving at a speed that means we’re not ready to control it? The progress over the last year has been really quite amazing, starting with the ability to write code and find cyber flaws, the ability to reason in biology, the ability to form relationships with kids or other people, the ability to disrupt the job market. The incredible power that exists today means that every one of those things will happen and society needs to be ready. Do you see that happening as a technology as a whole or in the products that are instantiated by the companies that are making AI today? What I mean is that AI is a broad set of models that exist in the world, some open source, some proprietary. Then there are the companies that make these products and there are the leaders of those companies that make these products. At every level, there’s a different relationship you or I might have to AI. Are you seeing these risks and these capabilities broadly in the field, or in the particular companies led by the particular people? The risk isn’t one model versus another model. Certainly, the near-term danger of models where you can remove all the safeguards is very high and quite different from models where you monitor to make sure that cyberattackers and bioterrorists are not able to exploit the capability of the model to do gigantic harm. The big near-term risk really comes from models without safeguards. On a longer timeframe, the control issue relates to any state-of-the-art model, but it’s always easier when you can make sure safeguards are maintained. The reason I’m asking that question that way is maybe you don’t trust Sam Altman today, but you trust Dario Amodei. Or maybe you don’t trust either one of those and you trust Satya Nadella at Microsoft, and that is a market dynamic where maybe we’re all going to pick the safest model or the safest company, and you think that is diffuse. You think eventually the technology will just get to a place where it’s harmful or can cause these harms because it exists? For somebody doing a cyberattack with the model, it’s not about choosing a model. It doesn’t matter what model you choose. If Anthropic has safeguards in place, maybe it can’t. This is their approach currently. I’m just pushing on that. Yes, certainly the models where they make sure the safeguards are not removed and they’re putting a lot of effort in seeing how those models are being used, monitoring the activity, the near-term risk from those models is not gigantic. It’s more where somebody can remove all the safeguards where the cyberattacks are available today. When you say cyberattacks, is it the things like the Hugging Face breach and the other cybersecurity incidents we’ve seen out of the labs that have made you feel that thresholds have been crossed, and you need to speak up more about the controls that are needed? It’s the basic power of the models towards everything: social relationships, the job market, cyberattacks, bioterrorism attacks. We’ve crossed the threshold of capability that this is by far the most dangerous technology ever invented, and it’ll have pervasive effects in the economy and how war is fought. The industry is actually speaking up about that quite a bit, but the awareness or even the willingness to believe these things about, “This time is different,” once you get outside the industry, it’s very, very low. People are often looking at the past and saying, “All the fears about technology in terms of its disruption, including to the job market, never were borne out. So this must be another example just like those. These people who are warning of all these different problems must just be wrong and we can ignore them.” Some outsiders say, “Get better PR companies.” But that ignores the fact that these warnings are the truth We see this with our audience as well, right? “We can’t release the model, it’s too dangerous.” “This is just hype to prop up the bubble.” And on and on we go. Yeah. None of the warnings being made about these models by industry insiders are at all insincere. They’re absolutely the truth and it’s pretty much universal.

title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
abstract: Back to Articles OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 5 Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai 🤗 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌎 Embeddings Explorer | 🗺️ Interactive story Today, we’re releasing OlmoEarth v1.3 , a state-of-the-art satellite embedding model. Alongside OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re sharing precomputed, annual embeddings for the whole planet (10m, 64- and 128-dimensions), plus a new browser-based tool to explore and customize maps based on those embeddings — the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer . This means anyone can put OlmoEarth v1.3 to work right away, from tracking change over time to finding similar places—no sign-in, and no advanced technical knowledge required. Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio: training a model for each task and running it over satellite imagery to make a map. That requires GPU access and the ability to download and store the imagery . Embedding models compress satellite data into ready-to-use features that can be reused cheaply for many tasks. With OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re excited to give users more ways to explore and engage with planetary artifacts in whatever way suits them best. Compute once, reuse everywhere An embedding represents what the model learned from millions of images. OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a year of radar (Sentinel-1) and multispectral (Sentinel-2 and Landsat) satellite time series and produces one 128-dimensional vector for every 10-meter pixel on Earth; the first 64 dimensions also work on their own as a smaller embedding. Foundation models and global embeddings are expensive to produce, and to make sure everyone is able to access the benefits, we’ve computed these embeddings for the entire planet and shared them with the community on Source Cooperative . From there, a crop map, a land-cover map, or a change analysis becomes a lightweight modeling problem: train a small classifier on top and run it locally. How OlmoEarth v1.3 makes an embedding: a vision transformer reads the satellite data, an Attention Pooler pools it into one vector per patch of land, and a linear layer reduces it to 128 numbers. State-of-the-art embeddings We evaluated OlmoEarth v1.3's embeddings against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2 across 27 evaluations, covering six continents and many different tasks. OlmoEarth’s 128-dimensional embeddings score highest on 20 of 27 evals and rank highest overall. The 64-dimensional version, at half the size, still leads on 18 of 27 evals. As part of this evaluation, we introduce PLANTEUR, a new crop-type benchmark for tropical farming , and the embeddings generalize best to places a classifier has never seen (PLANTEUR technical report is available here ). Everything behind them is fully open: the model weights, the pretraining data, and the pretraining code. In practice, this means a small classifier trained on the OlmoEarth embeddings is enough to map what’s on the ground: think classifying smallholder crops in Kenya, detecting brick kilns west of Dhaka, assessing fire damage in Indonesia, and tracking gold mining in the Peruvian Amazon. Compared to previous generations of OlmoEarth models, OlmoEarth v1.3 was also our cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of our last version (v1.2) and 18% of our first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. And it also remains a strong fine-tuning model, matching v1.2's performance across research and partner labels. Our latest model builds on the same foundation as earlier OlmoEarth versions, tuned so the embeddings stay lightweight without giving up accuracy across tasks, and that efficiency work carries forward into the versions ahead. Full results and methodology are in our technical report . If you wanted to reproduce it, pre-training OlmoEarth v1.3 Base would cost roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, data, and code are all open. One place, nine years How much each pixel’s embedding changed between 2017 and 2020 (left) and 2020 and 2025 (right). Magenta is the largest change. Left: mining spreading southeast, the big patch at lower right. Right: that corner has gone quiet; the change now sits in the older mining zone to the west, part regrowth, part renewed digging. Explore it yourself in the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer. In Peru's Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve, according to Amazon Conservation's MAAP monitoring program . In February 2019, Peru's Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. The question ever since has been, did it stay down? The embeddings help answer that. Compare each pixel's vector across years, no model training required, and the 2017 to 2020 pair lights up where the mining was spreading to the southeast. Run the same comparison from 2020 to 2025, and the signal shifts. The crackdown is visible in the embeddings. The more interesting part is what the second map still shows. It is not dark. According to MAAP , pockets in the northwest kept operating, and the old mining zone keeps changing as the land recovers. The embeddings register that too. The reprieve was brief, and the pressure is building again. In August 2026, the Associated Press reported, Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve after prosecutors found mining had crossed into Tambopata itself. Our interactive story opens on this stretch of Madre de Dios, and walks through several other examples from there. The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer is an interactive analysis tool built from the embeddings themselves, rendered as a false-color map of the planet. Pan anywhere, flip between years to see how landscapes have changed, and pull up the underlying Sentinel-2 imagery to check the map against the real thing. Then start asking questions: click a place to find others that look similar, or drop a few labeled points and train a small classifier on the spot, then export the result as a GeoTIFF. No account, no setup required. For many teams, testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds. You can analyze entire regions from a handful of labels, no GPU needed. When a task calls for fine-tuning, the embeddings can help you decide whether it deserves the compute, and where the model falls short. The archive behind the Explorer holds embeddings at 10-meter resolution, roughly 150 TB per year, covering land and adjacent coastal waters. At launch, 2025, 2024, and 2023 are global, and 2017 to 2022 cover select countries, with more coverage on the way. You can retrieve the embeddings in the full 128-dimensional version or the lighter 64-dimensional version. Every embedding also comes with a record of where it came from. For each 20-kilometer tile and year, open provenance tables list the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat scenes the model read, with links to the public catalogs that host them, so you can trace any pixel back to the imagery behind it. Get started This release includes the OlmoEarth v1.3 Base model, the precomputed global embeddings, the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, and the technical report. If your work needs a specific time window, OlmoEarth Studio runs the same model over the dates, modalities, and resolution that you choose, and a tutorial shows how to generate embeddings on your own compute. These tools work together: explore in the Embeddings Explorer, fine-tune in Studio when a task calls for it, and take your map from there. Everything is published under the OlmoEarth Artifact License, the same open license as v1 and v1.2. Pull the embeddings for a place you care about, put your question to them, and show us what you find.

title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
abstract:
Back to Articles Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 13 +7 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less
guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from
Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ],
) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" ,
) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 ,
) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast
combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations
have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" ,
) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models
forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit
the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results
with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores
are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations.
Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations.

title: Liquid AI Launches RIPL, a Real-Time Inference Engine for Sub-50 ms LFMs
abstract: Liquid AI just announced Liquid RIPL , short for Real-time Inference Pipeline. RIPL is a low-latency engine that serves Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) inside a live request path. It returns complete generated responses end-to-end in under 50 ms. It also claims that latency holds while traffic arrives continuously at peak load. For developers, the message is simple. Swap gradient-boosted trees for a generative model, and keep the latency budget. Most serving stacks target large batches and long agentic jobs. A few seconds per request is acceptable there. Search ranking, fraud checks and payment authorization need answers in milliseconds. Liquid AI argues teams default to classical models for these paths because LLM serving is too slow. RIPL is built to remove that trade-off. Liquid AI describes RIPL as optimizing the full path, from request arrival to completed response. In several workloads, Liquid AI plots the same model, LFM2.5-350M, on vLLM and on RIPL. RIPL’s p95 line sits well below the vLLM line in each case. That isolates part of the gain to the engine, not just the model architecture. The LFM2.5 models themselves are hybrids. LFM2.5-1.2B-Instruct has 16 layers: 10 double-gated convolution blocks and 6 GQA blocks. LFM2.5-2.6B has 30 layers: 22 convolution blocks and 8 GQA blocks. Liquid measured p95 end-to-end latency under open-loop Poisson arrivals on one B200. LFMs ran on RIPL. Baselines, including MiniCPM5 and Granite 4.2, ran on vLLM. Source: Liquid AI blog, Figure 2 . Sealf-reported. Liquid AI also mapped 6 real-time workloads against fixed budgets: Yes, according to Liquid AI. Shopify is deploying LFMs across latency-sensitive commerce workloads. In search enhancement, LFMs run with sub-20 ms inference on production traffic. According to Liquid AI’s blog, they use about 50% fewer parameters than alternatives and deliver 2 to 10x faster inference. Check out the RIPL announcement , try the latency calculator , and see the LFM2.5 model cards .. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Gradium Open-Sources Phonon, a 31M-Parameter On-Device TTS Model Under Apache 2.0
abstract: Gradium has open-sourced Phonon , a family of small text-to-speech models built to run on the device. The Gradium Phonon on-device TTS model comes in 31M and 40M sizes. The English Phonon 31m ships under Apache 2.0 and fits in a 64.5 MB file. Developers get natural speech with no cloud call, no GPU and no per-character bill. Phonon is an open-weight TTS family from Gradium , a Paris voice AI company spun out of Kyutai. It generates speech locally on phones, laptops, boards and browsers. Phonon uses a causal transformer backbone. Its prefix combines text and speaker embeddings. A SentencePiece tokenizer with a 4,000-token vocabulary reads raw text, with no phoneme conversion. The backbone generates 1 latent vector per 80 ms frame. A flow-matching head turns that vector plus noise into an audio embedding in a single step. A smaller variant of Kyutai’s Mimi decoder then outputs 24 kHz PCM audio. A separate end-of-speech head decides when to stop. Phonon 31m uses 6 transformer layers, width 512 and 8 attention heads. Phonon 40m uses 9 layers at the same width. Both are distilled from a larger Phonon teacher. Training ran on an NVIDIA H100 cluster with NCCL and CUDA Graphs. The work builds on Kyutai’s Continuous Audio Language Models research and Pocket TTS. Gradium ran blind pairwise listening tests with 1,189 raters and 17,270 votes. In US English, Phonon 40m scored 2117 Elo and Phonon 31m scored 2098. Kokoro scored 2043, NeuTTS 2034 and Magpie 1939. Accuracy was tested on a public hard-sentence set . It holds 500 sentences per language, full of phone numbers, emails and postal codes. Phonon 31m scored 1.70% WER against 3.50% for Kokoro and 8.71% for NeuTTS Nano. Built-in text normalization drives much of that gap. On the easier Seed-TTS set, the gap closes. Phonon 31m scored 0.51% LLM WER, while Kokoro scored 0.45%. On a MacBook Air M5 CPU with 4 threads, Phonon 31m reaches first audio in 6.9 ms. It runs 29.9x faster than real time. Kokoro takes 517 ms, because it does not stream. With Arm KleidiAI and Apple Accelerate, Phonon 31m reaches 46.7x real time. On a Raspberry Pi 5, Phonon 31m starts in 38 ms and runs 3.7x faster than real time. Gradium says Kokoro needs 7 seconds to start there. On Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, Phonon starts in 7.5 ms at 24x real time. On an NVIDIA L40S, CUDA reaches first speech in 5 ms. An AMD EPYC 7413 CPU takes 43 ms, per the press release . Benchmark rows come from Gradium’s blog and model card . Size, language and license rows come from each model’s own card. The runtime is MIT or Apache-2.0 licensed. It covers Rust, Python ( pip install ptts ), Swift, C, C++ and the browser via phonon-tts . It also ships an OpenAI-compatible server and a WebSocket server. Phonon loads in Transformers, MLX-Audio, Ollama and LM Studio. Voice cloning and voice design run in Gradium Studio, then the voice runs locally. Check out the technical blog , model card , GitHub runtime and hard-sentence dataset . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . title: Cohere Releases Rerank 5 With Passage-Level Context Focus and Calibrated Scores
abstract: Cohere AI has released Rerank 5 , a new reranker family in Pro and Fast tiers. Cohere Rerank 5 is a retrieval model that reorders search results before they reach an LLM. It adds 2 developer features: Context Focus, which returns relevant passages inside each document, and calibrated relevance scores. For RAG and agent builders, the message is simple. Send fewer, better tokens to the LLM. Rerank 5 ships as two models. Pro targets ranking quality on reasoning-heavy queries and long, domain-specific documents. Fast targets low latency and high throughput for agents running many searches. Both models support over 100 languages and a 32K context window. They also rerank semi-structured data such as JSON, tables and YAML records. Upgrading needs no re-indexing. Developers change the model parameter and keep their existing keyword, vector or hybrid search. Context Focus is an optional feature, off by default. A single Rerank call returns document scores plus scored character spans. Each span carries start and end offsets into the original text. Developers set it through the relevant_spans field, with a threshold and max_spans value. Cohere tested it on 30 QA datasets . Removing half the retrieved text kept 96% of answer quality. Removing three quarters kept 87%. Cohere says teams can push to 10x less context at some quality cost. In a search-agent test across 17 datasets, BM25 alone scored 46% accuracy. Adding Rerank 5 Pro raised it to 49%. Context Focus at the default 0.1 threshold cut tokens per task by 19% and reached 57%. At 0.4, tokens fell 34% and accuracy hit 58%. Versus BM25 alone, the full stack used 35% fewer tokens. On 6 deep-search benchmarks, tokens fell 41% and accuracy rose from 39% to 52%. Rerank 5 scores read as probabilities. A score of 0.7 means a 70% chance the document is useful. Cohere team measured expected calibration error (ECE) against blind human graders and NIST TREC-DL assessors. Rerank 5 scores about 0.06 on both. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 0.234 and 0.307. Rerank 4 Pro scores 0.384 and 0.309. In practice, dev teams can filter by threshold instead of a fixed top-k. An agent can also detect when nothing relevant came back. All scores below are self-reported by Cohere using RCP-nDCG@10 , a Cohere-developed variant of nDCG. Cohere ran the competitor models itself. Pro leads all four main benchmarks. It scores 92.2 on ViDoRe V3 , 90.4 on BEIR , 82.2 on BRIGHT and 87.3 on nanoMTEB. BRIGHT shows the largest jump: 12.4 points over Rerank 4 Pro. Fast beats Voyage AI Rerank 3 Lite, Qwen3-Reranker-8B and Rerank 4 Pro on all 4. It ties Voyage AI Rerank 3 on ViDoRe V3 at 90.6. It trails it on BEIR, 88.1 versus 88.6. On parsed PDFs, averaged over 47 datasets, Pro scores 89.9 and Fast 88.5. Voyage AI Rerank 3 scores 88.4. Pro ranks first on 14 of 19 non-English languages in Cohere’s internal suite. *Scores are RCP-nDCG@10 or ECE from Cohere’s Rerank 5 post , measured by Cohere. Not independently verified. Rerank 5 is generally available on the Cohere API and Model Vault . It also runs on Microsoft Foundry ( Pro , Fast ) and Amazon SageMaker ( Pro , Fast ). It is also available to all North users. API pricing is $0.05 per 1M tokens for Pro and $0.02 for Fast. Model Vault lists $4.00 per instance-hour for both tiers on its Medium tier. Integrations include LangChain, Haystack, Elasticsearch and Weaviate, per Cohere’s integration docs . Check out the official announcement , the Rerank 5 changelog and the full results sheet . title: A Developer’s Guide to OmniParseBench: Leaderboard Benchmarks and OCR Testing
abstract: In this tutorial, we implement OmniParseBench , Datalab’s open benchmark for document parsers, which grades a parser’s output with 16,288 small pass-or-fail tests across 2,937 pages, from scanned forms and handwriting to arXiv math and dense tables. Rather than trust the leaderboard, we rebuild it from the verdicts Datalab released for 27 parsers, after feeding the scorer a hand-made page to see which mistakes flip a verdict. We then measure ranking certainty, slice it by document type, test whether the two models the card names as helping build tests behave differently on tests a model corrected, and run Tesseract and Indra OCR ourselves on a 50-page sample. Along the way, we find that the top two parsers are statistically tied, the leader changes on most slices, and one launch figure doesn’t match the released files. We install omni-parse-bench pinned to 1.0.0rc1, because a bare pip install still resolves to 0.2.0, an older release with a different API. The benchmark extra brings the parser adapters, the Hugging Face client, and pyarrow for the manifest, and on Colab we add Tesseract with its script models through apt. We also pin the dataset to one commit, since the repository changes as parsers are added. Printing the families shows the structure the benchmark rests on: present, order, and repeat tests form the text family; table_cell forms the tables family; and layout_kind forms the layout family. Before trusting a score, we want to see what a verdict means, so we write a gold file by hand with thirteen tests on an invented page and grade predictions with unit_tests.score, the function the benchmark itself uses. A base prediction passes everything, and each variant changes one thing. A one-letter typo, a lost minus sign, a different symbol in an equation, swapped headings and a mislabelled block each flip exactly one test to fail, with a reason attached. The controls still pass : capitals, a dropped thousands separator and dfrac in place of frac, because text is folded and equations are compared after KaTeX renders them. With the scorer understood, we download the manifest, the gold files, and the published verdicts at the pinned revision, skip the 1.5 GB of page images, and read every page’s tests through unit_tests.gold. The counts match the dataset card, including 92 languages once the undetermined and no-language codes are removed. Two fields deserve attention . Tags such as handwriting, rotated, or table never decide a verdict; they only let us slice results. Derivation records how each answer was established, from publisher markup and text layers to model panels and human review, which lets us test later whether test construction favored any parser. Because results.parquet holds one row per parser per test, we can rebuild the leaderboard by passing each parser’s rows to unit_tests.summarize. The headline is the mean of the text, tables and layout pass rates with unsupported tests left out, so a parser that cannot return layout blocks, such as Tesseract, gets no headline at all. All 108 entries in the card’s table match its one-decimal values. The recomputation also exposes a near tie at the top: Datalab accurate and Gemini 3.8 Flash both round to 92.9, 0.024 points apart, and pooling every test instead of averaging families puts Gemini first. A gap that small raises the question of how much of the order is noise. T ests on one document tend to pass or fail together, so we resample documents rather than tests : each of 2,000 draws picks 2,343 documents with replacement and recomputes every headline from per-document pass counts with one matrix product. The gap between the top two runs ranges from about -0.9 to +0.9 points, and each leads in roughly half the draws, so the honest reading is a tie. Datalab balanced, 1.35 points behind the leader, is clearly separated from it, and so is every parser below. Slicing by tag shows what a single headline hides about the documents we actually have. We r ecompute the headline on handwriting, rotated pages, tables, single scripts , and other slices with the same family-mean rule, after an assertion confirms that the rule reproduces the official headlines on the full set. The overall leader comes first on only three of thirteen slices. Gemini 3.8 Flash leads on handwriting, math, and forms; Claude Sonnet 5.5 on rotated pages; and Mistral OCR on Greek. Armenian and Lao rest on six and five documents, so we treat them as hints rather than rankings. The dataset card marks Gemini 3.8 Flash and Claude Sonnet 5.5 as used in creating and verifying some tests without saying which, so we ask a narrower question with a difference-in-differences : does a parser’s pass rate on one derivation split, relative to its rate elsewhere, change differently for the starred pair? On the 102 model_review tests, which a vision model corrected, both groups pass far less often than elsewhere, but the starred pair falls about 25 points less. The human_review placebo shows a smaller gap in the same direction and model_panel runs the other way, so we report a flag, not proof. Rebuilding a leaderboard from published verdicts is one thing; producing verdicts ourselves is another. data.select picks a fixed 50-page sample spread over all 22 suites, and we download only those pages. The loop is the benchmark’s own: needs lists the outputs a page still lacks, harness. predict runs the parser; record saves the prediction and grades the folder, so an interrupted run can resume. On Ubuntu we also link Tesseract’s script models into the layout the adapter expects. Tesseract passes 30.4% of the sample’s text tests against 17.6% on the full set, a gap that depends on which pages were sampled. Indra OCR is an open CPU model, and the package ships the HTTP server its adapter talks to, so we install the versions pinned in that server’s Dockerfile into a separate environment and start it in the background. Against the published verdicts on the same pages, Tesseract agrees on every scored test, so its sample score matches the published one. Indra agrees on 203 of 221, and all of its table differences sit on one page, which accounts for the whole gap between its published tables score of 36.1 and our 69.4. One page moving a family that far is the clearest argument for resampling documents. Any parser can be graded without an adapter: we write one predictions file per page and call benchmark.grade, declaring the outputs we cannot produce as unsupported. Our parser reads a PDF’s embedded text layer with pypdfium2 and returns an empty string for images, which have none. On PDF pages it passes exactly as many text tests as Tesseract, 42.3% each, without any OCR, while on images it has nothing and Indra OCR still passes 43.1%. Plain text fails every table test, since a pass needs cell structure, so the mix of PDFs and images matters whenever two parsers are compared. Instead of repeating the launch claims, we check each one against the files. The counts hold exactly, from tests and pages to languages and subsets, and the Claude and Tesseract rows match. Datalab ‘s own row does not: the launch article and blog give Datalab an accurate 92.7 and place it second behind Gemini, while the released verdicts give 92.92 against 92.89, a tie that rounds to the same figure. The no-judge claim holds for the scorer itself, whose modules import no model or HTTP client; KaTeX runs in an embedded JavaScript engine to compare equations. Latency and price cannot be checked from these files. The summary prints each step’s one-line result and every check the run decided, marking which held and which did not: 13 of 17 held, and the four that did not are findings rather than failures, namely the placebo gap, Indra’s reproduction and Datalab’s two launch figures. It also lists what we did not run here: the hosted parsers that need paid keys, the GPU models, latency and cost, and the full set of 2,937 pages.

title: IBM AI Releases Granite Speech 5.0 2B for Multilingual Transcription and Translation
abstract: IBM has released Granite Speech 5.0 2B , a new open speech-language model for transcription and translation. Granite Speech 5.0 2B is a 2B-parameter model from IBM that turns speech into text in 6 languages. It ships under Apache 2.0. IBM also updated 2 existing models : the edge-focused Turbo CTC and the diarization-focused 4.1 2B Plus. For developers, the release covers accurate transcription, fast on-device transcription and speaker-attributed transcripts. The model has 3 parts, per the model card . A speech encoder of 16 Conformer blocks is trained with CTC. It uses block attention over 4-second audio blocks. A 2-layer window q-former then projects and downsamples the acoustic embeddings. Total downsampling is 10x, so the LLM sees embeddings at 10 Hz. The LLM is an intermediate checkpoint of granite-4.0-1b-base . IBM extended it to 16k positions with YaRN and fine-tuned it with LoRA adapters. Training used 390,000 hours of public audio plus synthetic data. The synthetic sets target Japanese ASR, keyword biasing and translation. Training took 40 days on 8 H100 GPUs. On the Open ASR Leaderboard , IBM’s chart shows a 5.68% average English WER. That average covers 9 public and 2 private test sets, as of October 21, 2026. Only Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores better, at 5.40%. Note a source conflict. IBM’s blog reports 5.06% instead. That figure is unofficial, dated October 15, and averages public short-form sets only. Per-set results range widely. The model scores 0.99% on LibriSpeech Clean and 2.21% on LibriSpeech Other. It scores 13.79% on the private conversational set. On the noisy FFASR leaderboard , it ranks #4 of 42 at 14.80% average WER. Qwen3-ASR-1.7B scores 13.41% there. Multilingual CommonVoice WER is 2.60% for Portuguese and 3.50% for Spanish. Japanese is the weakest language at 10.74%. For translation, X-to-English CoVoST BLEU reaches 53.6 for Portuguese and 40.1 for German. English-to-Mandarin was not evaluated. Keyword biasing shows the clearest gain. On Earnings-22, keyword F1 rises from 67.2 to 90.1 with correct keyword lists. With 2,000-term lists mixing correct and wrong terms, it still reaches 82.8. *Leaderboard averages as charted in IBM’s model card from the Open ASR and FFASR leaderboards. Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC keeps its 470M footprint. It now transcribes 7 languages with native punctuation and capitalization. IBM compiled one Conformer block and reused its graph across the stack. That lifted throughput to 19,870 RTFx, up from about 12,600 at launch. The updated Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus is a drop-in weight update. Average timestamp shift falls from 210.86 to 98.54. Long-form WER drops from 13.53 to 10.22. Biased-keyword WER falls from 11.79 to 6.48. Granite Speech 5.0 2B runs in Transformers , vLLM, llama.cpp and mlx-audio. For GGUF, IBM recommends Q8_0. Lower-bit quantizations lose accuracy on audio longer than about 1 minute. Check out the model card , IBM blog and Granite Speech paper . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. title: Perplexity and NVIDIA Researchers Introduce JOLT: a Joint Teacher-Student Reinforcement Learning Method
abstract: Perplexity , along with NVIDIA team, has introduced JOLT, a new post-training method for language models. JOLT stands for Joint On-policy Learning and Teaching . It trains a single model in 2 roles. The teacher sees privileged information; the student does not. The key change is that the teacher is trained too, so its feedback stays usable. On MATH, JOLT matched GRPO’s accuracy with 6.5x fewer processed training tokens. For teams running RL post-training, that is a direct compute question. JOLT is a self-distillation method from Perplexity and NVIDIA that trains one model as teacher and student. It builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) . Outcome-reward RL, such as GRPO , gives one reward per attempt. That signal is sparse. It does not say which tokens helped. On long agentic tasks, successes are rare, so learning is slow. On-Policy Distillation fixes sparsity by having a stronger teacher score each student token. OPSD removes the separate teacher. The same model becomes the teacher when given privileged context, such as a verified solution. The research team argues this is not enough. A teacher holding the answer can take shortcuts the student cannot follow. Its guidance may sit beyond the student’s reach. In the paper, OPSD’s teacher-student disagreement grows during MATH training. JOLT trains both roles of one shared model at the same time: The research stands in the center on a ‘reward-consistent’ teacher. Its distillation update should point the same way as the student’s reward gradient. The ideal teacher favors high-advantage actions while staying near the student’s policy. The research team tested 5 settings, each with a different base model and type of privileged information: JOLT+ had the highest mean score in every setting. Against GRPO, the strongest baseline, it gained 1.5 points on GSM8K. It also gained 4.2 on MATH, 3.0 on LCBv6 and 9.9 on AppWorld. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 , JOLT+ reached 10.96% pass@1 and 34.83% pass@32. GRPO scored 8.25% and 30.34%. Even plain JOLT, with no student reward, beat GRPO on MATH: 72.14% versus 68.36%. On MATH, the research team fit accuracy curves against training-token budgets. At 63.44% accuracy, GRPO’s checkpoint used 8.40M processed training tokens. JOLT’s fitted curve needed 1.30M, a 6.5x reduction. Counting completion tokens only, the gap widens to about 13x. Across 55% to 65% accuracy targets, savings range from 4.3x to 7.4x on processed tokens. JOLT also levels off higher. It plateaus near 72%, against about 70% for GRPO and 62% for OPSD. All scores below come from Perplexity’s own runs in the JOLT paper , with hyperparameters tuned per method. Method descriptions link to each method’s own paper. Terminal-Bench base model: 5.18% pass@1, 22.81% pass@32. Check out the paper on arXiv and the Perplexity research blog post . All credit goes to the researcher of this project.
