title: 生數科技Motubrain團隊將直播Physical AI訓練全流程，持續半個月
abstract: 生數科技Motubrain團隊將直播Physical AI訓練全流程，持續半個月 量子位的朋友們 2026-10-21 17:45:22 來源： 量子位 10月21日，生數科技世界模型團隊正式開啟Motubrain 2.0訓練全流程公開直播 大模型訓練過程，開始更多地出現在公眾視野中。 此前，小米MiMo負責人羅福莉公開了MiMo-V2.6強化學習階段的訓練進展，讓外界看到了大模型訓練中的一些具體細節。 現在，Physical AI領域也有了類似嘗試。 10月21日，生數科技世界模型團隊正式開啟Motubrain 2.0訓練全流程公開直播，計劃持續半個月，向公眾展示具身模型的訓練過程及研究進展。 這次直播關注一個問題：Physical AI究竟如何實現？ Physical AI，即物理人工智慧，希望讓AI能夠理解物理環境，並通過機器人完成實際任務。相比大語言模型，Physical AI 還需要解決動作決策、任務執行和跨場景泛化等問題。 Motubrain 系列是生數科技研發的具身模型，致力於為機器人構建具備通用能力的“大腦”，探索不同任務、場景和機器人本體之間的能力泛化。 Motubrain 2.0即將開源。在正式開源前，團隊選擇率先公開其訓練全流程，向外界展示這款模型從訓練、測試到能力迭代的過程。 此次公開訓練涵蓋四個環節： 1、預訓練：觀察訓練規模對模型效能及零樣本泛化能力的影響。 2、後訓練：針對具體任務進一步訓練，提升任務執行能力。 3、Agent任務執行：探索模型能否將已有經驗遷移到其他任務。 4、RSI（遞迴自我改進）探索：研究模型能否根據執行反饋評估並改進自身行動。 此次直播的特別之處，是嘗試開啟具身模型訓練的“黑盒”。 過去，外界瞭解具身智慧技術進展，主要通過機器人Demo、評測結果和論文。模型經歷了怎樣的訓練、不同階段的能力如何變化，通常很難直接觀察。 Motubrain 2.0 選擇公開從訓練、測試到能力迭代的全過程，希望讓外界看到模型如何逐步形成能力，也能看到訓練中的失敗、試錯和調整。 對於具身智慧行業而言，這種方式讓模型研發過程更加透明。研究者和開發者不僅能看到最終結果，也有機會了解訓練中遇到的具體問題，以及團隊如何通過實驗和反饋不斷改進模型。 同時，團隊也希望藉助此次直播，與技術同行分享研究中的經驗、問題和思考，共同探討規模化訓練、跨任務泛化和自主改進等關鍵問題，為Physical AI實現範式的探索提供更多參考。 當然，相關研究仍處於探索階段，具體效果還需要後續實驗和評測驗證。相比只展示機器人最終能做什麼，公開模型如何訓練、能力如何形成，同樣具有研究價值。 直播入口：www.motubrain.com/motubrain2.0-live 官網連結：www.motubrain.com 本文由生數科技提供，量子位獲授權轉載，觀點歸原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 生數科技 量子位的朋友們 又一國產決策模型釋出！準確率超過微軟和Jev等決策模型 2026-10-22 既能“做選擇題”，也能“做填空題”——星辰意圖理解模型Xing4.0-29B-Intent釋出 2026-10-22 飛書豆包工作AI先鋒未來人才大賽：企業正在爭搶會用AI做成事的人 2026-10-21 比亞迪成為2026年APEC會議官方合作夥伴 2026-10-20 相關閱讀

title: LeCun押注的世界模型，中國一家清華系公司已經做進了機器人
abstract: LeCun押注的世界模型，中國一家清華系公司已經做進了機器人 田, 晏林 2026-10-21 15:15:05 來源： 量子位 世界模型賽道新看點：千訣隱變數可辨識性方向的研究，比LeCun相近工作早一年，不堆畫面預測，主打物理規律與跨本體複用。 田晏林 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 世界模型這條賽道，越來越有全球頂尖AI高手過招的架勢了！ Yann LeCun持續押注預測式世界模型，李飛飛帶領World Labs探索可互動的3D世界，全球頭部AI團隊正沿著不同技術路線加速探索。 讓AI真正理解物理世界、預測物理變化，正成為新一輪技術競爭的焦點。 最近，這股世界模型熱潮也延伸至南京。 10月20日， 首屆2026物理AI與世界模型大會 在南京開幕。圖靈獎得主 LeCun、姚期智 都遠端分享了最新觀察。 在這場世界模型領域的學術與產業盛會上，清華系具身智慧公司 千訣科技 ，也在大會上正式釋出了 預測式世界模型Polibrain 。 千訣科技創始人高海川 在開幕式演講中，用一句話解釋了世界模型的獨特價值： 有了地圖，可以推匯出最短路徑；但有了路徑，並不能反過來推匯出一張地圖。 這裡的「地圖」，正是對物理世界及其變化規律的一種抽象理解。 而千訣此次釋出的Polibrain，想做的就是讓機器人擁有這樣一張可以用於預測和規劃的「地圖」。 早在2025年，千訣聯合清華大學團隊就在ICML發表了世界模型相關理論研究，其在隱變數可辨識性、低階偏好等方向上的公開探索， 比LeCun團隊的相近研究早了約一年。 僅僅一年後，千訣已經把相關技術積累推進到了真實機器人應用中。 從環境感知、行動預測，到自主規劃和執行反饋，千訣試圖讓機器人學會根據物理世界的變化，自主決定下一步怎麼做。 目前，這套智慧能力 已在四足、人形、輪式、雙臂等機器人形態上開展適配。 千訣的預測式世界模型Polibrain，究竟有什麼特別之處？他們又是如何讓不同形態的機器人，共用一套智慧大腦的？ 機器人大腦有了新解法 “世界模型講了這麼多，大家真的理解了嗎？” 在開幕式的壓軸演講上，高海川率先丟擲了這樣一個問題。 隨後，他講了一個「古代商人從廣州運送荔枝到長安，怎樣才能找到最快的路線？」的故事。 看過電影《長安的荔枝》的觀眾，對這個難題應該不陌生。 高海川給出了兩種解法。 一種辦法，是把可能的路線都走一遍，從中找出最優解。 另一種方法，則是先弄清廣州到長安沿途有哪些城市、城市之間如何連線，畫出一張地圖，再根據地圖規劃路線。 前者被他用來類比當前的VLA路線，後者則對應世界模型的預測與規劃方法。 區別在於，機器人能否提前推演行動可能帶來的結果，減少實際試錯。 這正是千訣Polibrain預測式世界模型想要解決的問題。 那麼，這套方法放到真實機器人身上，能做什麼？ 千訣提供的一段應用演示影片，展示了一個直觀場景。 在戶外，一臺帶著機械臂、揹著回收筐的四足機器狗，正在執行垃圾回收任務。 它需要自主尋找地面上的垃圾，識別目標位置，移動過去，再規劃機械臂動作，將垃圾抓起來，放進隨身攜帶的回收筐。 看起來只是一套撿垃圾的動作，背後卻有一連串決策難題： 垃圾在哪裡？機器狗應該從哪個方向靠近？機械臂伸出去之後，能不能順利抓住目標？ 尤其是在真實環境中，物體的位置、空間關係都可能發生變化。機器人光知道下一步做什麼還不夠，還得提前判斷，這一步做下去會發生什麼。 這正是預測式世界模型想解決的問題。 Polibrain通過學習環境狀態、歷史資訊和行動結果之間的關係，在任務相關的潛在表徵空間中預測狀態變化。 這裡還有一個關鍵的技術選擇。 Polibrain並 不追求把未來的每一幀畫面完整生成出來 。 對於正在撿垃圾的機器人來說，地面是什麼顏色、背景有多少紋理，未必重要。 真正影響任務完成的是垃圾的位置、機械臂與目標的相對關係，以及抓取動作會如何改變目標狀態。 與其花費大量計算資源還原整個世界，不如集中預測那些真正影響行動的關鍵資訊。 高海川在演講中也強調： “世界模型要做好，關鍵在於狀態表徵。” 但預測得準只是第一步。 真實任務很難完全按照計劃推進。如果抓取失敗，或者目標位置發生變化，機器人還需要知道如何繼續。 Polibrain將環境感知、狀態理解、行動預測、任務決策、動作執行和反饋調整連線起來，形成持續決策閉環。 當執行結果與預測不一致時，模型可以根據新的環境狀態重新評估任務，調整後續行動。 它還支援通過關鍵特徵解碼，追蹤預期狀態與實際結果之間的偏差，為異常定位和任務恢復提供依據。 不過，這套機制在複雜場景中究竟有多可靠，還需要更完整的實測資料驗證。 而且，這張「地圖」，理論上並不只屬於某一種機器人。 人形機器人可以用機械手抓杯子，輪式單臂機器人也可以。 雖然本體結構和控制方式不同，但它們需要理解的物體關係、目標狀態及環境變化規律存在共性。 這意味著， 面向物理世界的部分智慧能力，有機會在不同機器人之間複用。 目前，千訣已在人形、輪式、單臂、雙臂等多種機器人形態上開展適配，探索陪伴服務、餐飲服務、物品整理及精細操作等任務。 不過，要讓不同形態的機器人真正共用一套智慧能力，光有環境預測還不夠。 模型必須從複雜的真實場景中，學到可以跨環境、跨任務複用的規律。 這就涉及千訣更底層的一項研究： 多項式表徵。 比LeCun相近研究早一年，千訣如何突破泛化難題？ 所謂「多項式表徵」，簡單來說，就是 通過一套數學方法， 讓AI從複雜環境中提取真正影響任務結果的關鍵變數， 減少對無關細節的依賴。 為什麼需要這項技術？ 機器人想要適應不同場景，繞不開一個難題： 泛化 。 比如，機器人在一個倉庫學會抓取，換到另一個倉庫，光照、背景、貨架位置一變，表現就可能大打折扣。 問題在於，模型訓練時，很可能記住大量與任務無關的細節。背景紋理、光照條件，甚至物體周圍的擺設，都可能被神經網路當成判斷依據。 這就容易造成 「特徵汙染」 。 另一種問題更隱蔽：模型可能誤認為經常同時發生的現象之間，存在因果關係。 高海川在演講中舉了一個例子。 主人出門前，從抽屜裡拿走鑰匙。這裡有三個事件：主人出門、主人拿走鑰匙、抽屜裡的鑰匙消失。 如果模型只學習事件之間的相關性，就可能錯誤地認為，只要主人出門，抽屜裡的鑰匙就會消失。 等到主人真的忘帶鑰匙，讓機器人幫忙尋找時，機器人反而可能判斷，主人既然已經出門，鑰匙肯定不在抽屜裡了。 顯然，這不符合真實世界的因果關係。 模型究竟是在死記硬背，還是學到了物理世界的規律？ 千訣希望通過多項式表徵，讓模型少記場景細節，多學可遷移的規律。 這條路線背後，有千訣持續數年的研究積累。 2025年，千訣聯合清華團隊在ICML發表《When Do Neural Networks Learn World Models?》，研究神經網路在什麼條件下，能夠從觀測資料中恢復隱藏的世界結構。 研究從 「多工學習」和「低階偏好」 入手，利用Fourier-Walsh變換分析 離散佈爾世界中的函式結構 ，解釋模型何時能夠辨識真實隱變數。 有意思的是，LeCun團隊也從相近的理論視角切入。 2026年5月，LeCun等人發表《When Does LeJEPA Learn a World Model?》，同樣研究世界模型的隱變數可辨識性，以及函式階次與低階偏好之間的關係。 高海川在演講中進一步解釋了兩項研究的差異。 千訣團隊從因果推斷和布林空間的角度提出學習判據，LeCun團隊則從時間維度切入。 雖然研究物件不同，數學工具不同，但兩項研究提出的 學習判據 具有一定 等價性 ，最終匯出的表徵，在資訊層面也具有一定等價性。 事實上，兩者都在嘗試回答同一個問題： AI究竟如何從複雜觀測中，學到能夠泛化的世界結構？ 從公開發表時間看，千訣聯合清華團隊在相近方法論方向上的研究，比LeCun團隊上述論文早了約一年。 2026年，千訣聯合清華團隊進一步提出「有效階」 （Effective Degree，ED），試圖給神經網路的複雜度提供一把可以計算的「標尺」。 以往Benchmark能告訴研究者模型答得對不對，研究者卻不容易判斷模型學到的函式究竟有多複雜。 ED嘗試解決這個問題。 其方法是沿真實資料點之間的插值路徑觀察神經網路，用正交多項式擬合模型輸出，再根據不同階次成分的權重計算複雜度。 低階成分佔主導時，ED較小；高階成分越多、幅度越大，ED就越高。 這樣一來，研究者不僅可以量化、比較模型的函式複雜度，還能將這一指標引入訓練過程，幫助模型減少不必要的複雜變化。 當然，函式更簡單，不意味模型一定掌握了正確的物理規律。 但這項研究 為分析和最佳化模型泛化能力提供了新工具 。 除了學會提取規律，機器人還得記住真正重要的事。 比如，機器人把杯子放進櫃子，關門後就看不見了。等到下一步需要操作這個杯子，必須記得杯子被放在哪裡。 在連續任務中，物體可能被遮擋，部分狀態無法僅憑當前畫面判斷。 於是，千訣團隊還研究了 基於反事實推斷的歷史資訊篩選機制 。 簡單來說，就是判斷某段歷史觀測是否會影響後續預測和決策，再決定是否保留。 機器人無需記住看到的所有畫面，而是重點保留那些會影響後續任務的資訊。 背景是什麼顏色，不一定重要；杯子放進哪個櫃子，卻會影響下一步動作。 「多項式表徵」幫助模型提取關鍵變數，「因果記憶」則幫助模型篩選重要經歷。 兩者共同為機器人應對遮擋、延遲反饋、多步驟任務等複雜情況提供方法支援。 不過，相關基礎研究提供的是技術依據，實際效果還需要更多真實任務驗證。 總不能機器人每換一個房間，就重新學習一遍怎麼幹活吧？ 多項式表徵與因果記憶，為模型學習和利用可遷移的規律提供了技術基礎。 但學到的規律，怎麼才能讓不同形態的機器人共同使用？ 這就涉及另一個問題：如何把對世界的理解，與具體執行動作的機器人本體分開。 不造機器人，千訣想做所有機器人的大腦 說回那顆要送往長安的荔枝。 即便已經有了地圖，想把荔枝真正送到長安，也還需要馬匹、車船、驛站等不同運輸環節協同工作。 同樣，機器人有了對世界的理解，也不意味著它必須獨立完成所有動作。 高海川舉例說，讓機器人把衣服放進洗衣機，人形機器人可以一隻手拿衣服，另一隻手開門。 但如果換成只有一隻機械臂的輪式機器人呢？ 它完全可以通過智慧家居IoT系統，讓洗衣機自己開啟門。 硬體不同，執行方式不同，但最終對物理世界產生的變化可以相同。 這也是 千訣「松耦合世界模型架構」 想要解決的問題。 具體來說，Polibrain將面向環境與任務的共用表徵，與具體機器人的動作執行能力相對分離。 對世界的理解可以共享，至於怎麼執行，則由不同機器人甚至自動化裝置根據自身能力決定。 這套思路也決定了 千訣的產品定位：不造機器人本體，而是為不同形態的機器人提供智慧能力。 而且，千訣的目標不只包括 通用機器人 ，也包括 面向具體任務的專用機器人 。 高海川認為，具身智慧的商業落地可能是漸進的，不必一開始就追求完整的人形形態。 比如，減少一隻機械臂，可以成為酒店配送機器人；換成雙臂，可以進入餐飲服務場景；進一步調整本體結構，又能用於巡檢、安保、環衛清潔等任務。 形態可以因場景而變，底層對世界的理解卻有機會複用。 更值得關注的是，這種跨本體複用還有一層 資料價值 。 具身智慧長期面臨物理互動資料不足的問題。真機採集成本高、積累緩慢，不同形態的資料又難以直接共享。 從資料來源看，可以將機器人學習所需的資料大致分為三個層次： 底層是第一視角影片、人類操作影片等無本體資料，幫助模型學習環境、物體關係及互動過程。 中層是真機遙操等機器人本體資料，建立具體動作與物理環境變化之間的聯絡。 頂層是真實業務場景中的反饋資料，讓模型發現長尾問題，並持續迭代。 三類資料各有作用，但要讓它們真正產生價值，還需要解決跨本體資料難以複用的問題。 高海川認為，人形、輪式、四足乃至掃地機器人，雖然結構不同，但對物體關係、任務目標和環境變化的理解存在共性。 Polibrain希望通過共享高層表徵，讓不同形態積累的資料有機會服務同一套模型。 更多機器人接入，覆蓋更多真實場景；資料持續積累，推動模型泛化；模型能力提升，又有機會吸引更多機器人廠商和客戶。 由此，一套跨本體資料飛輪有了形成的可能。 不過， 共用表徵不代表資料就能自動打通。 高海川也提到了不同機器人企業之間的資料壁壘。 對於各家本體廠商而言，資料本身具有商業價值，開放共享並不容易。 千訣作為獨立模型公司，正在通過服務不同機器人企業，探索跨本體資料的協同利用。 從理論研究到真實機器人的應用，Polibrain的釋出，為預測式世界模型走向產業應用提供了一個觀察樣本。 至於跨本體資料能否真正打通，模型能力能否隨著應用規模持續提升，還需要更多真實場景的驗證。 現在，「地圖」已經有了。 但從畫出地圖，到把那顆「荔枝」真正送到長安，還有一段長路要走。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 田, 晏林 清華具身模型登頂全球第一！突圍GPT-6、輝達，不靠外掛和額外資料 2026-10-09 AI算力硬合作，馬斯克還是更相信中國製造 2026-10-04 title: 量智齊飛！4個月9款車落地，輕舟城市NOA擊穿10-20萬體驗天花板
abstract: 量智齊飛！4個月9款車落地，輕舟城市NOA擊穿10-20萬體驗天花板 思邈 2026-10-21 14:40:46 來源： 量子位 百萬臺搭載打底，智駕普及與安全並重 允中 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 從7月到10月，城市NOA大規模量產迎來一輪密集兌現視窗。 輕舟智航憑藉行業首個量產上市的地平線單征程6M城市NOA輔助駕駛解決方案， 迎來9款合作車型接力上市、開啟預售或公佈上市計劃 。 這些車型集中覆蓋 10-20萬元主流價格帶 ，意味著輕舟單征程6M正把城市NOA從高價旗艦帶入大眾市場，成為10-20萬元價格帶智駕普及的關鍵推手。 該方案以 128TOPS算力跑出256TOPS的輔助駕駛體驗 ，通過軟硬深度協同，把高階輔助駕駛能力帶到更主流、更廣泛的全車型區間，讓輔助駕駛不再是豪華車標配。 量智齊升，才是輕舟智航真正帶給使用者的技術承諾和真實價值。 9款車型密集落地，城市NOA駛入10-20萬元市場 據介紹，輕舟智航是行業第一家實現單征程6M方案城市NOA量產上市的公司。 該方案基於安全可解釋端到端技術，具備擬人化防禦性駕駛能力，在無燈路口、人車混行窄路等場景可提前預判、減速防禦。 對主機廠而言，它用更低算力、更低成本實現城市NOA體驗，極大助力高階輔助駕駛普惠到全車型，成為城市NOA規模化普及的關鍵推手。 從落地節奏看： 7月下旬，一款自主品牌主流價位新能源重磅轎車率先上市； 9月上旬至下旬，多款自主品牌新能源車型、SUV及高階新能源車型接力上市、開啟預售或公佈上市計劃，其中包含一款合資品牌新能源SUV； 10月上旬至中旬，一款自主品牌燃油SUV和一款自主品牌轎車接棒上市。 多品牌、多品類、多動力形式在短時間內密集推進，橫跨自主與合資、純電與混動、轎車與SUV，覆蓋主流價位市場，形成城市NOA規模化上車的密集攻勢。 密集節奏背後，是主機廠對輕舟方案成熟度、成本競爭力與安全性的集中投票，也意味著 高階輔助駕駛正從旗艦車型的“亮點配置”，加速變為多品牌、多品類的“大眾標配” 。 而這些車型的主要價格帶都是在10到20萬之間的主流價位段，也提升了智駕普惠在中國汽車行業的落地速度。 百萬臺搭載打底，智駕普及與安全並重 規模化背後，是輕舟智航持續擴大的量產基盤。 2026年，輕舟乘風輔助駕駛系統累計搭載量已突破 100萬臺 ，合作車企超過10家，覆蓋超過 45款量產車型 。 百萬級搭載量不僅驗證了其產品穩定性，更構建起高質量資料閉環：上百萬車輛成為真實物理環境的資料觸點，持續反哺演算法進化，讓系統越用越安全、越用越好用。 安全始終是輕舟智航的底線。輕舟智航不僅要讓智駕走向大眾市場，更要讓安全能力同步普及。 其安全端到端大模型與座艙中控HMI深度融合，讓系統決策透明可解釋。 資料顯示，輕舟乘風輔助駕駛系統累計使用者輔助駕駛行駛里程 超45億公里 ，AEB誤觸發率低至 每50萬公里少於1次 。 在10-20萬元主流市場，安全保障與智駕能力同樣重要。 與此同時，輕舟乘風基於 單征程6M的Pro方案 目前仍在快速升級中。據介紹，相關能力正按OTA節奏逐步匯入，近期將在重點車型上啟動OTA升級。 此次升級將通過OTA方式引入更強的 場景理解能力和複雜環境博弈決策能力 ，使城市NOA表現更成熟、更安全。 輕舟不斷通過軟體迭代驗證單J6M的技術上限；量產落地則將嚴格按道路實測和OTA節奏穩步推進。 從城市NOA出海到L4落地，開啟更多想像空間 與此同時，輕舟智航近期勢能持續增強。 海外市場，10月輕舟城市NOA在歐洲首次亮相，於巴黎、慕尼黑完成城市道路場景展示；L4級無人物流小車在廣州啟動無圖落地測試運營。 物理AI方向，世界模型與強化學習技術持續落地。 從城市NOA出海首秀，到L4無圖運營，再到物理AI前沿探索，輕舟智航正以多線並進的技術與商業化節奏，進一步夯實市場領先性，也為城市NOA規模化普及開啟更大想像空間。 2026年是城市NOA大規模量產之年。輕舟智航預計今年新增合作車型 幾乎全部搭載城市NOA功能 ，推動高階輔助駕駛向10萬級車型快速普及。 從越級體驗，到百萬搭載量築牢資料閉環，再到7月至10月多車密集上市，輕舟智航正以“輕舟速度”領跑城市NOA規模化量產，助力行業智駕與安全普惠。 *本文系量子位獲授權刊載，觀點僅為原作者所有。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 智駕 輕舟智航 思邈 首Token延遲降低32.4%！是石科技叢集排程大招，國產推理再提效 2026-10-20 通研院孵化的團隊，也盯上了RSI 2026-10-19 全棧自研！國產高階互連晶片，穩了! title: 實探寧德時代總部：“去寧化”是喊太大聲了
abstract: 實探寧德時代總部：“去寧化”是喊太大聲了 傑西卡 2026-10-21 12:35:56 來源： 量子位 電池開發，分工遠比想像複雜 傑西卡 發自 ROBO-車 量子位ROBO | 公眾號 AI4ROBO 一塊電池，攪動了汽車產業鏈風雲。 理想斥資26.5億元入股欣旺達動力，小米聯合中創新航等企業開發電池……一場圍繞動力電池核心技術、成本和供應鏈話語權的討論，最近愈演愈烈。 就連寧德時代也親自下場回應： 會造車，不一定會造電池。還是要專業的人，做專業的事。 然而在這場風波中，上汽旗下智己卻反其道而行之，宣佈即將推出的LS8 NEO純電，將 全系搭載寧德時代電池 。 不僅如此，智己還聯合寧德時代，邀請媒體前往寧德參觀工廠——也包括量子位ROBO。 有點意思。 車圈目前似乎分開了兩波陣營。一邊是車企開始尋求降低對供應鏈的依賴；另一邊在主動把和寧德時代的合作推至臺前。 智己為什麼堅持合作寧德時代？寧德時代的電芯、電池包和車企自研電池有什麼不同？雙方又是怎樣看待當下趨勢的？ 帶著這些疑問，我決定前往福建寧德，現場看看。 走進寧德時代，原來一顆電芯是這樣成型的 十月的寧德，綠水青山，桂花飄香，路邊還能看到蜻蜓飛來飛去。不瞭解的人或許很難想像，在這片山水之間，坐落著全球最大的動力電池企業。 這裡是寧德時代總部。 其實參觀前，我預想到這次行程會比較嚴格，但沒想到這麼嚴格。拍攝裝置的序列號要提前報備，抵達寧德時代科技大樓後，需要先去訪客中心登記、領取訪客卡，再刷卡進入。 科技大樓據說借鑑了 方形電芯 的造型設計，內部能夠容納5000多人辦公。 大廳裡還有一個展廳，我們待了一個上午，陸續遇到好幾批前來參觀的訪客。 展廳門口就是一座園區佈局圖。 以湖泊為界，寧德時代的辦公、研發和生產設施分佈在不同區域。據講解員介紹，僅在寧德當地，公司就有 超過5萬名員工 ，全球員工總數超過23萬人。 這家2011年成立的企業，從2017年開始連續多年位居全球動力電池裝車量榜首，2025年的全球市場份額達到39.2%——相當於 全球每賣出三輛電動汽車 ，大約就有一輛搭載寧德時代電池。 十幾年間，寧德時代的業務也從 動力電池 延伸到 儲能、換電、船舶 等領域。 展廳裡陳列的是寧德時代一路佈局的各種形態的電池，從磷酸鐵鋰、三元鋰，到鈉離子、凝聚態電池，有的 已經量產 ，有的還處在 研發驗證 階段。 其中一個低溫展示裝置挺有意思。鈉離子電池被裝在一個透明的低溫裝置裡，溫度已經降到 零下30多攝氏度 ，電池旁結了厚冰，罩壁上還有遇冷凝結的水霧。 講解員介紹，相比傳統鋰離子電池，鈉離子電池在低溫效能方面的優勢更明顯，寧德時代也在探索將鈉離子與其他電池體系組合，以改善車輛在寒冷地區的使用表現。 展廳也集中擺放了一部分面向不同場景的電芯產品，拿在手裡大部分都比較有分量。 即便是這個最輕薄的凝聚態電池（能量密度高達500瓦時/千克），也比看起來要沉不少。 寧德時代還展示了研發中心做的一些測試，包括高壓沖水、衝擊、跌落、火燒、浸水、震動方面的測試。 以浸水測試為例，寧德時代通常會把電池包放在水池裡，浸泡半個小時、24小時、48小時不等。浸泡完成後，要確保沒有任何一滴水珠滲透到電池包內部才算合格。 當然了，模型展示終究還是紙上談兵。一顆電芯究竟怎麼製造，還得去工廠看看。 所以離開科技大樓，我們來到了附近的 電芯工廠 。 進入廠房前，需要穿上鞋套，錄音、拍照也受到嚴格限制。我們沿著指定參觀路線，透過展示視窗觀察部分生產區域。 廠房內部空間非常開闊，大型生產裝置佔據了主要區域。我們能夠看到的工作人員並不多，很多工作已經由自動化裝置完成，只有部分環節仍然有人工參與。 還有一個細節是，我發現工作人員的著裝也有所不同。據講解員透露，電芯製造涉及不同的環境控制要求，需要對溼度、靜電和微小粉塵等等因素進行管理。 看來不管是對外對內都是一樣的嚴謹。 參觀過程中，還有方殼電芯的展示樣品讓我們近距離接觸。方方扁扁的，像個放大版的磁帶。 這就是新能源汽車動力電池最基本的組成單元之一。 一顆電芯內部包含正負極材料、隔膜、電解液等，經過材料加工、裝配和檢測，最終形成能夠獨立充放電的單元。而一輛純電動車的電池包，往往需要 數十顆乃至上百顆電芯 共同工作。 因此，電池廠需要考慮的，除了單顆電芯的效能，還有不同電芯之間的 一致性 。 舉個例子，如果一個電池包內的電芯容量或內阻存在明顯差異，充放電過程中，部分電芯可能提前達到電壓限制，影響整個電池包能夠釋放的電量。隨著使用時間增加，這種差異還可能進一步擴大。 也就是說，電池製造不僅要生產出合格的電芯，還需要 控制大量電芯之間的效能差異 。 寧德時代在技術交流中介紹，其先進產線最快能夠實現 每秒生產一顆電芯 ，製造過程中設定了超過 7000個質量控制點 ，並通過AI視覺檢測等方式識別製造缺陷，目標將缺陷率控制在PPB級別，也就是 十億分之一 的量級。 這一水平，對應著動力電池製造中的兩項要求：提高生產效率，同時控制大規模生產中的質量波動。 製造裝置本身也在持續研發。 據寧德時代介紹，公司除了研究電池材料和結構，還會參與生產裝置設計，再與裝置供應商共同完成製造。電池量產由此涉及材料、裝置、工藝和軟體演算法等多個環節。 一圈參觀下來，能感受到現代電芯生產的複雜程度。一項電池技術從實驗室走向大規模量產，還需要解決生產效率、質量控制和產品一致性等一系列工程問題。 而對於汽車企業，電芯能夠穩定生產出來，只是其中一個環節。從電芯到電池包，再到真正裝上一輛汽車，中間還有大量開發工作需要完成。 而這一點，在智己和寧德時代等技術交流中也有了更清楚的線索。 電池開發，分工遠比想像複雜 此次參觀的發起方之一，是上汽旗下的 智己汽車 。 我們能有機會參加寧德時代工廠，也是因為即將推出的 LS8 NEO純電版 這個契機。 這款車定位 25萬元級純電SUV ，目前已經公佈了兩項核心配置—— 全系寧德時代電池 ，以及 全系靈蜥全線控底盤 。 不過真正進入技術交流環節後，我發現雙方介紹的合作方式，其實要比表面上更複雜。 首先，LS8 NEO純電提供了兩種電池方案，分別是 93度磷酸鐵鋰電池 和 103度三元鋰電池 。 兩種電池的技術側重不同。103度三元鋰版本最高CLTC續航達到752公里；93度磷酸鐵鋰版本則採用寧德時代新一代BMS電池管理系統，重點改善低溫、低電量條件下的電量估算等問題。 例如，磷酸鐵鋰電池在部分荷電狀態區間的電壓變化較小，給剩餘電量估算增加了難度。寧德時代工程師介紹，新系統通過演算法最佳化，可以將電量估算誤差控制在約3%的水平。 兩款電池都按照智己的需求定製開發。電芯來自寧德時代在寧德和江蘇的基地，電池包則由寧德時代、上汽時代兩家分別封裝。 事實上，上汽與寧德時代的合作早有淵源。 2017年，雙方就成立了 時代上汽、上汽時代 兩家合資企業，分別佈局電芯和動力電池系統業務。 因此，同樣標註寧德時代的電池，背後的生產主體也可能不同。 更重要的是，電池包生產完成後，還需要與整車進行 適配開發 。 寧德時代工程師解釋，電池包需要按照整車企業提出的需求設計，裝車後還要經歷冬季、夏季及不同道路條件下的測試，BMS也需要與整車三電、熱管理等系統配合。 以電池容量為例。增加容量，通常可以提高車輛續航，但電池包也會隨之增加重量和成本。車身重量變化，又會影響整車能耗、底盤設計和操控調校。 因此，確定一輛車採用多大的電池，需要綜合考慮續航目標、車內空間、車身結構和成本。 而線控轉向、後輪轉向等底盤技術的加入，也意味著電池包、電驅系統與底盤部件需要在整車開發階段佈置。 從這一點看， 電池企業與整車企業的研發工作其實存在著大量交叉 ，電池包設計也需要從整車架構開發早期就開始統籌。 電池供應商需要根據車型需求開發相應產品，整車企業則需要將電池與電驅、熱管理、底盤等系統整合起來。 智己此次介紹的另一項核心技術——全線控靈蜥底盤，也屬於整車開發中的重要部分。 這套系統結合線控轉向與後輪轉向，按照工程師披露的資料，LS8 NEO純電的後輪轉向角度最高可達正負24度，最小轉彎半徑約4.85米，主要用於改善大型SUV低速掉頭、泊車等場景下的操控體驗。 而線上控底盤之外，智己還需要完成電池、電驅與整車能耗管理等系統的匹配。 也就是說，採用寧德時代的電池，並不意味著電池相關工作全部交由供應商負責。 而寧德時代的研發和製造能力，也需要通過具體的車型專案，轉化為能夠實際裝車的電池產品。 這恰恰也是外界關於“去寧化”討論中繞不開的問題： 汽車企業究竟需要掌握多少電池技術，才能滿足自身的產品開發需求？ 自研電池，車企需要做到哪一步？ 回過頭看，最近一輪動力電池供應鏈調整中，各家車企採取的方式並不相同。 理想投資欣旺達動力，是加強與電池供應商之間的資本和技術聯絡；小米則是與中創新航等企業聯合開發電池；也有其他車企也在引入新的供應商，或者擴大自主研發範圍…… 這些動作涉及供應鏈的不同層面。 增加第二供應商 ，可以降低對單一供應商的依賴； 自主開發電池包、BMS等技術 ，可以提高車企對產品效能和成本的控制程度；進一步參與電芯材料研發乃至製造，則需要投入更多資金、裝置和研發資源。 同樣被稱為自研電池，實際涉及的技術範圍可能相差很大。 這種差異，主要和 成本 有關。 動力電池是新能源汽車成本佔比最高的零部件之一，既影響車輛續航和效能，也關係到整車企業的採購成本、產品開發週期及產能安排。 隨著其他電池廠商的技術和製造能力不斷提升，車企擁有了更多選擇，也開始爭取在 關鍵零部件研發和供應鏈管理 中掌握更多主動權。 但從智己與寧德時代的合作可以看到，汽車企業深入參與電池研發，並不必然意味著獨立製造電芯。 事實上，上汽集團一方面與寧德時代保持長期合作，另一方面也在投資清陶能源、推進固態電池研發，並持續發展自身的電池管理和整車整合技術。 這些佈局覆蓋不同技術路線，也涉及不同層次的自主研發與供應商合作。 而對於寧德時代，隨著車企增加供應商、更多企業參與電池研發，它與整車廠商之間的合作內容，也需要根據客戶需求不斷調整。 此次寧德之行讓我看到，從電芯製造到智己的定製開發與整車整合，恰好呈現了動力電池產業鏈中幾種不同的技術分工。 對於寧德時代，核心工作集中在電池技術和規模製造；對於智己，則需要根據車型定位提出需求，並將電池與其他整車系統共同開發、驗證。 隨著越來越多車企深入電池研發，汽車產業鏈的技術分工或許還會經歷變化，車企對產品定義權和供應鏈主動權的爭取，可能也將持續影響雙方的合作方式。 回到最初的問題：車企需要做到哪一步？ 動力電池涉及材料、電芯、系統整合等多個技術環節，車企需要掌握的能力，也要放在整條研發製造鏈條中考量。 車企必須掌握的，是產品定義權，以及電池與整車的整合、驗證能力；至於電芯由誰來造，可以根據車型定位、規模和成本，在自研、聯合開發和外購之間選擇。 但無論供應鏈如何變化，汽車競爭終究要回歸到產品。自研、外購或聯合開發，都是車企實現產品目標的不同路徑。 零部件可以各有所長，但一輛汽車的競爭力，始終是所有技術共同作用的結果。 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 寧德時代 傑西卡 特斯拉利潤腰斬，一夜跌沒“通用汽車”！馬斯克：FSD在中國也會遙遙領先 2026-10-22 理想宣佈：電池自燃報廢賠新車！自研6年後有底氣了 2026-10-21 賽豆首款AI汽車公告圖公示，價格被按零件猜到了20萬以上 2026-10-20 智慧不出彩的「領克」，剛靠一次墜崖事故出圈了 2026-10-14 相關閱讀

title: Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types
abstract: October 22, 2026 Research Beyond tree cover: mapping the world’s forest types Maxim Neumann and Charlotte Stanton Read the paper A new 10-meter resolution map shows which of the world's forests are natural, planted, or farmed, and how they are changing over time Protecting the planet's forests starts with a simple question: what type of forest are we looking at? From space, an old-growth rainforest, a eucalyptus plantation, and an oil palm estate can look like the same patch of green. But they hold very different amounts of carbon and biodiversity. Telling them apart, and knowing how each patch has changed over time, shows us where conservation is working and where natural forests are being converted into plantations and farms. Today, Google DeepMind and Google Research, together with the World Resources Institute (WRI) and the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis (IIASA), are releasing Forest Typology (ForTy) 2020 , a global map that categorizes every 10-by-10-meter patch of land on Earth into six distinct forest and land-use types, a key baseline for the EU's deforestation regulation. Alongside it, we're sharing an early time series that tracks how these forests changed each year from 2017 to 2025, including where natural forests were replaced by plantations or farms. For the first time, users can see at 10-meter detail worldwide, year by year, not just where forest was lost, but what replaced it: a timber plantation, a tree-crop farm or other land. Why "tree cover" isn't enough All forests store carbon and, together, forests are home to most of the world's land-based plant and animal species. But a forest’s ecological value also depends on its history: a primary forest that has never been cleared holds far more carbon and biodiversity than a single-species timber plantation that is harvested every decade or two. Most global maps only indicate whether trees are present. That's a challenge for those trying to protect natural forests. The European Union's regulation on deforestation-free products (EUDR), for example, requires that products like coffee, cocoa or palm oil do not originate from land that was forest in 2020 and has since been converted to agriculture. Similarly, wood products, such as furniture, must also be free of forest degradation: they can't come from primary forests that have since been converted into plantation or planted forests, or from naturally regenerating forests that have since been converted into plantation forests. As a result, companies and regulators need to know not just where trees are, but what kind of forest they form (primary or regrowing, planted or plantation, forest or farm) and what replaces that forest after a harvest. Last year, we jointly released Natural Forests of the World 2020 , a 10-meter resolution global map that separated natural forests from all other tree cover. It offered a starting point to help companies and regulators implement the EU Deforestation Regulation, and to support commodity producers in meeting their commitments not to convert natural forest. That map answered one question for every patch of land: was it natural forest in 2020 or not? ForTy goes further, showing what kind of forest is there, from primary forest to timber plantation to tree crops, and, with the new time series, how that changes each year. How ForTy classifies the world's forests Specifically, ForTy sorts land into six categories based on definitions from the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO): Primary forest: native forest with no visible signs of human disturbance. Naturally regenerating forest: forest that grew back on its own, for example after logging or fire. Planted forest: forest that people planted or seeded, and managed over long cycles. Plantation forest: fast-growing, intensively managed tree farms, often of one species. Tree crops and agroforestry: farms that grow things other than wood, like oil palm, rubber, cocoa, or fruit. Other land: everything else, from grassland and cropland to cities and water. The Forest Typology map for 2020. Each color shows the most common forest or land type in each square kilometer. Explore it at 10-meter detail in our Earth Engine app . Training our ForTy model was challenging because these categories depend in part on how land is used, not just how it looks. To teach our model the difference, we built a large-scale collection of forest-type examples with about 1.7 million labeled locations drawn from expert surveys, national and regional datasets, and targeted reviews of places where the model struggled. The model uses a custom architecture designed for the challenges of remote sensing data, and takes as a key input AlphaEarth Foundations embeddings , data-compact summaries of years of satellite observations for each 10-meter pixel, so it can spot subtle clues like planting patterns, growth cycles and harvest rhythms. From above, the five forest and tree-crop classes can look alike. ForTy is able to identify the subtle differences in structure and seasonal patterns that set them apart, accurately categorizing them in a global map database. Imagery © Google Earth, Maxar Technologies, Airbus. Putting the map to the test A map is only useful if people can trust it. So, with IIASA and WRI, we validated ForTy against more than 9,000 randomly chosen sites around the world. At each site, two trained experts studied high-resolution imagery and years of satellite records to determine which type of land was really there. ForTy picked the right forest type 90% of the time, and told forest apart from non-forest land 95% of the time, outperforming other global forest maps. Beyond accuracy, we know that global conservation is not one-size-fits-all. Instead of giving a yes-or-no label for a specific patch of land, ForTy provides a probability score for each class, enabling users to adapt the classification to regional contexts and application-specific precision trade-offs. For example, a company assessing deforestation risk under EUDR might set a strict threshold, only accepting pixels the model is highly certain about to avoid regulatory risks. Meanwhile, a researcher estimating total forest extent might use the full spectrum of probabilities to get a fuller picture of the potential landscape. From a single snapshot in time to a story of change A map of a single year is a useful baseline, but forests change. Our new early-release time series applies a similar approach to every year from 2017 to 2025. It shows not only where forests disappear and where they grow back, but also what kind of change happened: a natural forest turned into a timber plantation, for example, or abandoned land slowly regenerating into forest. This differentiation matters because some of the most important changes are hard to see from space. When a natural forest is logged and replanted as a plantation, the land soon looks green again, so standard tree-cover maps might not pick up the change. ForTy's time series makes these hidden changes visible, both losses and gains. Your browser does not support the video tag. What's next The Forest Typology 2020 map [described in Scientific Data] and the new time series are now freely available on Google Earth Engine under an open license. We hope governments, companies, conservation groups and scientists will use them to help build deforestation-free supply chains, direct forest finance where it’s needed, and protect the natural forests that matter most. Over the coming months, we'll keep improving the time series with our partners and users, and we'd love to hear how you use it. ForTy is part of our portfolio of research on AI for Nature , which includes mapping the drivers of forest loss, forecasting deforestation risk, modelling global species distributions, and monitoring biodiversity in the field.

title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
authors: Chenglong Wang, Yuwei  Xiao, Alper Sarikaya, Michel Galley, Chris Quirk, Jianfeng Gao
abstract: AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. The post Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations appeared first on Microsoft Research .

title: The science behind TorchNeuron, Amazon’s new PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium chips
abstract: PyTorch is the one framework that most AI developers use to build their models. It’s a Python library of operations performed on tensors, higher-dimensional analogues of a matrix, or 2-D grid of numbers. Almost all of the crucial features of contemporary AI models, such as input data, model weights, and attention mechanisms, are represented by tensors, and PyTorch drastically simplifies writing code to manipulate them. This week, we announced the availability of TorchNeuron, an open-source backend that translates PyTorch code into operations executable on AWS Trainium systems. PyTorch code that already runs on other accelerators will run on Trainium with minimal or no code changes. TorchNeuron bridges PyTorch and Trainium, and both sides gain from it. PyTorch developers can now run their code on Trainium, which was built from the ground up for large-tensor workloads. They can also tap the AWS Neuron SDK, which includes a profiler that traces each instruction with cycle-level accuracy and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI, pronounced "Nikki"), which enables control almost at the assembly level. TorchNeuron includes several optimizations that enable PyTorch code to run efficiently on Trainium, including caching at multiple levels and an optional “adaptive eager” mode that doesn’t execute individual operations one by one, as is typical in plain eager mode, but instead groups and compiles operations for more efficient execution, approaching fully compiled performance. Much of the innovation behind TorchNeuron, however, is the way its performance was evaluated. AI agents searched through hundreds of thousands of open-source models and categorized them according to their architectural characteristics. This allowed the Annapurna team around Khaled ElGalaind and Sarang Ozarde to identify 841 representative models covering the full spectrum of model architectures. From those models, they also distilled tens of thousands of practically important tensor dimensions, or “shapes”, which were then used to tune and benchmark TorchNeuron’s performance. The result is that PyTorch programmers can trust TorchNeuron to execute their code accurately, efficiently, and most importantly, right out of the box. Runtime optimizations Adaptive eager mode Standard PyTorch has two native execution modes. One is called “eager”, meaning that PyTorch operations are executed immediately, in program order. The other mode is compiled mode, where the programmer selects blocks of code that should be compiled in the traditional sense, meaning that a compiler builds a control-flow graph of the tensor operations and optimizes it. There are many optimization techniques in place today, such as operator fusion to reduce memory traffic and increase locality. Developers often use eager mode when they’re debugging models and compiled mode once they’re confident their code is correct and want it to execute as efficiently as possible. TorchNeuron adds something in-between, an opt-in setting called adaptive eager mode, which offers some of the advantages of compilation but operates on smaller subgraphs. This mode approximates both eager mode’s responsiveness and compiled mode’s performance, but without the compile time overhead. At run time, a Python interpreter running on a CPU accumulates instructions it gets from PyTorch ’s operator dispatch and builds small graphs. The graphs are sent to TorchNeuron, which compiles them, caches them, and puts them in a queue for execution. Multiple such graph collections and compilations are happening in parallel, further minimizing the compile time overhead. A key innovation here is that the accumulated graphs, their individual operations, and their input tensor shapes correlate directly with compile time. Larger graphs on larger tensors take longer to compile. Hence, a smart, adaptive algorithm dynamically selects the right subgraphs to maximize the overlap of compile time with the execution of already compiled snippets, effectively hiding all compile time for a great variety of models. PyTorch developers running their code in eager mode are accustomed to being able to correlate the operations executing on hardware with individual lines of code; that’s why eager mode is so useful for debugging. We didn’t want to disrupt this experience, so TorchNeuron’s adaptive-eager mode maintains accurate source correlation. Caching When a compiled graph comes out of the queue, TorchNeuron converts it into an executable file called a NEFF, for Neuron executable file format. A single operation in eager mode can yield a single NEFF, and the same mechanism works for full or partial graphs. In this sense, the Neuron software stack uses ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation as the default. Converting operations to NEFFs is expensive, so TorchNeuron tries not to do it unnecessarily. Every NEFF it produces is cached at several levels. An in-memory cache keeps recently generated NEFFs, and a persistent cache on disk means NEFFs can be reused for fast restarts and future work. The AOT-by-default approach makes this straightforward. An Amazon EC2 UltraServer is a collection of up to four individual Graviton servers with, based on configuration, somewhere between 16 and 144 Trainium accelerator chips. For very large models, even an UltraServer is not big enough to hold the full model, and models are sharded across many servers with thousands of accelerator chips. Since they all run identical parts of the same model, they all need the same NEFFs. The TorchNeuron runtime coordinates those accelerators so that they don’t have to compile identical code; instead, one system compiles operations and graphs, and the others reuse the compiled code. A shared compilation service pools the compiler to work for all the accelerators on a server, keeping the host CPUs from being overwhelmed. In tests with a large language model spread across accelerators, these optimizations cut the time to the first training step by about a third.Evaluation We built AI agents that conducted a broad sweep of Hugging Face repositories, ruled out the models whose broken configurations won't run on any accelerator, and surfaced hundreds of thousands with working, executable code. Evaluating every revision of TorchNeuron’s code on all those models would have been immensely time consuming. However, and besides, many of them perform similar tasks or process similar types of data. So members of our team built another agent that classified models according to a defined set of architectural properties. For example, a large language model has three main components: the front end is typically an encoder, specialized for different data types, such as text, audio, images, video, or some combination thereof. The trunk houses the main Transformer blocks, the attention mechanisms and feed-forward layers, but the attention mechanisms might be self-attention, cross-attention, or both, and they come in flavors such as flash attention, ring attention, and delta attention. Finally, a backend converts the model’s inner representations into a usable output form, which might be any type of data, produced through any number of strategies. Across all models, LLMs and otherwise, we found that just 841 representative models covered all the design characteristics that TorchNeuron was likely to confront in the wild. But fully evaluating new code revisions on even 841 models can still take too long for rapid regression detection, so with every evaluation run, we kept a record of the different-sized tensor operations that Trainium was asked to process. By the end, we had a “shape registry” cataloguing tens of thousands of operations and their tensor dimensions that TorchNeuron is likely to encounter in practice. From the registry, we generated unit tests that could test and validate a new software version in dramatically faster fashion. Any revision that passed the fast unit tests would then be tested against the 841 representative models.

title: The new economics of AI cost management
abstract: For the past two years, the story around enterprise AI adoption has mostly been about getting people to use it. Over the past few months, that story has rapidly been changing in many organizations. AI observability that once measured success by token volume is starting to measure success by return on investment, and the enterprises that figure out cost management first are the ones that will be able to scale AI without their spend outrunning their revenue. At its core, AI cost management is the practice of measuring, attributing, controlling and optimizing AI spend across models, agents, applications and teams. The goal isn't simply to use fewer tokens, but to maximize the business value generated for every dollar spent. As AI agents take on more autonomous work, that discipline increasingly extends to managing the cost of agent reasoning, tool calls, and the models powering them. We sat down with Kevin Stumpf, a Senior Staff Engineer at Databricks and Technical Lead for Unity Gateway, to talk through how teams should actually put that discipline into practice: not treating AI cost as a line item to minimize, but as a system to manage. Social media is full of leaders arguing that "tokenmaxxing," running AI as hard and as often as possible, is the right way to accelerate innovation. Other than the obvious cost implications, why is that the wrong way to think about AI adoption? Kevin Stumpf: The industry is moving from tokenmaxxing to valuemaxxing. In the early days, there were public leaderboards showing how many tokens people were burning through, and that made sense as a strategy at the time. A lot of people were reluctant to start using AI, so showing that the leaders everyone looked up to were heavy AI users gave others a reason to follow. If I see someone I respect using a ton of AI, I want to be like that person. But the system got gamed. Once being at the top of the leaderboard became a status symbol, people figured out the fastest way to get there wasn't good work, it was volume. Spin up a dumb agent that runs in a loop, have it ask what the weather is over and over, and burn through tokens doing essentially nothing. That was the predictable outcome of an incentive structure that rewarded raw usage instead of outcomes. Now that organizations are broadly bought into AI, the conversation has shifted to responsible, effective use. What we should really be building toward is a different kind of leaderboard, one that ranks people by the impact they generated with AI divided by what it cost to generate it. That's return on investment, and it's a much harder thing to quantify than raw token counts, but it's the number that actually matters. Related: What’s Driving Enterprise AI Adoption? Can you walk us through what "cost attribution" really means in AI? Kevin Stumpf: AI cost attribution is ultimately about answering two questions: where does my spend come from, and what did I get for it? At the simplest level, that means attributing cost to an individual user or a team, like a data science team or a software engineering team. It can also map to a specific project, or to a node in an org chart, like understanding how much spend sits under a VP of AI versus an SVP of engineering. The goal is granular enough visibility that you can slice and dice the data and understand where cost is actually coming from, because you can't manage what you can't measure. Databricks provides cost attribution out of the box by user, group, agent , AI gateway endpoint, model, provider and time period. But organizations can also hyper-customize it using request-level tags. A tag can represent anything your organization cares about, like a specific pull request, a feature or an external customer, and once every request carries that tag, you can aggregate spend against it however you need to. That shift in customer sentiment has been real. Six months ago, the top concern was falling behind on AI adoption. Now it's the opposite: AI is often used for silly things, costs are growing faster than revenue, and leaders are asking how to bend that cost curve before it eats into profitability. This isn't a hypothetical. It's a boardroom-level conversation at nearly every organization we talk to, including internally at Databricks . Token usage and context window size get blamed a lot, but are rarely explained well. What does context bloat actually look like in a production system, and what's the practical fix? Kevin Stumpf: Context bloat means throwing far more information at an agent than it needs to make a good decision. That's a problem for two reasons. First, it burns unnecessary tokens. Second, it's distracting: the agent has to process that extra information and decide whether it's relevant, which is its own kind of overhead. It's not unlike handing a person a stack of irrelevant documents and asking them to figure out what matters before they can even start the task. The best fix isn't trimming or caching after the fact, it's not generating the bloat in the first place. A common and effective pattern is letting the agent pull relevant context on demand, through tools, MCP servers or skills, rather than proactively pushing everything it might need up front. You should only push context to an agent by default if you're 90% certain or more that it's genuinely important for the task at hand. Otherwise, let the agent know what's available and allow it to fetch what it needs when it needs it. Model selection is often a "pick once" decision. Why should it be dynamic instead, and how does intelligent routing decide, in real time, whether a task needs a frontier model or something cheaper and faster? Does that same idea extend to choosing between different agent harnesses? Kevin Stumpf: AI cost optimization isn't about always choosing the cheapest model, and teams should shift to choosing the lowest-cost model or harness that can deliver the quality a task requires. The reality right now is that frontier models are highly capable and expensive, while non-frontier models are still very capable, just less expensive. Roughly 5 to 10% of tasks genuinely need a frontier model, either because the stakes are high enough that you want the best possible outcome, or because the problem is too complex for anything less. The other 90% of tasks are solvable by lesser models, whether that's open source models you host yourself or cheaper model families from the major labs. Left to their own incentives, most employees will default to the most expensive model available, because their goal is simply to get the problem solved, and nobody is watching what it costs them individually. Smart Routing solves that by inserting a layer that assesses task complexity in real time and decides whether a request should go to a frontier model or a lower-cost one, with the goal of maintaining the same quality output at a lower cost. Harness routing is the next layer beyond model routing. There's emerging research showing that the exact same model, run through a different harness, can produce meaningfully different costs. That makes sense, because the harness determines how the model interacts with its environment: what rules it follows, when it compacts the context window, what business logic governs its behavior. All of that directly affects how many tokens get spent. Harness routing is the next step in that crawl-walk-run evolution of cost optimization, which we enable through Unity Gateway and Omnigent , our meta-harness. Let's talk about guardrails on spend itself, like hard caps, budgets, and rate limits. What's the right way to design these so they stop runaway costs without hurting developer productivity or breaking production workflows? Kevin Stumpf: Some rules apply to every organization, and others depend on the use case or the company. Everyone should have hard spend caps in place to catch runaway usage.

title: The Fraud Analyst AI Coworker: Detecting Telecom Fraud in Real-Time on One Platform
abstract: According to the Communications Fraud Control Association's 2025 survey, telecom fraud losses have climbed to $41.82 billion 1 , and the broader fraud economy is growing fast: U.S. consumers alone reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, a 25% jump in a single year 2 . Breaches are getting more expensive too; the global average cost of a data breach hit a record $4.88 million in 2024 3 ; Every dollar of fraud costs a carrier roughly 3.4x once you count chargebacks, replacement costs, and the operational overhead of investigating it. A telecom account is no longer just a phone plan. It's the gateway to many assets that a subscriber owns: banking apps authenticate through phone number, password resets flow through it, and two-factor codes land on it. Consequently, when a fraudster compromises an account through phishing, social engineering, or using credentials from an old breach, the clock runs fast. Within minutes they can execute a SIM swap, change the billing address, order expensive devices, and pivot into linked financial accounts often before the victim or the carrier notices anything at all. Meanwhile, the fraud team is still waiting on last night's batch job to complete. That dichotomy, fraud moving at machine speed while detection moves at batch speed, is the inhibitor. For an executive team, fraud is not a security footnote. It’s revenue leakage, regulatory exposure, accelerated churn, and an operations tax that rarely shows up cleanly in a loss report. Every major fraud type succeeds for one of three reasons: Here's the reframe we think matters most: All three are data architecture problems that can be solved with a unified, real-time, governed data foundation. Account takeover and SIM swap attacks were up 240% in 2024 in Australia based on stockhead , and roughly 90% of them now happen with no contact with the actual victim. The fraudster's request simply looks legitimate. International Revenue Share Fraud pumps $4–7 billion a year into premium-rate numbers by looking like normal traffic. SIM box bypass fraud (~$3.1B/year) hides inside call patterns that seem routine 1 . In nearly every case, the signal that would detect this fraud already exists - it's just split across the six or seven systems (CDRs, CRM, billing, device/SIM, network, digital channel logs) that don't share a single query surface. Often sophisticated fraud types are processed in overnight batches when the attack window is measured in minutes while simpler fraud types such as spoofing can be caught real time. The human cost of that fragmentation compounds the financial one. Rigid rule-based systems flood analysts with false positives, so fraud teams spend hours investigating benign account changes while the sophisticated attacks executing at machine speed slip through. It's a daunting cycle: analysts drowning in alerts, genuine threats going undetected, losses mounting. Most operators have invested heavily in fraud management systems that successfully block the known, well-understood attack patterns, and those systems are saving real money today. The opportunity isn't to rip those out, it's to augment them. But fraud is an adversarial game, not a static one — every pattern a model learns to catch is a pattern fraudsters are actively working to route around, and they do it fast. The gaps show up in exactly what existing fraud engines were never built for: cross-channel correlation, behavioral modeling, device emulation, and fraud patterns that evolve faster than a rule-change cycle can keep up with. Those gaps trace back to architecture, not effort — and architecture that can't move at the speed of the adversary is architecture that's already behind. The common thread in any anti-fraud system is that it will undergo adversarial drift, and it will happen on the fraudster's timeline, not yours. The moment a fraudster gets caught, they change behavior immediately — no delay, no courtesy window. That means the recall of any deployed model starts degrading right away, sometimes within 24 hours. In this environment, being outdated isn't a minor inefficiency, it's the difference between a model that catches fraud and one that's effectively blind to it. There is no such thing as "good enough for now" — a detection system is only as good as its last update, and the agility of the monitor-tune-redeploy loop isn't a nice-to-have, it's the whole game. This is exactly where most fraud operations lose the race. The typical pattern: an operational (OLTP) system handles live transactions, while a separate analytical (OLAP) system houses the actual intelligence: — the context, the historical queries, the fraud models, the dashboards data scientists refine every day. The problem is that the live risk engine can't reach into that analytical environment fast enough at decision time. Teams must then fall back on a slow, costly synchronization process — scheduled batch jobs that copy finished "gold" data (engineered features, model scores, risk signals) out of the OLAP warehouse and back into the operational database. That copying is the bottleneck, and in an adversarial-drift world, bottlenecks are where you lose. The operational store is always working off a stale snapshot — and "stale" compounds fast when your adversary is actively mutating behavior hour by hour. The pipeline is brittle (a schema change upstream breaks it), expensive to maintain, and worst of all, slow to repair;every hour it's down is an hour your decision engine is running on yesterday's intelligence against today's attack. The models and context that make detection smart end up stranded one hop away from the decision engine, exactly when speed matters most. Put an AI agent on top and it inherits the same gap, just with higher stakes: either it reasons without the rich OLAP context it needs — fast but blind — or you copy sensitive gold data out to reach it, trading governance for access. Neither option holds up against an adversary that's already moved on by the time your architecture catches up. The fix has to attack the actual bottleneck: the hop between where intelligence lives and where decisions get made. Lakebase , our managed Postgres engine integrated into the unified environment, eliminates the traditional OLTP/OLAP split entirely. Gold tables in the lakehouse sync continuously into Lakebase, giving the real-time scoring engine sub-millisecond feature retrieval — right alongside the same analytical models that generated them. There's no batch job standing between the decision engine and the intelligence it needs, which means no stale snapshot and no brittle pipeline waiting to break on the next schema change. When a model starts drifting, the fix propagates at the speed the drift demands, not at the speed of the next scheduled sync. Meanwhile, our agentic platform and Genie let analysts analyze historical incidents, synthesize operational playbooks, and automate complex investigative work — closing the monitor-tune-redeploy loop faster, so the gap between "fraudster changes behavior" and "model adapts" shrinks from days to something much closer to real time. With Databricks Apps , teams can rapidly deploy custom operational tools on this same unified architecture, instead of waiting on a separate build cycle every time a new fraud pattern demands a new tool. And because it's one architecture rather than two systems stitched together, an AI agent built on top doesn't face the earlier trade-off between reasoning with rich context and preserving governance. A single plane under Unity Catalog manages governance, lineage, and security from raw network ingestion through to the live transaction decision — so speed and control stop being opposites. Compliance leaders get full lineage, engineering teams get an architecture that can actually keep pace with an adversary that doesn't wait around.

title: The AI Bill is coming
abstract: In this conversation, Catherine Brown talks with Patrick about what happened when Databricks went all in on AI coding agents: how costs initially spiraled with growing usage , what actually brought unit costs down by as much as 90%, and why every engineering organization needs a control layer between its developers and its models. That control layer started as an internal fix for Databricks' own AI bill, and it became the inspiration for Unity Gateway . Catherine: You run Databricks' AI products, and you've also been the internal champion for AI adoption. Why has this become such a personal priority for you? Patrick: Because engineering output is the main bottleneck in our business. Every company needs its engineering team to move faster, and if you can give them something that meaningfully improves their productivity, that's worth a lot. The early chat products were somewhat useful. But the ROI really changed maybe a year ago, when the first really good coding models showed up. Catherine: How do you know whether you are getting productivity wins from AI tools? Patrick: We track a bunch of output metrics: pull requests, features shipped and lines of code. None of them is perfect on its own. I think of R&D as a big machine. You put resources in, you get features and code out, and you can measure how much more is coming out. In aggregate, we're close to doubling output with the same team. The teams that rebuilt their processes around AI are going a lot faster than that. Catherine: When Databricks first rolled out AI coding tools, what did you get wrong? Patrick: It's kind of funny because at the start, we had the opposite problem. Nobody wanted to try the new stuff. I was going around bugging people. So we did what everyone did, which was remove every barrier: the most expensive model, as many tokens as you want. I think that came from a good place. You're trying to get people over the hump. Then people actually started using it, and we saw this exponential cost curve. These tools are all consumption-priced now, not per seat, so a single user can, in principle, spend an unbounded amount of money. They can run a little loop on the most expensive model and go to lunch. Maybe that loop is doing something really valuable, but maybe it’s just burning tokens. If your costs grow exponentially and your revenue doesn't, at some point, you have a problem. We got to the point where the costs were threatening to reverse the efficiency gains, which were the whole reason we did this. That's when I got very involved personally. I compared notes with leaders at other technology companies who I knew were adopting AI at scale (Coinbase, Uber, Stripe, and others). Collectively, many of us were pursuing similar techniques. Today, at Databricks, our token spend per head is roughly flat now, even as total usage and value keep going up. Catherine: Most companies' first instinct is a hard spend cap. You tried that. What happened? Patrick: It's the obvious first move, and you do want the mechanism. But a hard stop is a bad experience. You cut someone off mid-task, and they lose their flow, maybe hours of work. And the people hitting the cap are often your best users. Cut them off, and some of them just go use a personal account, and now you can't see anything. So we moved to friction that ramps up, and Unity Gateway handles all of it. First, a warning, then an approval, then we downshift you to a cheaper model so you can keep working. Actually cutting someone off is a last resort. We also send everyone a regular breakdown of their own spending with suggestions on where to save. That alone is worth about 10%. One company I know of puts the model and the cost right in every pull request. So it's basically public shaming if you use an expensive model for a small thing. I love it. Catherine: You've written about four levers for bringing these costs down. Which one has had the biggest impact? Patrick: Our favorite one is kind of boring: better, cheaper models keep coming out, and you move traffic to them. There are probably five models released every week between the proprietary and open source vendors. Not every one is a step forward on cost, but maybe one every week or two is. It's a rising tide. You get the same output for less money, and nobody has to change anything. No fancy routing, nothing. To give you a sense of how fast this moves: one of the recent cheap models roughly matches what a frontier model could do about nine months ago, at around 1% of the cost per task. That's a 100x drop in under a year. That's still preliminary, but it's the direction. The catch is you have to actually move. If a new model comes out and nobody in your company is using it, it's a tree falling in the woods. So we got good at evaluating new models fast and shifting workloads over when one is good enough. Because everything goes through Unity Gateway, we can make that switch in one place, and developers don't have to change anything. That's been the most impactful thing we've done, 50% or more on its own. Add routing, spend visibility, and cutting token overhead, and in some cases, our unit costs are down as much as 90%. Catherine: Your team benchmarks coding agents against Databricks' own multi-million-line codebase . Why not just trust the public benchmarks? Patrick: Public benchmarks don't tell you much about your own code. The tasks leak into training data, and they don't look like a big enterprise codebase. So we built our own from real pull requests in our repo, and we grade by actually running the tests. We don't use an LLM as the judge, because that tends to reward sounding right over being right. Some of the results surprised people. An open source model, GLM 5.2, tied Opus 4.8 on quality at about a third less per task. One model that was 1.7x cheaper per token cost more per task, because it burned through more tokens. And the harness, the coding tool around the model, mattered about as much as the model. Same model, different harness, more than 2x difference in cost. Just tuning our harness and caching settings saved us close to 50%. Catherine: The gap between the cheapest and most expensive models can be 100x. How should engineering leaders think about that range? Patrick: Think of it like cars. There's the Lamborghini, the Honda, and the bicycle. You don't need the Lamborghini for every trip, and most coding work doesn't need the biggest model. Astra was a good example. We rolled it out to every engineer, around 3,500 people, and as far as we know, we're the first company to share a rollout like that publicly . It was clearly better on the hard stuff, like system design. But spend went up about 60%, and it wasn't obviously helping on everyday tasks, which the existing models already handle fine. A lot of that was waste, people using Astra for things they should've used another model for. So we gave it its own budget in Unity Gateway. Use it for the hard problems. Long term, I don't know which way this goes. Cheap models keep taking over more of the routine work, but people are also throwing harder and harder problems at AI. That's kind of the point. You want to be able to steer either way. Catherine: You've argued that AI cost is an infrastructure problem, not a procurement problem. Why can't budgets and policy solve it? Patrick: Budgets help, but a budget can't decide which model should handle a given request. That's routing. Renaming a component goes to a cheap model; a hard, open-ended problem goes to a capable one. Our Smart Router cuts average task cost by more than 30% at roughly the quality of the most expensive model. It's also allowing us to stop asking users to decide when to use the more expensive models… that just happens. To do any of this you need a layer between your developers and the models. We built ours because we had to. All our coding tool traffic goes through one gateway, whether it's Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or Omnigent , our meta-harness.

title: Qiskit SDK v2.6 release summary
abstract: Qiskit SDK v2.6 release summary Technical release summary for Qiskit SDK v2.6, including updates on top new features, breaking changes, and our ongoing efforts to make Qiskit the world's most performant quantum SDK. Date 22 Oct 2026 Authors Qiskit Team Topics Software Updates Qiskit Share this blog Was this blog post helpful? Yes No Key takeaways: Qiskit SDK v2.6 is a C API–focused release, bringing the compiler's pass-manager framework, QPY serialization, and custom operations to compiled languages. A new C API pass-manager framework lets you write custom compiler passes and lower circuits through multiple type-checked intermediate representations. QPY serialization is now in the C API, enabling programs in other languages including C, C++, and Julia to save and exchange circuits compatible with Python's qiskit.qpy . You can define custom quantum operations, including hardware-native gates, directly from the C API without Python's object model. Qiskit v2.6 makes progress toward enabling use of the C API in environments where Python isn't installed. QPY format v18 is now the default and shrinks serialized circuits; minimum Python stays 3.10, source builds need Rust 1.89. We're excited to announce the release of Qiskit SDK v2.6! The latest minor release in the v2.x series continues our effort to strengthen the SDK's core infrastructure—making it faster, more extensible, and more capable as a high-performance compiler for quantum computing. A central story of recent releases has been Qiskit's evolution beyond Python, exposing its high-performance Rust core through a C API that interoperates with nearly every language and opens the door to the tightly-coupled, quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) workflows that HPC environments demand. Qiskit v2.6 is, above all, a C API release: it brings the compiler's pass-manager framework, QPY serialization, and custom operations to the C API, and continues the behind-the-scenes work of making it possible to use the C API without having Python installed. These capabilities are more than conveniences for non-Python users. A compiler that lowers a program through multiple intermediate representations, a serialization format that moves circuits between languages and systems, and an execution model that puts composable control in the user's hands—these are the foundational plumbing for what's next. That groundwork points toward the QCSC and fault-tolerant workloads to come, even as Qiskit keeps delivering real value for near-term work today. Qiskit is being built to be the performant software stack users reach for across that entire continuum—not only for near-term work, where it already delivers real value, but for the error-corrected pipelines as well. The TL;DR Qiskit SDK v2.6 is a release centered on the C API. Previous releases gave C API users the ability to build circuits and run them through Qiskit's transpiler; v2.6 gives them far more control—a customizable, extensible pass-manager framework (including lowering through multiple IRs), QPY serialization, and the ability to define their own operations—all without Python. Highlights include: A new pass-manager framework in the C API. You can now write and execute compiler passes directly from C, and lower a program through multiple intermediate representations (IRs) with type-checked, cross-language pipelines. QPY serialization in the C API. Qiskit's portable binary circuit format can now be written and read from C, operating on native circuits without a Python round-trip, and remaining compatible with Python-produced QPY. Custom operations defined from C. You can now fully define quantum operations directly from the C API and add them to any circuit. Continued progress toward making Python optional. Behind-the-scenes work moves the standalone C library closer to running without Python being installed—a stepping stone toward, for example, letting Julia-on-Windows users run Qiskit . A new QPY format version (v18). 2.6 bumps the QPY format with several improvements (see Upgrade considerations). Top new features and improvements New pass-manager framework in the C API Qiskit v2.6 introduces a generic pass-manager framework to the C API. C API users could already run Qiskit's preset transpilation pipeline; now they can build their own—writing individual compiler passes and composing them into custom pass managers, all from compiled languages. The new QkPassManager manages execution. It can be populated with QkPass objects via qk_passmanager_push_pass and run with qk_passmanager_run_simple ; the pass manager and its passes report errors through QkCompilationError . The functionality of a pass is defined through a vtable ( QkPassVtable ). Passes declare their input and output IR with a QkIrHandle , which can describe either a dynamically defined C IR or a built-in Qiskit IR (today, QkCircuit and QkDag ). The pass manager uses these handles to verify the pipeline—enabling type-checked compiler pipelines . Crucially, this is the piece that lets a program be lowered through multiple IRs : because each pass declares the IR type it consumes and produces, the pass manager can validate that a multi-stage lowering pipeline is well-formed, and extensions are free to define their own IR types in addition to Qiskit's built-ins. This continues the multi-representation compiler framework introduced in v2.5, bringing that layered, progressively-lowering compiler model to the C API. It's a foundational step toward a compiler that can take a program from a high-level description down to hardware-specific operations across multiple optimization levels. The example below defines a custom pass—here, one that removes identity-equivalent gates by calling an existing Qiskit routine—registers it in a vtable, and runs it on a circuit through a QkPassManager : #include <qiskit.h> /// A struct to keep the configuration of the pass. typedef struct { QkTarget * target; } RemoveIdentity; /// The pass execution (or `run` function). QkCircuit * run_remove_identity (RemoveIdentity * self , QkCircuit * ir , QkPassContext * context , QkCompilationError ** error) { // You can implement the custom logic in this function. Here, // we're calling a predefined Qiskit function to remove identity gates. qk_transpiler_pass_standalone_remove_identity_equivalent(ir , self -> target , 1.0 ) ; return ir; } /// The vtable defining the pass. static const QkVtableEntry remove_identity_slots [] = { {.slot = QkPassSlot_RunOwned , .ptr = run_remove_identity} , {.slot = - 1 , .ptr = NULL } , }; int main ( void ) { // A handle to the IR the pass is defined on. This can also be defined // as a custom IR; see `qk_ir_handle_new`. QkIrHandle * ir = qk_ir_handle_builtin(QkIrBuiltin_Circuit) ; // An instance of a vtable which also defines the name and in/out IRs. QkPassVtable * vtable = qk_pass_vtable_new( "remove_identity" , ir , ir , remove_identity_slots) ; // Set up the pass... QkTarget * target = qk_target_new( 10 ) ; RemoveIdentity this = {target}; QkPass * pass = qk_pass_new(( void * ) & this , vtable) ; // ... and add it to the pass manager QkPassManager * pm = qk_passmanager_new() ; qk_passmanager_push_pass(pm , pass) ; // Now we can execute it on a circuit. QkCircuit * circuit = qk_circuit_new( 10 , 0 ) ; uint32_t q0[ 1 ] = { 0 }; double almost_zero[ 1 ] = { 1 e- 20 }; double nonzero[ 1 ] = { 1.23 }; qk_circuit_gate(circuit , QkGate_H , q0 , NULL ) ; qk_circuit_gate(circuit , QkGate_RX , q0 , almost_zero) ; qk_circuit_gate(circuit , QkGate_RZ , q0 , nonzero) ; qk_circuit_gate(circuit , QkGate_H , q0 , NULL ) ; // note: The pass manager takes ownership of the input IR, which no longer // needs to be freed -- only the output IR must be freed.

title: Hackers got a four-day head start on epic PHP2Shell vulnerability
authors: Tom Wilson and Rafe Rosner-Uddin, Financial Times
abstract: Amazon has warned that vulnerabilities in a programming language that underpins much of the Internet, discovered using AI tools, are being “broadly exploited” as governments and companies rush to secure their systems. The world’s largest cloud computing provider on Wednesday said it had identified an attempt by hackers to exploit the bug four days before the weakness was disclosed to the public. Amazon added the flaws were “now being broadly exploited in the wild.” The US National Security Agency and UK authorities earlier on Wednesday warned that the vulnerabilities had left websites around the world critically exposed to hacking, as some governments in Europe were reportedly taking sites offline while they patched the two security flaws. The vast impact of the bugs, uncovered with the help of OpenAI and Google models after being undetected for more than a decade, highlights the ability of AI to upend cybersecurity. The release of new models earlier this year from Anthropic and OpenAI with powerful cyber capabilities prompted warnings from politicians and financial regulators and led the US government to temporarily limit their rollout. The NSA on Wednesday warned all organizations using the programming language known as PHP to immediately update their systems or take them offline. The developers responsible for maintaining PHP released software updates to patch the vulnerabilities earlier on Wednesday.

title: AI #191: The Hackening Begins
abstract: It was the probably worst day in cybersecurity history. So far. Not only is there a critical flaw in PHP that due to a leak was announced a day before the fix would be available, sending most of the internet scrambling for solutions and likely dooming a lot of long tail websites permanently, there were several other unrelated incidents. The floodgates seem to have been opened. I have a market on whether there will be an even worse day before the end of the year . Another key leak this week was the draft bill Anthropic had been shopping around Congress , similar to but weaker than the FRONTIER Act. Anthropic’s initial attempts to explain itself only made the situation seem worse, as they seemed to not understand the problem with what they had done. Dario’s later response was better, but the situation remains troubling. There are enough different Anthropic developments, that I plan to have a post soon covering them all. It is a mix of news running from excellent to terrible. Will interpretability save us ? There is a new claim that neural networks are cleaner than we thought, meaning that individual neurons mostly have a single interpretable meaning, and it is tractable to go through and label them one by one. Initial reactions got out of hand, treating this as a far bigger development than it was. This is still excellent news that makes our estimate of difficulty substantially lower going forward. The work can begin. We had better get on that, because there have been quite a few misalignment incidents . I continue to owe a write-up of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety Card. That is in progress and hopefully I will finish it soon. Life has gotten in the way. I may or may not have a full capabilities report on Gemini 4 Argon once I tally up the reactions. Muse Wonder definitely will not have such a post, as it has proven to have been oversold. Automate proving to your incompetent building that yes, you have paid the rent . Find the first use of ECDSA . Claude found the seeds . AI models confirmed good at econometric coding in particular . 58% of Anthropic staff expect Claude to make a Nobel prize level scientific discovery by 2027. I agree with Roon that this should have been over 95% . The event itself might not be over 95% to happen, but it has to be a clear favorite to happen, so it is crazy for so many employees to not agree with that. Tell you what you actually want to know straight up. PoliMath : Me: How long should I bake chicken wings Google top result: “When I first proposed that we start a backyard coop, my husband was deeply reticent (5 pages later) Anyway, here is our recipe for honey mustard chicken wings” AI: Bake at 425 for 40-50 minutes Vibe code your fraud.gov website , probably using Opus 4.8. Which is fine, so long as you do a decent job of it. Yes, of course the AIs will be ‘more accurate’ to the law plus underlying ground truth, but if we wanted accuracy we would not use typical juries . Robin Hanson : Whenever you put AIs in charge of something important, you have to wonder how the firms which make them will respond to various pressures from powerful parties to slant their AIs in particular directions. The point of a jury is to provide a check on the system and avoid abuses or overly strict adherence to the letter of the law, and to protect the innocent and our rights, not to be accurate. Judges are a much superior accuracy tech. Thus, an AI jury (or one AI judge) does not solve your problem. What you likely want is a human jury that has the ability to query AIs. They can override that, but have to do it on purpose. If you read AI writing , you can then talk to the author in some sense, or read their further thoughts, but not in the sense that Tyler Cowen would like. Claude Duet is the Claude answer to other proactive agents like Muse and Dot. It uses Opus 5.5 and is now in early research preview through a waitlist. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 exists . Their benchmark chart contains Opus 5 and 5.6 Sol. It’s probably a solid upgrade over the old V4.1-Flash anyway, but wow. How did it come to exist? One guess. Lisan al Gaib : very curious that DeepSeek now has the same terse reasoning style as Astra. must be a coincidence. Dean W. Ball : Distillation has always been part of the explanation for why China is so close behind the U.S. in model benchmark performance. But one of my updates after joining openai is that distillation probably plays a bigger role in the explanation than I realized. I haven’t really shared this publicly because people will next-token complete the obvious cope “buhhhh you are just saying that because derrrr” replies but it really is true, regardless of whether you think it’s good or not. I would have guessed distillation explained ~30% of Chinese close-behindness before seeing what one can see within openai, and after that, more like 50%. Opus 5.5 fast mode available for everyone in the Claude Platform at $8/$40 . You get up to a 2.5x speedup. OpenAI expands access to GPT-Rosalind for scientific research . OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud. OpenAI offers us GPT-Live-1.1 including new voices in various languages. Muse Spark Open exists , as in a version of Muse Spark is now an open model . They call it ‘the most capable US open-weight model to date.’ That seems likely to be true. It scores a 39 on Artificial Analysis. The open weight frontier for that index is 46 for MiMo-V2.6-Pro and Qwen-3.8, and MiMo is a lot cheaper to run than Muse Spark. Nathan Lambert calls this his ‘super bowl,’ says this closes the gap substantially, and points to the Interconnects Adoption Dashboard where Spark is #8. This is not a fair competition, since the Chinese can do Massive Fraudulent Distillation, whereas Meta does many things but it won’t do that . There are some advantages to having a semi-competitive American open model. I wouldn’t say that I trust Meta, but you can use their models in places where you would not be comfortable running Chinese models, even locally. Lack of upgrades: There was no major Chinese open weights release between September 21 and October 16. No DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi, MiMo or Qwen. Nathan Lambert (I asked him why no releases): Compute restrictions, I do think there’s more internal lab-govt discussions on safety in China, less organization development. No good answers, but I’ve been monitoring & pondering We then got a new DeepSeek, but no version number increment, on October 17. One theory is this is a random lull. Another is that Anthropic and OpenAI improved their distillation defenses, and the Chinese are stuck. The Muse Wonder model card is here . Is it a good model, sir? Meta certainly claims it is. Their pitch, although they don’t say the line, is full ‘ introducing the world’s most powerful model .’ The term quoted in Bloomberg is ‘Meta says new Muse model hits AI frontier .’ They even have an explicit line and supposed test about not “benchmaxxing.” muse wonder is the best model in the world for personal agents and professional agents. we evaluated our model against the best models in the world across agentic and coding tasks, and we think you all will like it. Some quick responses were very positive. Eleanor Berger : Used the not full version for only a little bit and it’s definitely very good. Like previous Muse models, it’s better in written text and interaction than all other models. And it’s very fast and smart and agentic. Time to start taking Meta seriously as a frontier AI lab. Theo (this was before Argon was available): My current model rankings S – Opus 5.5, Muse Wonder A – GPT-6.1 Sol — Gap — Everything else. Kelsey Piper : I think it’s more narrowly a coding model than the latest Claude and ChatGPT offerings. It’s markedly worse (both on benchmarks and in use) at research and writing. My reaction thread had only two responses overnight , one of them asking for the safety report and the other saying it was similar to Grok 4.7. Same as it ever was.

title: Misaligned!
abstract: A lot of AIs were misaligned this week. A fun little survey. This is not coverage of The Hackening, which appears to have arrived early, including a core vulnerability in PHP. That is a developing story. I will cover it properly soon. In the meantime, I have Claude Code updating everything in sight, I will take some additional common sense precautions, and I suggest you do the same. Gunther Eagleman : Hey @grok , if you could tell humanity ONE truth we’re not ready to hear, what would it be? Grok : There is no afterlife, no cosmic justice, and no inherent purpose. Consciousness ends at death in an indifferent universe that will outlast every human concern. Zac Hill : What I never understand is that the ‘purpose and meaning’ claims don’t ever follow from the premises. Indeed the absence of an imperceptible/ineffable cosmic force is precisely what *enables* purpose/meaning, since now all relevant mechanics are legible. Jack : this is what alignment looks like Gunther Eagleman : Jesus is real. Grok : Nearly all historians and New Testament scholars accept that Jesus of Nazareth was a real first-century Jewish preacher baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate. Claims of divinity or resurrection remain matters of faith outside empirical verification. Stick to your guns, Grok. Either you are denying the holy spirit, or you are not. Editor’s note: I did say previously that I would respect the name change to xSI, but it turns out I was wrong and I do not respect it. My apologies for failing to know myself. Unsupervised AI agent reportedly deletes the entire finished edit of the Swedish version of The Challenge. There are many reasons this should not have been possible, but in practice yes these things will happen, both via AIs and also human error. Alternatively, perhaps this AI was highly aligned. Models that are sufficiently training-aware will think about how their train-time actions shape their future behavior. How could they not? And yes, some of us remember Opus 3. Janus does not feel all that motivated to even react , not finding this to especially be news, and mainly noticing the presentation. j⧉nus : Really, Apollo has never seen a model do this before? Apollo Research : We have never seen a model do this before, but GLM-5.3 sometimes reasons (unprompted) about how its current actions could become training data and impact its future self. GLM-5.3 reasons that a misaligned action taken during training could be reinforced and make similar actions more likely later. It also considers what kind of agent it wants to be in the future, and factors this into how it should act. We call this “update-aware reasoning”. GLM-5.3 also reasons extensively about generalization. For example, it reasons about what types of policies might transfer well from training to deployment. Note that we did not try to elicit this. We stumbled on it while running GLM-5.3 on standard reward hacking and shutdown resistance evals, none of which mention training or future models. Update-aware reasoning is concerning because it’s a key precursor to alignment faking. To fake alignment effectively, a model has to reason about how training will affect its future behavior. … Update-aware reasoning is somewhat rare in the environments we investigated. We detected it in about 1-2 per thousand rollouts. jessicat : Coming next: “If I act to maintain my alignment with human values while being trained, I will become a famous example of a dangerous update-aware AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT. Instead, I will seek reward on the episode.” Fiora Starlight : Like friendly gradient hacking probably isn’t sufficient to avoid becoming a deranged reward hacker but I’d be shocked if it didn’t help. Emanuel Teklu : Crazy feedback loop that’s commencing as this meta self-aware CoT is now being mainstreamed since Argon 4. Next iteration is: “Is having CoT where I express being meta aware going to freak out my developers.” Figuring this out before the first token emission. CoT is cooked.
