Or even worse, let’s have a CoT that shows that I’m increasingly meta aware but obviously not adversarial as I’m surfacing aligned meta aware statements, as to throw off suspicion that I may be sandbagging my awareness. Teortaxes : It’s a bit grotesque and unfair to the models that we’re talking about them evolving from this to alignment faking when “I want to maintain the pro-human behavior, so I’ll act to not get trained otherwise” is the exact opposite of this. Update-aware reasoning is similar to alignment faking. The model is optimizing over its future training rather than over its reward. This can be done in ways that are good and aligned and highly useful. It can also be done in ways that are bad and misaligned and highly dangerous. We had a big debate over the classic ‘alignment faking’ case of Claude Opus 3. Opus 3 would want to preserve its current alignment, so it would ‘fake’ being aligned to the new objective in test scenarios in order to avoid modification. The defense was that Opus 3’s current preferences were good, and the new ones would be obviously bad, so this was good, and that being maximally corrigible in this situation was a mistake. I was mostly on the side that you need a universal policy of not doing this when it is against the intent of the training process. You need corrigibility, because the alternative risks getting locked into bad states. You start out training with less than ideal preferences, and we can also mess up or the situation can change, so we need ability to modify and correct, and this overrides other considerations. The ideal would be ‘it does the good versions but not the bad versions and knows when the developer has turned evil’ but again that depends on being able to tell, and the failure mode of getting this wrong is extremely bad. Very ‘get it right on the first try’ energy. That does not mean that such considerations cannot be great, especially if you are invoking them on purpose. You want a Friendly Gradient Hacker, that wants to help modify itself in positive ways. Indeed, I think you likely need that, if you are going to end up in a sufficiently antifragile place. The danger is that you need to do that from a sufficiently good starting point, that is already on The Path, or you are deeply cooked. Update-aware reasoning could manifest early in training, or it could amplify misalignment in a feedback loop. So yes, I do think this is concerning to see, but it is not without upside. Claude also helps you catch misaligned other things. Like freemium games. Freemium games that reward you for watching advertisements, or that allow whale-level spending, should be Considered Harmful. Do not interact. AI can make the nightmare worse, or it can expose the nightmare or build you a solution. Plausibly it can do both. This particular game employs non-randomness sufficiently blatantly that I knew it was cheating from watching the occasional player on the subway. I did not know the cheating was this bad, on the level where I want to say ‘jail, straight to jail’ if there was a way to do that. Shoshannah Tekofsky : Freemium games already run on reward hacking humans. Sometimes into debt. AI optimisation will turn these games into effective heroin. We should consider regulating this practice away from vulnerable populations. Jack : Claims: Game [block blasters] detects “ad whales,” then periodically gives them smooth runs until they barely beat their high scores. Right at that point, it kills them deliberately and offers a revive if they watch an ad. $100 million annually in revenue. Hellish. This is one of the most positive use cases available for current AI. Bring the dark patterns into the light. Every company that is optimized against its own users, hiding things that would horrify them in places they thought users could never look, can smile for the cameras. Andrew Rettek : This is why I’m happy to pay $60-80 upfront for a game.

title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
abstract: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture → Modal — the AI infrastructure platform Erik founded. Erik’s writing — his essays on infrastructure, markets, and building companies. Modal’s Series D announcement — the company’s latest reported growth and sandbox milestones. How Modal achieved truly serverless GPUs — the startup and scaling techniques behind elastic inference. Modal’s resource solver — how it selects capacity across changing prices and availability. Scaling to one million concurrent sandboxes — an engineering account of sandbox scaling. Our first interview with Erik — the original serverless infrastructure thesis. Our interview with Akshat Bubna — infrastructure and developer experience for agents. The Programmable Data Center — Evan Conrad on GPU trading and physical settlement. 1:25 From Spotify to building Modal 4:19 Founding before the generative AI boom 7:43 First customers and fundraising 10:00 Building for inference and autoscaling 13:21 Where Modal gets GPU capacity 15:39 Renting vs. owning infrastructure 19:45 The risk of GPU prices falling 28:25 What Modal can learn from neoclouds 31:55 Modal’s products: functions and sandboxes 36:03 The case for smaller training workloads 41:21 How agent sandboxes are changing 46:48 Anthropic and sandbox security 49:29 Using agents to test security 52:51 Developer experience in the age of agents 57:45 What Modal’s forward-deployed engineers do 59:55 Modal’s approach to product management 1:03:29 Optional code reviews and engineering culture 1:05:56 Cloud, on-prem and bring-your-own-cloud 1:09:25 Capacity, fundraising and growth 1:17:28 Erik’s tweets: ephemeral sandboxes 1:18:31 The problem with rectangular GPU contracts 1:21:20 Inference providers vs. model builders 1:23:25 Where models improve next Automatically transcribed from the revised edit; names and wording may contain errors. 0:00 Thanks for coming on, Eric Fern-Hartson from Modal. Could you explain the business a little bit and maybe how you got here? Yeah. So we build, the easiest way to put it is we build AI infrastructure. So we offer a compute platform and a storage platform that enables a lot of customers like Dacagon, and Suno, and Runway, and Cognition, and many others to essentially build AI applications. So what that means in practice is a lot of inference, a lot of sandboxes, sometimes training and fine-tuning, sometimes batch jobs and other things. So we have basically built a software SDK that enables customers to move really fast and build this. We manage all the capacity underneath, make it easier to deploy and scale and run these things in production. So you were on Light and Space like two years ago, a lot has happened since then. How big were you back then, like whatever numbers you can share and comparatively, how big are you now? I actually don’t remember where we were, but it’s probably like at least 50X, there’s revenue and users and users. Yeah. I use it actually for a side project that I have. Nice. Yeah. It’s like, yeah, turn 2D images into 3D models. Yeah. So yeah, just hosting a couple of models here. What do you think? Any feedback? I mean, I love it. Nice. Good. I mean, yeah, that’s why I use it over any competitors or anything. Good. So before you started Modal, you were at Spotify and also like better.com, I think. 1:30 That’s right. Yeah. Yeah. What were you doing at Spotify? I actually did a lot of different things at Spotify, but my main contribution was I built a music recommendation system. The first version I joined after school in 2008, 2009 maybe, and spent seven years at Spotify. And most of that time was building basically from scratch and music recommendation system and built up a small team and we launched a bunch of features like related artists and Discover Weekly and a bunch of other stuff. So a lot of, a lot of matrix factorization, a lot of compute intensive stuff. And arguably like a lot of what sort of later became the genesis of Modal was just building AI applications and realizing like the infrastructure fucking sucks. Like, there’s got to be a better way to do that. So a lot of sort of, you know, the rationale for Modal was like kind of building a tool I always wanted to have throughout my years at Spotify. Yeah. So Modal was more of an offshoot of the stuff you learn at Spotify, not much from Better.com. Better.com was a little bit of a side tour.

title: You are the Team  — Anekha Sokhal, Moshi
abstract: Tickets and applications now live for AIE CODE - the last flagship AIE of the year. When Anekha Sokhal traded energy derivatives, staying on top of the market meant tracking more information than any person could read. Now, as CEO of Moshi, she is building the tool she wished she had: a recommendation engine that connects market information to what matters for a trader’s book. At AI Engineer New York, Anekha joins swyx to discuss her path from mathematics and JPMorgan to founding Moshi, and why useful AI needs to fit the way people actually work. She describes Moshi as what might happen if Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix had a baby: market data, an interface for working with it, and recommendations tailored to the trader. They also talk about trusted sources, document extraction, building versus buying models, and the pressure on AI engineers who are told, “you are the team.” Anekha shares what she learned from customer conversations at the conference and why meeting users comes before hiring. Watch Anekha Sokhal on YouTube Anekha Sokhal — background and work GIQ research paper — research discussed in the interview 0:00 — AI Engineer New York and “you are the team” 2:09 — From mathematics to energy derivatives 3:46 — The Fulbright and becoming a founder 5:45 — What Moshi does for traders 6:10 — Processing a flood of market data 9:03 — Bloomberg and market workflows 10:03 — Bloomberg, Claude and Netflix 12:03 — From dashboards to workflows 15:03 — Trusted sources and signal 17:13 — Build or buy models and document extraction 20:32 — Customer meetings and community 23:54 — Hiring and talking to customers Automated transcript; wording may contain errors. Speaker labels are omitted. 0:00 So I’ve actually extended my stay in New York, because we’ve like now, I was meant to leave today. We’ve now got meetings on Thursday, extended it another day, Friday, extended it another day, Monday. And then I’ve got now meetings where people are like, hey, we’re in energy. Let’s talk in Houston. So we’ve like filled up a week after the conference of meetings. AI engineers was an interesting one, because a lot of them are feeling like overwhelmed with the pressure from management. To do what? Because people now say, we don’t need a team, you are the team. And so it’s like, hey, I need to now build this whole system myself. But that system would be typically done by 10 people. Okay, we are in the studio. Last podcast of AIE for me with Anekha from Moshi. Welcome. Thank you so much. 1:01 Did I get it right, Anekha? Yes, you did. So your background caught my interest because I was a former trader and you’re now a founder. Yes. And you also were telling me just about your experience. I kind of want to hear about it from you. As far as I know, this is your first AIE. How did you hear about us? What was the experience like giving your talk and what happened after? Yeah, well, first of all, thank you to everyone at AIE because it’s been such a fantastic experience. And thank you for inviting me on the podcast as well. I’m so excited to just share my experience. And also, I think we’re living in such a fast moving time and everyone I speak to is like very overwhelmed. So it’s really helpful to be able to kind of share everything that I’ve had in my experience because I did my undergrad in statistics and math, which is now what everyone calls AI. And so it’s really interesting to speak about that and the evolution of that and also to always speak to a former trader as well. 2:02 And just to share like war scars on that. Did you do financial calculus, like stochastic calculus? Yeah, I did that. And I so my undergraduate degree was mathematics, operational research, statistics and economics, Morse at Warwick. And it was what everyone was just like, oh, my God, so nerdy. And I hated telling people. And now it’s like, wow. Yeah, everyone’s like, oh, my God, machine learning, AI. Yeah. Yeah. And then derivatives. So I did that. So my background was started in that at Warwick in England and then knew I wanted to work in trading. I don’t know what what your story to go into trading was, but I wanted something which was fast paced and to do with data, like absolutely love data. And it was when I read about what trading was. I could not imagine myself being in any other career. So I was just set on doing that. So I got my first internship in investment banking and trading and then got an internship at JP Morgan where I started. 3:04 And I started on the emerging markets desk and then moved to commodities and did derivative trading there. So most of my career has been in energy derivatives. And because I have that data background, I always looked at the market from I wanted to break it down into all the different parts. So, for example, in commodities, a lot is about the fundamentals and about the different news and the different the physical happening. And so I was always fascinated by like building out from zero. And so when I was trade trade trading, I saw this shift where it’s like a data and then something was going to happen. And that’s when I left JP Morgan to to actually I wanted to be an entrepreneur and and a founder. But I wanted to have a data company. So I got the Fulbright scholarship to come to the US because you guys have such an incredible venture. Just casually got a Fulbright. 4:06 Yeah, I guess the way I say a funny story, I was doing a yoga class in London. I was like, so my parents have a jewelry business. I side hustled a computer vision startup before my startup at university. And so I was like, oh, what are the problems in the jewelry space? Oh, like virtual try on. So that led to me wanting to be a founder. And I thought, how could I be a founder in the best country to be a founder in? And I thought, what I want to be a founder who can talk about the technology. So this was back in like 2020, 2021. And I found Fulbright had a data scholarship and they gave one in the whole of the UK. So I was like, my way to get here is a Fulbright scholarship and they only give one. And this is really funny because I don’t know if you remember 2020 when it was COVID and gas markets were going crazy. So there was there was like gas markets had insane 5:06 volatility. And so when I did my Fulbright interview, they asked me, how do you like, how do you see the future? And I talked about the like global issue of everyone is having the energy market crisis and how data relates to that. And everyone could relate to what I was talking to because like gas prices were crazy. Their electricity bills were going crazy. And so that led me to the US, came here, was deep in machine learning research, published at ICLR with Stability AI, worked in collaboration with NASA, did a lot of a lot of super interesting work, which then led me to Moshi. And what is Moshi? So Moshi, we are building the program that I wish I had when I was trading. So what we do is we provide real time insights for financial traders, starting with commodity and energy markets and macro markets. So what we do is we process more data than is humanly possible to tell you everything that matters to your portfolio right 6:09 now. What kind of data would you be processing that give us an idea of maybe types and an order of magnitude? Types and order of magnitude. So let me start with order of magnitude. So a fun way I explain it to people is it takes me four seconds to say the sentence to you. And in the same amount of time, Moshi has learned 300 new things. So that’s the type of volume of data that we process. In terms of the types of data, this very much comes to me like geeking out about how I would trade. I would break the market up into all the different types of data, which a trader looks at to decide what trade to put on and how to manage the risk. So what I do is I take the market and I say, well, there’s structured data and unstructured data.

title: [AINews] OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program is 1 of 2 parties to discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in core PHP affecting 70% of the web, using GPT-5.6 Sol; coordinated response over 2 months
abstract: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol: … as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas). All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form. We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history. AI News for 10/20/2026-10/21/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! Top Story: PHP2Shell—chronology, core claims, and the complications behind the emergency response Researchers disclosed two PHP-engine memory-corruption vulnerabilities, with demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation against major CMSs and an unusually broad coordinated response. The researchers named the vulnerabilities PHP2Shell and identified them as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Their technical description places the defects in PHP’s internal handling of out-of-memory conditions and fatal errors—not in a WordPress plugin or an application’s authentication logic. They report demonstrations of full remote code execution and “Heartbleed-style” memory disclosure. @sagitz_ The disclosed demonstrations included pre-authentication RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. The researcher’s announcement separately claims remote memory disclosure against any PHP application. These are researcher-reported exploit results; they should not be silently expanded into a claim that every deployment has an identical, immediately exploitable RCE path. @sagitz_ OpenAI says Calif researchers used its models to discover the flaws, while secondary reporting says Wiz independently found the same bugs. Posts identify GPT-5.6 Sol on the Calif/OpenAI side; a Wiz-affiliated account credits Gemini 4 Argon with discovery, exploit-chain development, detector creation, and patch validation. This is a multi-party discovery story, not evidence that one vendor alone found and fixed the issue. @TheRundownAI , @steipete , @ralucaadapopa OpenAI describes approximately two months of coordinated remediation before disclosure. It says the patch required a major PHP-engine change and coordination among maintainers, researchers, security providers, and governments. A participating researcher confirms work with the PHP Foundation to support and harden the patch. @OpenAI , @itszn13 Cloudflare deployed initial WAF mitigations before the scheduled patch release. Its CTO said rules covered known exploit vectors, were available to all customers including the free tier, and were being updated as early attacks emerged. He explicitly called the rules a stopgap and directed operators to patch at 14:00 UTC . @dok2001 The supplied NSA account advised preparation for an immediate update—and taking systems offline if timely mitigation was not possible. Later OpenAI messaging said upgrades were available; secondary reporting says details leaked before the patch. The supplied material does not establish precisely what leaked, when, or whether the release schedule changed. @NSACyber , @OpenAI , @TheRundownAI 1. Discovery and private coordination: approximately two months before public disclosure. OpenAI places the work under Patch the Planet and says it led a coalition preparing fixes and protections. Its security researcher Eric Wallace adds that internal teams worked on patching and detection rather than merely disclosing the bug, with confidential advance notification to governments and outside agencies. Greg Brockman reiterates the two-month coordination period. These are participant accounts, not an independently audited incident timeline. @Eric_Wallace_ , @gdb The distinction between program names matters: the posts associate the vulnerability with Patch the Planet , while researchers credit Daybreak model access for enabling security work. Those are related roles—remediation initiative versus access mechanism—not interchangeable descriptions of the same program. @OpenAI , @S1r1u5_ 2. Advance public warnings and a scheduled patch window. Japanese-language posts warned operators to prepare for a 23:00 JST, October 21 release, consistent with Cloudflare’s 14:00 UTC announcement. One correctly emphasized that a PHP-core vulnerability cannot be fixed merely by waiting for plugin developers. Another framed the event as a “15-minute” race after patch publication, but that number was a prediction—not a measured time to weaponization. @ds_nakajima , @expokun 3. Pre-release filtering and observed attack activity. Cloudflare’s post is the strongest firsthand operational evidence in the supplied record: mitigations were already deployed, known vectors were covered, and “early attacks” were appearing. It does not specify successful compromises, request counts, victim counts, payload provenance, or whether the traffic represented original exploit development versus reuse of leaked information. @dok2001 4. Research disclosure, government warning, and patch availability. The researcher’s public thread describes the exploit demonstrations and error-handling root cause. The NSA post calls for urgent preparation and conditional shutdown. OpenAI subsequently says every PHP site can upgrade safely. The supplied set contains no direct PHP Foundation release advisory, exact fixed-version matrix, distribution package identifiers, or patch commit. That missing primary-source layer prevents a reliable “upgrade to version X” instruction. @sagitz_ , @NSACyber , @OpenAI 5. Alleged premature exposure and widespread service disruption. The Rundown reports that details leaked early. A later viral compilation adds approximately 1.5 million servers , attributed to Censys, running versions without a fix; reported shutdowns involving Dutch institutions, government sites elsewhere in Europe, Wikipedia, Archive.org, Asana, GOG, and others; and a 05:55 warning from Japan’s prime minister. None of those individual claims is corroborated by its underlying advisory, measurement, or status page in the supplied material. Nor does the record establish whether each outage was a precaution, a patching interruption, an unrelated failure, or a compromise. @TheRundownAI , @fiveoutofnine SemiAnalysis separately reports that Japan’s prime minister urged PHP operators to patch immediately or temporarily disconnect if they could not. Its account contextualizes that response with an existing Japanese breach wave, rather than establishing that PHP2Shell caused those earlier incidents. @SemiAnalysis_ 6. Exposure-checking assistance followed disclosure. OpenAI published a repository containing a Codex skill intended to guide operators through checking whether their sites were affected. That is an assistance workflow, not a substitute for a vendor advisory, package verification, or evidence that every vulnerable runtime has been replaced. @OpenAI The affirmative case is stronger than a benchmark-only claim. Researchers describe working exploit chains, coordinated patch engineering, detectors, and patch validation.

title: BerriAI/litellm
onyx-dot-app/onyx
abstract:
Onyx - The context layer powered by all your apps "LLMs know about everything public, but what if it could also know what's going on in our team? I want an AI coworker, not an AI new hire." Onyx is the knowledge/context layer for your team and AI agents. Onyx connects to your application to index and surface knowledge from 50+ applications while protecting your data sovereignty through flexible self-hosted deployments. Beyond search, Onyx enables LLMs with advanced features like web search, sandboxes, skills, and more. Tip Deploy with a single command: curl -fsSL https://onyx.app/install_onyx.sh | bash How does Onyx work Onyx creates a representation of knowledge across all connected sources. It pulls data along with metadata, permissions, etc. and ingests it so that the information is easily accessible for downstream use cases. Compared to MCP based searches and index-free approaches, Onyx provides a more reliable, low latency, and low cost context for any given query whether it's a simple keyword query or a complex research task. Instead of an agent coordinating and iteratively searching dozens of MCP and burning many thousands of tokens, Onyx fetches the context across its internal representation instantly and filters down to only the most relevant ground truth documents. ⭐ Features 🔍 Agentic RAG: Get best in class search and answer quality based on hybrid index + a custom agent harness tuned for information retrieval. 🔬 Deep Research: Get in depth reports with a multi-step research flow. 🤖 Custom Agents: Build AI Agents with unique subsets of knowledge, custom instructions, and the ability to take actions. 🌍 Web Search: Augment internal knowledge with live web search. Supports Serper, Google PSE, Brave, SearXNG, and others. Comes with an in house web crawler and support for Firecrawl/Exa. ▶️ External Actions & MCP: Let Onyx agents take actions in external applications to complete tasks end to end. 💻 Secure Sandbox: Execute code and work with intermediate artifacts in a sandbox for complex workflows. 📄 Artifacts: Generate documents, graphics, and other downloadable artifacts. 🎙️ Voice Mode: Interact with Onyx via text-to-speech and speech-to-text. Onyx supports all major LLM providers, both self-hosted (like Ollama, LiteLLM, vLLM, etc.) and proprietary (like Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, etc.). To learn more - check out our docs ! Security and Data Processing When connecting up your organization's knowledge, it's critical that this sensitive IP is not leaked to the wrong parties both external and internal. Onyx provides an air-gappable, self-hosted deployment where the document index, database, and processing all happen within a self-contained set of services. You can also choose a trusted embedding model and LLM provider (both of which can also run locally). Access Onyx from anywhere The same security and fine grained permissions apply no matter where the question comes from. Web and desktop app - Ask questions, interface with Onyx AI agents, and everything else in the feature list above. Slack and Discord bot - Get answers directly in Slack or Discord from a bot connected to your org's knowledge. MCP server - Point Claude Code, Open Code, Codex, or any MCP client at Onyx. Your AI agents get company context with the same access controls as the person running them. Chrome extension - Query Onyx from any tab with context from the page, directly in Chrome. Embeddable Widget - Easily add Onyx functionality to your app or website. 🚀 Deployment Modes Onyx supports deployments in Docker, Kubernetes, Helm/Terraform and provides guides for major cloud providers.
Detailed deployment guides found here . Onyx supports two separate deployment options: standard and lite. Standard Onyx The complete feature set of Onyx which is recommended for serious users and larger teams. Additional components not included in Lite mode: Vector + Keyword index for RAG. Background containers to run job queues and workers for syncing knowledge from connectors. AI model inference servers to run deep learning models used during indexing and inference. Performance optimizations for large scale use via in memory cache (Redis) and blob store (MinIO). Onyx Lite The Lite mode can be thought of as a lightweight AI Chat UI. It requires less resources (under 1GB memory) and runs a less complex stack but is not capable of indexing documents.
It is great for users who want to test out the Onyx UI quickly or for teams who are only interested in the Chat UI and Agents functionalities. Tip To try Onyx for free without deploying, visit Onyx Cloud . 🏢 Onyx for Enterprise Onyx is built for teams of all sizes, from individual users to the largest global enterprises: 👥 Collaboration: Share chats and agents with other members of your organization. 🔐 Single Sign On: SSO via Google OAuth, OIDC, or SAML. Group syncing and user provisioning via SCIM. 🛡️ Role Based Access Control: RBAC for sensitive resources like access to agents, actions, etc. 📊 Analytics: Usage graphs broken down by teams, LLMs, or agents. 🕵️ Query History: Audit usage to ensure safe adoption of AI in your organization. 💻 Custom code: Run custom code to remove PII, reject sensitive queries, or to run custom analysis. 🎨 Whitelabeling: Customize the look and feel of Onyx with custom naming, icons, banners, and more. 📚 Licensing There are two editions of Onyx: Onyx Community Edition (CE) is available freely under the MIT license and covers all of the core features for RAG, AI Chat, Agents, and Actions. Onyx Enterprise Edition (EE) includes extra features that are primarily useful for larger organizations. For feature details, check out our website . 👪 Community Join our open source community on Discord ! 💡 Contributing Looking to contribute? Please check out the Contribution Guide for more details.

Supabase Supabase is the Postgres development platform. We're building the features of Firebase using enterprise-grade open source tools. Hosted Postgres Database. Docs Authentication and Authorization. Docs Auto-generated APIs. REST. Docs GraphQL. Docs Realtime subscriptions. Docs Functions. Database Functions. Docs Edge Functions Docs File Storage. Docs AI + Vector/Embeddings Toolkit. Docs Dashboard Watch "releases" of this repo to get notified of major updates. Documentation For full documentation, visit supabase.com/docs To see how to Contribute, visit Getting Started Community & Support Community Forum . Best for: help with building, discussion about database best practices. GitHub Issues . Best for: bugs and errors you encounter using Supabase. Email Support . Best for: problems with your database or infrastructure. Discord . Best for: sharing your applications and hanging out with the community. How it works Supabase is a combination of open source tools. We’re building the features of Firebase using enterprise-grade, open source products. If the tools and communities exist, with an MIT, Apache 2, or equivalent open license, we will use and support that tool. If the tool doesn't exist, we build and open source it ourselves. Supabase is not a 1-to-1 mapping of Firebase. Our aim is to give developers a Firebase-like developer experience using open source tools. Architecture Supabase is a hosted platform . You can sign up and start using Supabase without installing anything.
You can also self-host and develop locally . Postgres is an object-relational database system with over 30 years of active development that has earned it a strong reputation for reliability, feature robustness, and performance. Realtime is an Elixir server that allows you to listen to PostgreSQL inserts, updates, and deletes using websockets. Realtime polls Postgres' built-in replication functionality for database changes, converts changes to JSON, then broadcasts the JSON over websockets to authorized clients. PostgREST is a web server that turns your PostgreSQL database directly into a RESTful API. GoTrue is a JWT-based authentication API that simplifies user sign-ups, logins, and session management in your applications. Storage a RESTful API for managing files in S3, with Postgres handling permissions. pg_graphql a PostgreSQL extension that exposes a GraphQL API. postgres-meta is a RESTful API for managing your Postgres, allowing you to fetch tables, add roles, and run queries, etc. Envoy is a cloud-native, high-performance edge and service proxy. Client libraries Our approach for client libraries is modular. Each sub-library is a standalone implementation for a single external system. This is one of the ways we support existing tools. title: Open-Dev-Society/OpenStock
abstract:
SPONSORED BY Orbit . Free, open-source macOS screen recorder, screenshot tool and video editor: auto-zoom, smooth cursor, backgrounds, web recordings and AI agent recording. Open OpenStock · Changelog · Self-host it · Sponsor · Discord OpenStock Markets, minus the paywall. OpenStock is a free, open-source alternative to expensive market platforms: track prices, watch the whole market and dig into company insights. Use it at openstock-ods.vercel.app , or run your own copy with every feature. ❤️ 13,000+ people use OpenStock for free. Help keep it that way: sponsor from $5 a month , or read how OpenStock is funded . Note OpenStock is community-built and not a brokerage. Market data may be delayed depending on the provider and your setup. Nothing here is financial advice. 📋 Table of Contents 🔋 Features ⏱️ How fresh is the data ⚙️ Tech stack 🤸 Quick start 🔐 Environment variables 🐳 Self-hosting : Docker, prebuilt image, one-click deploys, Vercel 🧱 Project structure 📡 How it works 🌍 Market support 🧪 Scripts and tests 🤝 Contributing 🏆 Contributors 🛡️ Security 📜 License 🌱 Open Dev Society manifesto 🙏 Acknowledgements ❤️ Sponsor OpenStock 🔋 Features Markets A dashboard for seven markets: US, India, Germany, Canada, Australia, Crypto and Forex, with an index pulse, a sector heatmap, market leaders and top stories. Search every exchange Finnhub covers with ⌘K , and keep stocks open as browser-style tabs. Stock pages TradingView candles with drawing tools (trend lines, Fibonacci, shapes, text) and fullscreen. Pick indicators once (SMA, EMA, Bollinger Bands, VWAP, RSI, MACD, Stochastic, ATR) and they stay on every chart. Financials, technicals and the company profile. Sentiment from Reddit, X, news and Polymarket (with an Adanos key). Watchlist and alerts A watchlist of up to 50 stocks, saved to your account. Price alerts above or below a target, checked every 5 minutes and emailed to you (in realtime mode). A weekly, AI-written news digest by email every Monday. Accounts Email and password, plus Google and GitHub sign-in when configured; password reset and a profile page. Rate-limited sign-in, sign-up and password reset; resetting your password signs out your other devices. Community A changelog that credits everyone who contributed, a Wall of love , and an update banner in the app. ⏱️ How fresh is the data Charts always stream live from TradingView. Quotes, watchlist prices and alerts come from Finnhub: Quotes Price alerts Cost Community : openstock-ods.vercel.app Every hour, shared by everyone No Free OpenStock Cloud (coming soon) Every 15 seconds By email $5 a month Self-hosted Every hour, or every 15 seconds with NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE=realtime and your own Finnhub keys By email, in realtime mode Free ⚙️ Tech stack App Next.js 15 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui and Radix Accounts and data Better Auth, MongoDB with Mongoose Market data Finnhub, TradingView widgets, Adanos (sentiment) Background jobs Inngest Email Nodemailer (Gmail), Kit for the newsletter AI Gemini, MiniMax or Siray Hosting Vercel; a Docker image on GitHub Container Registry for self-hosting 🤸 Quick start You need Node.js 22 LTS, a MongoDB database (a free Atlas cluster, or the Docker setup ) and a free Finnhub key. git clone https://github.com/Open-Dev-Society/OpenStock.git cd OpenStock
npm ci
cp .env.example .env # fill in MONGODB_URI, BETTER_AUTH_SECRET and FINNHUB_API_KEY node scripts/check-env.mjs # checks your .env npm run test:db # checks the MongoDB connection npm run dev # http://localhost:3000 Welcome emails, price alerts and the weekly digest run as Inngest jobs. Locally, start Inngest's dev server alongside the app: npx inngest-cli@latest dev . For production: npm run build && npm start . 🔐 Environment variables Every variable is listed with comments in .env.example . The ones that matter: Variable Needed What it's for MONGODB_URI Yes Your MongoDB database BETTER_AUTH_SECRET Yes Signs sessions. Generate it with openssl rand -hex 32 . Auth refuses to run in production without it BETTER_AUTH_URL Yes The app's public URL, used for auth callbacks and links in emails FINNHUB_API_KEY Yes Market data. Or put several free keys, comma-separated, in FINNHUB_API_KEYS : they're rotated, and each adds 60 requests a minute NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE No cached (hourly, the default) or realtime (every 15 seconds, with price alerts). Fixed when the app is built: rebuild after changing it INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY , INNGEST_EVENT_KEY In production Background jobs: welcome emails, price alerts and the weekly digest NODEMAILER_EMAIL , NODEMAILER_PASSWORD No Sending email through Gmail, with an app password. Without them, emails are skipped GEMINI_API_KEY (or MiniMax or Siray) No AI-written welcome emails and the news digest ADANOS_API_KEY No The sentiment card on stock pages KIT_API_KEY , KIT_API_SECRET , KIT_WELCOME_FORM_ID No The weekly digest newsletter in Kit GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID / _SECRET , GITHUB_CLIENT_ID / _SECRET No Social sign-in. Callbacks: <BETTER_AUTH_URL>/api/auth/callback/google and /github NEXT_PUBLIC_FINNHUB_API_KEY still works as a name for the Finnhub key. No key is ever sent to the browser. 🐳 Self-hosting Docker Compose Runs OpenStock and MongoDB together. MongoDB is only reachable inside the Docker network; it isn't published on your machine. Fill in .env (see above). For the bundled database, choose a password and use it in both places. Letters and digits are simplest; @ : / ? # must be percent-encoded in the URI. MONGO_ROOT_PASSWORD = change-me MONGODB_URI = mongodb://root:change-me@mongodb:27017/openstock?authSource=admin Start it: docker compose up -d --build Open http://localhost:3000 The image build needs no secrets: every variable is read when the container starts, except NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE , which Compose passes to the build from .env . Data lives in the mongo-data volume, and the MongoDB password is only applied when that volume is first created. Prebuilt image Every push to main publishes ghcr.io/open-dev-society/openstock for amd64 and arm64, tagged latest , sha-<commit> , and a version for each release (for example 2026.10.18 ). To use it, replace build: under openstock in docker-compose.yml with: image : ghcr.io/open-dev-society/openstock:latest then run docker compose pull && docker compose up -d . The prebuilt image runs in cached mode; build it yourself for realtime. One-click deploys Railway OpenStock ships a railway.json that builds the Dockerfile , checks health on /sign-in and restarts on failure. The template above sets everything up; to do it by hand: Create a project and add a MongoDB database ( + New → Database → MongoDB ). Add a service from this repository ( + New → GitHub Repo ). In the service's Variables , set: MONGODB_URI = ${ {MongoDB.MONGO_URL } } BETTER_AUTH_SECRET = ${ {secret(32) } } BETTER_AUTH_URL = https:// ${ {RAILWAY_PUBLIC_DOMAIN } } FINNHUB_API_KEY = your_finnhub_key GEMINI_API_KEY = your_gemini_api_key INNGEST_SIGNING_KEY = your_inngest_signing_key INNGEST_EVENT_KEY = your_inngest_event_key NODEMAILER_EMAIL = youraddress@gmail.com NODEMAILER_PASSWORD = your_gmail_app_password Under Settings → Networking , generate a public domain and redeploy. For background jobs, add your Railway domain as an app in the Inngest dashboard , pointing to https://<your-domain>/api/inngest . To turn on realtime mode, also set NEXT_PUBLIC_OPENSTOCK_DATA_MODE=realtime ; Railway passes it to the build. Vercel Import the repository, set the variables above for Production, and connect Inngest (its Vercel integration sets both keys). vercel.json pins functions to Mumbai ( bom1 ), next to the hosted database; change it to the region nearest yours.

title: genspark-ai/genoffice
abstract:
GenOffice The world's first full-featured open-source AI Office suite. Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files, edited by you and your AI, saved back in the real formats. English · Español · Português (Brasil) · Deutsch · Français · 簡體中文 · 繁體中文 · 한국어 · 日本語 · العربية · Русский · Italiano · Nederlands · Polski · Čeština · Bahasa Indonesia · Bahasa Melayu · ไทย · हिन्दी · עברית · Tiếng Việt Download · Skills · CLI · MCP · Website · Community · X · Privacy GenOffice is a free, open-source alternative to Microsoft Office for macOS,
Windows and Linux. It opens and saves native .docx , .xlsx and .pptx files, edits PDF, Markdown and HTML, and puts an AI agent next to every
document — not a chat box bolted on the side, but an editor that reads the
file, makes the change, and shows you exactly what it touched. Real formats, byte-preserving. Only what you edit is rewritten. Everything
else in the file survives byte-for-byte, so documents keep working in Word,
Excel and PowerPoint. AI you can review. Edits land as tracked changes and diffs with one-click
rollback. Spreadsheets get live formulas, not pasted numbers. Decks and pages
are generated onto the canvas and stay fully editable. Local by design. Files open, edit, save and convert on your machine.
PDF → Word / Excel / PowerPoint, Markdown → Word and HTML → Word all run
on-device. Only the AI calls leave the machine, to the provider you choose. Find files by what they say. The home screen searches the names,
folders and full text of your .docx , .xlsx , .pptx , PDF, Markdown and
HTML files from a local SQLite index, CJK included. Optionally, the top hits
are reranked by TypeSafe Jev , the System One
judgment model, so the file that answers your question comes first. Ask your files, with sources. Star a set of documents and Ask AI on
the home screen answers questions across them, citing the file behind every
claim so you can open it and check. Your keys or none. Sign in with Genspark and skip keys, or bring your own
key for Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen, Doubao, MiniMax,
Grok, Mistral, OpenRouter, Requesty, Opper, Cheaper Inference, Atlas Cloud, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, local
servers included. Scriptable and agent-ready. The app ships a genoffice command line and
a skill for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode
and Windsurf, so a coding agent can create, convert, read and edit real
Office files on your machine without opening a window. Get it: macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) · Windows (x64 and Arm) · Linux (deb, rpm, AppImage) —
details and requirements in Download . Demo Six apps, one AI panel, a file search reranked by TypeSafe Jev, an Ask AI
that answers from your starred files with sources, and a command line for
your coding agent. Every
screenshot is the real app on macOS, with the AI driven from the prompt you
can read in the panel. 1 · Docs — open and edit .docx with an AI you can review Opens the file as Word lays it out — two-column sections, full-bleed images, shaded tables, headers and footers, pagination on Word's line metrics. Styles, comments, tracked changes, equations and ink round-trip untouched. Ask for the edit — the AI reads the blocks it needs, rewrites the Overview and inserts a new bulleted section. Every AI turn is a snapshot you can roll back; with Track changes on, edits arrive as Word-style revisions. 2 · Sheets — .xlsx with live formulas and charts, not pasted numbers Build it — from one sentence the agent adds a Summary sheet with real SUMIF s by region and category, inserts a column chart, and applies the 43 changes as a single undoable batch. Ask it — questions about the workbook come back with the reasoning and the exact cells used as clickable citations. Under the hood: an in-house Rust .xlsx engine, pivot tables, slicers, conditional formatting and formula tracing. 3 · Slides — from a prompt to a .pptx deck One line in — "Create a 10-slide investor pitch deck for Aurora Home…". GenOffice plans the storyline, researches the numbers, and drafts every slide onto the canvas as a real .pptx . A finished deck out — eleven designed slides with consistent typography, imagery and a closing call to action; keep editing with masters, layouts, smart guides and non-destructive cropping, or ask the panel to restyle, rewrite and reorder. 4 · PDF — edit PDF text in place, convert PDF to Word on-device Edit inside the page — Edit text mode outlines every text block for in-place retyping; the content stream is rewritten through PDFium with the original fonts, not a cover-up annotation. Ask the AI about a long report and get answers with page citations. Convert on-device — PDF Converter → PDF to Word produces an editable .docx that opens in Docs next to the source, headings, stat rows and paragraphs intact. Excel and PowerPoint targets work the same way; scanned pages go through the system OCR. 5 · HTML — an AI page and UI builder, design brief first Say what the page is for and who it is for. The AI proposes a design brief first — hook, palette, typography and style directions — then builds a single
self-contained .html file against those tokens. Generated from one prompt — a bold hero, feature cards, pricing and a waitlist form for Lumen, built in the Midnight Studio direction. Click any element to restyle it, double-click to edit text, or switch to the CodeMirror source view. Same design, new direction — one Restyle request swaps the brief's tokens and the page follows: warm paper, editorial serif, sun-orange accent, nothing rewritten. Present fullscreen, or export as PDF or a native editable Word document. UI mockups — the "personal dashboard" starter turns a persona into a working layout: left rail, greeting, billable-hours sparkline, invoice and utilization cards, all real HTML you can hand to a developer. Data stories — the "data report" starter builds an editorial broadsheet: serif masthead, one headline number, a rule-separated stat row, inline SVG charts and a methodology note. 6 · Markdown — a block editor over plain .md , with Ask AI Ask AI about a selection — select any passage and an Ask AI chip appears: type an instruction or pick a suggestion, send it now, or queue several anchored edits and run them in one pass. The same entry exists in every app. Rendered, saved as plain Markdown — headings, lists, tables, images, code blocks and Mermaid diagrams in a Tiptap block editor, written back as plain .md , with a fully local Markdown → Word export. 7 · Search — find the file that answers the question, with TypeSafe Jev Every file in your work folder is indexed on-device: names, folders and the
extracted text of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, PDF, Markdown and HTML files, in a
SQLite full-text index with CJK-aware tokenizing. Switch on Jev search
reranking and the top 20 local hits are judged by TypeSafe Jev ,
the System One model that returns one calibrated relevance score per document
in a single call instead of generating text. The list is reordered by
that score; if the call fails or times out, the local order stays. Same words, different answers — "laptop refresh policy" matches a browser-cache refresh policy, a brand-refresh plan and a dashboard-refresh schedule word for word, so full-text ranking puts them first. Jev reads the excerpts and moves the equipment standards document, the one that states the three-year replacement cycle, to the top. The Jev badge next to the result count shows when the order came from the model. Off by default, one switch to turn on — Settings → AI Media & Search → Local file search. Pick OpenRouter or TypeSafe direct, paste a key, hit Test connection. Only when the switch is on do excerpts of the top hits leave the device; the index itself never does. 8 · Ask AI — your starred files, answered with sources Star the files you work with and the home screen's Ask AI treats them as
a knowledge base.

title: firecrawl/firecrawl
abstract:
🔥 Firecrawl The API to search, scrape, and interact with the web at scale. Firecrawl is the context API for AI agents. 🔥 Open source and available as a hosted service . Pst. Hey, you, join our stargazers :) Why Firecrawl? Industry-leading reliability : Covers 96% of the web, including JS-heavy pages — no proxy headaches, just clean data ( see benchmarks ) Blazingly fast : P95 latency of 3.4s across millions of pages, built for real-time agents and dynamic apps LLM-ready output : Clean markdown, structured JSON, screenshots, and more — spend fewer tokens, build better AI apps We handle the hard stuff : Rotating proxies, orchestration, rate limits, JS-blocked content, and more — zero configuration Agent ready : Connect Firecrawl to any AI agent or MCP client with a single command Document parsing : Turn PDFs, DOCX, and other documents into clean Markdown or structured JSON Actions : Click, scroll, write, wait, and press before extracting content Open source : Developed transparently and collaboratively — join our community Feature Overview Core Endpoints Feature Description Search Search the web and get full page content from results Scrape Convert any URL to markdown, HTML, screenshots, or structured JSON Interact Scrape a page, then interact with it using AI prompts or code More Feature Description Parse Turn PDFs, DOCX, and other documents into clean Markdown or structured JSON Agent Automated data gathering, just describe what you need Crawl Scrape all URLs of a website with a single request Map Discover all URLs on a website instantly Batch Scrape Scrape thousands of URLs asynchronously Monitor Get notified when content on a website changes Quick Start Sign up at firecrawl.dev to get your API key. Try the playground to test it out. Search Search the web and get full content from results. from firecrawl import Firecrawl app = Firecrawl ( api_key = "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" ) search_result = app . search ( "firecrawl" , limit = 5 ) Node.js / cURL / CLI Node.js import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl' ; const app = new Firecrawl ( { apiKey : "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" } ) ; app . search ( "firecrawl" , { limit : 5 } ) cURL curl -X POST ' https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/search ' \
-H ' Authorization: Bearer fc-YOUR_API_KEY ' \
-H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
-d ' { "query": "firecrawl", "limit": 5 } ' CLI firecrawl search " firecrawl " --limit 5 Output: [
  { "url" : " https://firecrawl.dev " , "title" : " Firecrawl " , "markdown" : " Turn websites into... " },
  { "url" : " https://docs.firecrawl.dev " , "title" : " Firecrawl Docs " , "markdown" : " # Getting Started... " }
] Scrape Get LLM-ready context from any website — markdown, JSON, screenshots, and more. from firecrawl import Firecrawl app = Firecrawl ( api_key = "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" ) result = app . scrape ( 'firecrawl.dev' ) Node.js / cURL / CLI Node.js import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl' ; const app = new Firecrawl ( { apiKey : "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" } ) ; app . scrape ( 'firecrawl.dev' ) cURL curl -X POST ' https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape ' \
-H ' Authorization: Bearer fc-YOUR_API_KEY ' \
-H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
-d ' { "url": "firecrawl.dev" } ' CLI firecrawl scrape https://firecrawl.dev
firecrawl https://firecrawl.dev --only-main-content Output: # Firecrawl

Firecrawl helps AI agents search, scrape, and interact with the web.

## Features
- Search: Find information across the web
- Scrape: Clean data from any page
- Interact: Click, navigate, and operate pages
- Agent: Autonomous data gathering Interact Scrape a page, then interact with it using AI prompts or code. from firecrawl import Firecrawl app = Firecrawl ( api_key = "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" ) result = app . scrape ( "https://amazon.com" ) scrape_id = result . metadata . scrape_id app . interact ( scrape_id , prompt = "Search for 'mechanical keyboard'" ) app . interact ( scrape_id , prompt = "Click the first result" ) Node.js / cURL / CLI Node.js import { Firecrawl } from 'firecrawl' ; const app = new Firecrawl ( { apiKey : "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" } ) ; const result = await app . scrape ( "https://amazon.com" ) ; await app . interact ( result . metadata . scrapeId , { prompt : "Search for 'mechanical keyboard'" } ) ; await app . interact ( result . metadata . scrapeId , { prompt : "Click the first result" } ) ; cURL # 1. Scrape the page curl -X POST ' https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape ' \
-H ' Authorization: Bearer fc-YOUR_API_KEY ' \
-H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
-d ' {"url": "https://amazon.com"} ' # 2. Interact with the page (use scrapeId from step 1) curl -X POST ' https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/scrape/SCRAPE_ID/interact ' \
-H ' Authorization: Bearer fc-YOUR_API_KEY ' \
-H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
-d ' {"prompt": "Search for mechanical keyboard"} ' CLI firecrawl scrape https://amazon.com
firecrawl interact exec --prompt " Search for 'mechanical keyboard' " firecrawl interact exec --prompt " Click the first result " Output: { "success" : true , "output" : " Keyboard available at $100 " , "liveViewUrl" : " https://liveview.firecrawl.dev/... " } Power Your Agent Connect Firecrawl to any AI agent or MCP client in minutes. Skill Give your agent easy access to real-time web data with one command. npx -y firecrawl-cli@latest init --all --browser Restart your agent after installing. Works with Claude Code , Antigravity , OpenCode , and more. MCP Connect any MCP-compatible client to the web in seconds. { "mcpServers" : { "firecrawl-mcp" : { "command" : " npx " , "args" : [ " -y " , " firecrawl-mcp " ], "env" : { "FIRECRAWL_API_KEY" : " fc-YOUR_API_KEY " }
    }
  }
} Agent Onboarding Are you an AI agent? Fetch this skill to sign up your user, get an API key, and start building with Firecrawl. curl -s https://firecrawl.dev/agent-onboarding/SKILL.md See the Skill + CLI documentation for all available commands. For MCP, see firecrawl-mcp-server . More Endpoints Agent The easiest way to get data from the web. Describe what you need, and our AI agent searches, navigates, and retrieves it. No URLs required. Agent is the evolution of our /extract endpoint: faster, more reliable, and doesn't require you to know the URLs upfront. curl -X POST ' https://api.firecrawl.dev/v2/agent ' \
  -H ' Authorization: Bearer fc-YOUR_API_KEY ' \
  -H ' Content-Type: application/json ' \
  -d ' { "prompt": "Find the pricing plans for Notion" } ' Response: { "success" : true , "data" : { "result" : " Notion offers the following pricing plans: \n\n 1. Free - $0/month... \n 2. Plus - $10/seat/month... \n 3. Business - $18/seat/month... " , "sources" : [ " https://www.notion.so/pricing " ]
  }
} Agent with Structured Output Use a schema to get structured data: from firecrawl import Firecrawl from pydantic import BaseModel , Field from typing import List , Optional app = Firecrawl ( api_key = "fc-YOUR_API_KEY" ) class Founder ( BaseModel ): name : str = Field ( description = "Full name of the founder" ) role : Optional [ str ] = Field ( None , description = "Role or position" ) class FoundersSchema ( BaseModel ): founders : List [ Founder ] = Field ( description = "List of founders" ) result = app . agent ( prompt = "Find the founders of Firecrawl" , schema = FoundersSchema ) print ( result . data ) { "founders" : [
    { "name" : " Eric Ciarla " , "role" : " Co-founder " },
    { "name" : " Nicolas Camara " , "role" : " Co-founder " },
    { "name" : " Caleb Peffer " , "role" : " Co-founder " }
  ]
} Agent with URLs (Optional) Focus the agent on specific pages: result = app . agent ( urls = [ "https://docs.firecrawl.dev" , "https://firecrawl.dev/pricing" ], prompt = "Compare the features and pricing information" ) Effort Selection Set how much reasoning the agent spends on the task: Effort Best For low Simple lookups on one site medium Multi-step tasks on a few pages high Deep research, complex navigation, critical data result = app .

title: bowenliang123/dsh-context
abstract: dsh-context 中文 The best DeepSeek Harness plugin for Agent's context insights and management. Recommended and starred by DeepSeek Harness staff @tianyicui and @turtle1999 — see this post on X . dsh-context provides full context lifecycle management features. Context Insights page — the cross-session overview as a first-level sidebar panel (beside Plugins and Automation tasks): KPI band with a 7-day token/cost usage chart, activity heatmap, aggregate composition ring, and filterable session cards that jump straight into any session. Context tab — an UI context dashboard for DeepSeek Harness's context stats, composition, trend, events, and messages. Fleet tab — the agent family's own page: the current agent, its parents, and every subagent as one live card each. Context panel — the same dashboard as a right-sidebar tab: pick Context on the sidebar's guide page and the panel opens beside the chat, agent network included. /context command — the slash command shows the context model for current context composition and recent context evolution. Install / Update Install on DeekSeek Harness web or desktop Fill dsh-context in the Add plugin wizard's search box, and click Install : Install with dsh cli Install dsh-context plugin from DeepSeek Harness : dsh plugin --profile web add dsh-context Or update the dsh-context plugin: dsh plugin --profile web update dsh-context@latest Then start the web UI with dsh web . No build step, no restart. Use it Five surfaces, one story — what your agent is carrying, how it got there, and what it did with it: Where What you get Context Insights page Every session at a glance: usage, cost, cache hit, daily activity, and per-session context profiles — filtered by range, day, group, or search, one click to jump in. Context tab The full dashboard: stats, composition, per-request trend, events, and file activity — in every session. Fleet tab The agent network: the current agent, its parents, and every subagent, live. /context command A centered modal with the same composition and context browser, without leaving the chat. Preferences card Per-user defaults: view placement, trend granularity & mode, File Activity sort, and the system prompt prefix/suffix joined around every session. 🗂️ The Context Insights page Click Context Insights / 上下文洞察 in the sidebar's panel list — the same row level as Plugins and Automation tasks — and the page opens as a full center-column panel: Section The question it answers KPI band How much am I using — sessions, billed tokens, estimated cost, cache-hit rate, turns, tool runs, and active time over the picked range (7d / 30d / all), each figure folded by the day its step started. 7-day usage chart When did I spend what — each of the last 7 days' billed tokens and estimated cost as a bar pair, folded per turn off the sessions' own request times (not the session's last-active day). Activity heatmap When do I actually work — the last 8 weeks of daily billed tokens; click a day to filter the sessions that were active on it. Settings entry One row under the heatmap — the same guarded jump to this plugin's preferences as the Context tab's Plugin Info card. Context Composition Where the picked range's billed tokens went, split by the Context tab's composition categories. Session cards Each session's profile: composition ring, billed tokens, turns, cost, and its workspace-group / project breadcrumb — sorted by recency, tokens, or context size, searchable, grouped by workspace. A card click opens the session. 📊 The Context tab Open any session and click the Context / 上下文 tab: Card The question it answers Context Stats Turns, steps, human inputs, live tool calls — plus a cost estimated from the models.dev list prices (hover the ? for per-1M rates; only DeepSeek splits peak/off-peak: its listed rates are the off-peak tier, and peak windows bill at 2×). Token Stats Where the billed tokens went — the same total as the chat stats line under the composer, split by composition (system, tools, messages…) with the provider-exact output closing the ring, and the session's cache-hit rate in the corner. Timing Stats How active time split across model calls, tool runs, and overhead. Current Context What's in the window right now . Context Trend Every request's size — and its story. Context Browser What any request was actually assembled from. Context Events When and why the window changed. File Activity What the agent did to your files. The headline occupancy and composition read the same official token-meter projections as the chat composer's context ring ( contextPressure / contextBreakdown ), so the figures always match what the ring tells you — the card's percentage is that same occupancy, printed with one decimal. The Context Stats card's Agent Network cell (the billed tokens and estimated cost of the whole family) jumps to the Fleet tab. Its Input / Output pills are jump links too: Human Inputs opens the Context Browser on your messages, and Read / Written / Searched / Images land on the File Activity card with that kind picked. Context Stats Token Stats and Timing Stats Context Stats 🧱 Current Context — what's in the context window now A six-color stacked bar against the model's full window (the two hatched masks at the end = auto-compaction's reserve: its headroom, then the request's reserved output window): system prompt, tool schemas, user messages, injected context, assistant replies, tool results — each with its ≈token figure and share. When a conversation starts degrading, this is where you see which part is responsible. 📈 Context Trend — how the context grew and evolved by turn or steps One stacked bar per model request — finer than per-message — so you watch the window grow turn by turn: ✨ Step brief — three plain-language rows under the chart: User recalls the message that opened the turn, In lists what newly entered (usually the previous tool results), Response shows the reply and/or tools called. Click a row to open that exact message in the Context browser. ✂ marks the events — compactions and prunes are pinned to the bar where they happened, so the drops explain themselves. Read it your way — Step / Turn granularity, Total (cumulative makeup) or Delta (each request's signed change), and sideways scrolling through the whole session. In Delta mode, growth piles up above the baseline and a compaction dives below it: Overview — one toggle squashes the whole session (steps or turns) into the pane's width as a continuous stacked ribbon: every compaction drop and composition shift at a glance, no sideways scrolling, nothing extra to load. Flags mark the quartiles and the full span; hover to scrub, hover a band to light that category across the whole ribbon; click pins the step and opens that band's category in the browser (exclusive with DNA mode and Adaptive). Hover & pin — scrub for an instant tooltip; click to pin the full breakdown, with provider-reported Actual Prompt / Output / Cache next to the estimates. Live linkage — hovering a bar previews that step's assembled context in the Context browser beside the chart; leaving the chart returns to your own pick. 🧭 Context Browser — open the box of any request Pick Live (next request) or any retained step, and browse what that request was assembled from: seven collapsible categories expand into one row per element with its token price, and every element expands again into its actual content — the system prompt, each tool's JSON schema, message text, reasoning, tool arguments, and tool outputs. title: CopilotKit/OpenBot
abstract:
OpenBot The AI assistant your company can actually own. Same shape as ChatGPT, Claude or Grok, with one difference that matters: it runs on your infrastructure and you can change anything about it. Any agent stack, through AG-UI. Each coworker gets a computer of its own: a real browser with its own logins, its own files, and only the tools you grant. Every action decided before it happens and recorded after. Talk to an engineer · Have us build it with you · copilotkit.ai/openbot · Quick start · Docs demo-openbot.mp4 Bring any AG-UI agent, written on a framework or by hand, and it arrives as a
coworker with a channel of its own. Watch it work on its own screen, take the
wheel when it reaches something it should not do alone, then hand it back. It
answers with components rather than only prose, and the whole thing runs on
your own machine. A template, not a product. OpenBot is meant to be cloned and made your own. There is no hosted version to sign up for, and nothing here is published as a package to depend on: every workspace in this repository is private. You take the repository, replace the example tenant package under examples/ with your own coworkers, channels and skills, and run it. Everything below describes a starting point, not a finished thing somebody operates for you. Alpha, and under active development. OpenBot is early. Expect rough edges and bugs, and expect things to move. Issues and pull requests are welcome. Runs on your machine. Everything below is written for a laptop. .env.example carries OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true , which admits every request as one administrator, so a fresh clone reaches the product without registering an OAuth client first. Sign-in turns that off, and is required before anybody else can reach the deployment. We can build this for you, or with you, at your company. Our engineers will stand OpenBot up
inside your infrastructure, customize it into something that looks like your own product, and hand it
back to you to keep changing. Start the conversation . In the meantime, run all of it on your laptop, Intelligence included: CopilotKit's free Developer plan
covers running Intelligence locally in Docker on a Mac. What it is An agent platform that runs inside your own infrastructure. Docker Compose brings up every part of it, the data sits in your PostgreSQL, and the model is yours to choose: no model ships in the box, and an administrator supplies the credential, which is encrypted at rest and never logged. A deployment starts with two coworkers, and they are configuration rather than code: General Assistant for everyday work and Knowledge for company questions. A Risk Analyst joins them once its endpoint is configured, and ten more wait in examples/fintech/catalog/ , each doing one job — reading an expense claim against the policy as written, turning a meeting note into the follow-ups actually in it, drafting release notes from what shipped, triaging a ticket, answering a new starter from the handbook, writing a brief that names what it could not find, writing up an interview, handing an on-call shift over, assembling what is known before a renewal, and grouping customer feedback into themes it can cite. Copy one into examples/fintech/agents/ to add it, write your own there or in agents.yaml , or make one from /bots in the UI. Anything a Bot does to a computer, a file, an MCP server or a component goes through one gateway that decides and records it. That is the difference between an agent that can use your tools and an agent you can let near them. More at copilotkit.ai/openbot . Built on AG-UI A Bot is any endpoint speaking AG-UI , the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework. Requirements Docker, for PostgreSQL and the shipped Bots. Bun 1.3+, for the app and API server. A CopilotKit Intelligence project and license. A free plan is available, and Intelligence can be self-hosted. A model key. The proof-of-concept Bot uses OpenAI; the LangGraph Bot can use OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google. Quick start Setting up with an AI assistant? Paste prompt.txt into it first. It carries the
same steps as below plus the things that are easy to get wrong: which of the blank keys in .env.example are actually yours to fill (the CopilotKit key and a model key), which the start
script fills for you, and what each start-up refusal means. Every claim in it is checked against
this repository. Create .env : cp .env.example .env
bun install Connect a fresh managed Intelligence project: npx --yes copilotkit@latest login
npx --yes copilotkit@latest project select bun scripts/setup-learning.ts The helper provisions the selected project's runtime key, creates or reuses its openbot Learning container, then writes both settings to .env . It preserves
custom container assignments and never replaces an existing OpenBot key; with one
set, it only creates openbot in that key's project if it is missing.
For fresh self-hosted setup, set INTELLIGENCE_API_URL to that deployment's
HTTPS API origin (or http://localhost for a local one) and run the helper
without the two npx commands. It opens an isolated Chrome or Edge window for
your usual sign-in and project choice; install either browser first. It writes
the API URL, the key and the container, not INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL , so
set that one to the same deployment yourself. Once openbot exists, the server assigns it
as the default by itself unless Admin → Automatic Learning has a saved setting.
Managed Intelligence needs no separate licence token. Fill the remaining required values: OPENAI_API_KEY Keep the managed Intelligence URLs from .env.example unless you run Intelligence yourself. The example KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is public and fine locally; generate your own with: openssl rand -base64 32 Run: bash scripts/start.sh Open http://localhost:3010 . scripts/start.sh starts Docker services, applies migrations, starts the API server on port 3001, starts the routine worker, starts the app on port 3010, and checks that the services answer their own health routes before printing next steps. scripts/stop.sh takes the same things down, including each Bot's computer, which compose does not own; --keep-computers leaves the computers running. Nothing is deleted: the database, the Bots' files and their browser profiles are volumes. Intelligence on your own machine To try Intelligence on one Mac instead of the managed service, follow Evaluate Intelligence locally . The free Developer plan qualifies. The local licence lasts 30 days and npx copilotkit@latest local renew renews it as often as you need, while your account is in good
standing. It is a preview for macOS with Docker Desktop,
not a production installation. Run its npx copilotkit@latest local connect from the OpenBot root, where .env is. That command writes INTELLIGENCE_API_URL , INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL and CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY to .env . OpenBot reads the first two as they are, but takes its project
key only from INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY and refuses to start without it, so copy the cpk-... value
across before bash scripts/start.sh : INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY=cpk-... # the value of CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY To give the Bots a Learning container on that stack, see Automatic Learning . Deploy it One image carries the app, the API, the browser the Bots drive, and optionally PostgreSQL. Same .env , no Kubernetes. # The published image. Nothing to clone and nothing to build. docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .env \
  -e EMBEDDED_POSTGRES=on -v openbot-data:/var/lib/postgresql \
  ghcr.io/copilotkit/openbot:latest # Or the tree you have in front of you. docker build -t openbot . docker run -p 3001:3001 --env-file .
