title: NVIDIA/OpenShell
abstract:
Important New in OpenShell 0.1.x: a stable release cadence, new isolation primitives, an expanded extension surface, and new APIs. Read the 0.1.0 upgrade guide . OpenShell is the safe, private runtime for fleets of autonomous AI agents. Agents are most useful when they can read files, install packages, call APIs, and use credentials. OpenShell gives them that capability without giving them unrestricted access to your data, secrets, or network. You declare what each agent can touch in a policy, and OpenShell enforces it. How It Works OpenShell governs what agents can do in two ways: it instruments the kernel to enforce policy on every file access, system call, and network connection at runtime, and it uses formal verification to check what a policy change would allow before it is applied. Kernel-level enforcement. Each agent runs in an isolated sandbox. Kernel controls confine which files it can access and which system calls it can make, and every network connection passes through a policy check before it leaves the sandbox. Agents never see real credentials; OpenShell adds them only to requests bound for approved endpoints. Formally verified policy changes. Before a policy change is approved, OpenShell uses formal verification to flag risky new access it would grant, such as reaching a new host with credentials or calling a new API method, so those changes wait for human review. See Architecture for how the gateway, supervisor, and sandbox fit together. Quickstart You need Linux, macOS on Apple Silicon, or Windows with WSL 2 (experimental), plus Docker, Podman, or host virtualization. See the Support Matrix for details. curl -LsSf https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/main/install.sh | sh
openshell sandbox create --name demo The installer sets up the CLI and a local gateway. The default sandbox image is minimal Ubuntu with no agent installed. To run a real agent, follow Run Your First Agent : it runs OpenCode against a free OpenRouter model and shows how to approve new access as the agent needs it. Explore Further Sandboxes : images, runtimes, GPUs, and lifecycle. Policies : filesystem, network, and process rules, with the advisor and prover for reviewing changes. Providers : credentials that work only at approved endpoints, including inference . Gateways : the control plane for sandboxes, policy, and access. Kubernetes : deploy the gateway with Helm. Your CNI must enforce NetworkPolicy . Extensibility : middleware, interceptors, and compute drivers. Tutorials : step-by-step policy and agent walkthroughs. Prerelease and development builds : try an upcoming release or the latest commit on main . Agent Skills Install the public OpenShell skills for your coding agent: npx skills add NVIDIA/OpenShell The skills teach your agent to drive the OpenShell CLI, write sandbox policies, and debug gateways and inference routing. They live in skills/ and work without an OpenShell source checkout. SDKs SDKs connect applications to an OpenShell gateway. They do not install the CLI. Use the same OpenShell release for the SDK and the gateway when possible. Language Install Docs Python uv add openshell README TypeScript npm install @nvidia/openshell-sdk (GitHub Packages) README Go go get github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/sdk/go@latest README Rust cargo add openshell-sdk --git https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell --tag <release-tag> Installation and usage Community Questions and discussion: GitHub Discussions Bug reports and feature requests: GitHub Issues , using the issue templates Security vulnerabilities: follow SECURITY.md . Do not open a GitHub issue. Roadmap: OpenShell Roadmap and the RFC board Try it in the cloud: Brev Launchable OpenShell is built agent-first: it is developed with the same agent-driven workflows it enables. See CONTRIBUTING.md for development setup and the contribution workflow, and AGENTS.md for repository coding conventions. Telemetry OpenShell collects anonymous telemetry, limited to operational categories and counts, to help improve the project. It does not collect sandbox names, hostnames, file paths, prompts, credentials, provider or model names, or user content. To disable it, set OPENSHELL_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false on the gateway, or server.telemetryEnabled=false for Helm installs. You can also compile telemetry out entirely. title: Airbnb bans making guests do dishes and take out the trash
abstract:
Tech News Apps Airbnb bans making guests do dishes and take out the trash Airbnb’s new rules limit hosts to ‘reasonable’ requests like putting dirty dishes in the sink.﻿ Airbnb’s new rules limit hosts to ‘reasonable’ requests like putting dirty dishes in the sink.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Oct 21, 2026, 7:54 PM UTC If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Alex Castro / The Verge Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Checking out of your next Airbnb might be less of a hassle now that the company is banning hosts from including time-consuming chores in their house rules. Airbnb’s updated house rules policy , which starts with reservations booked on or after November 20th, says hosts can’t ask guests to “complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner.” According to Airbnb, that includes: Dishes: Guests shouldn’t be asked to wash and put away dishes, but you can ask them to put used dishes in the sink. Laundry: Guests shouldn’t be asked to remove sheets from the bed or start a load of laundry, but you can ask them to gather used towels. Trash: Guests shouldn’t be asked to take garbage off-site, but you can ask them to separate their trash and recycling into designated indoor bins. Utilities: Guests shouldn’t be asked to avoid using a listed amenity like air conditioning, but you can ask them to turn it off when they leave. Airbnb is displaying hosts’ requests more prominently now in a new “rules and requests” section on listings. You might see an “includes cleaning requests” warning if a host leaves chore requests in their listing after the new policy goes into effect. Hosts aren’t allowed to sneak in extra rules in messages to guests or on signs around their property, either. Some hosts pushed back on the house rules restrictions on Airbnb’s forums, saying they pose health risks and arguing that guests can simply choose not to stay at listings with overly-strict rules . Airbnb says there can be exceptions to the limits on checkout chores, like asking guests to “dispose of trash in an animal-proof container in bear country.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates. title: Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military
abstract:
Google staff resign in backlash over its AI contracts with military 1 day ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Christopher Giles BBC Eye investigations Reuters DeepMind is Google's AI company Google is facing a backlash from some staff members over the company's deployment of its AI technology for military use. The BBC has spoken to several tech workers who have either recently resigned from Google's AI company, Google DeepMind, or are in the process of leaving, over concerns with the tech firm's military contracts. Sofia Liguori, a London-based research engineer, is one of them. She resigned from Google DeepMind this week and spoke about her concerns exclusively with the BBC, despite her contract restricting her from doing so. "Realising my company is pushing more and more for AI systems in military operations makes me feel ashamed to work at Google," Liguori said, speaking in a personal capacity. Supplied Sofia Liguori resigned from Google, saying the company's push for more AI technology in the military made her feel "ashamed" to work there In response, a Google spokesperson told the BBC: "We work with public sector organisations worldwide and follow a consistent process for reviewing and entering these contracts, including compliance with our acceptable use policies and AI principles." "We also have dedicated channels for employees to safely raise any concerns - ranging from business ethics to misconduct - and have strict workplace policies in place to prevent retaliation of any kind." Google is one of several tech companies that signed contracts with the US military earlier this year to deploy AI across classified military environments. The US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has made integrating AI into the armed forces a key priority , saying the Trump administration will become an "AI-first warfighting force". But AI technology is evolving rapidly, and critics question whether it is reliable enough to be used in warfare without more testing, stronger guardrails and human oversight. After working for the company for three years, Liguori said she decided to resign over Google's increasing work with the US and Israeli militaries. "I don't agree with this direction and this has led me to lose faith in my company being true to its stated ethical values," she said. Those values, according to Google's AI Principles , include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning the technology with "international law and human rights". But former and current staff at the company, and experts the BBC spoke to, said they were concerned about the level of human oversight at critical moments. Getty Images US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth said in January that the US "will become an 'AI-first' warfighting force" The tech workers said they are particularly worried about the AI military deals signed this year, because they greatly increase the scope of what the Pentagon can use the technology for. Andreas Kirsch, an AI researcher, also resigned from Google DeepMind earlier this month over his concerns. Kirsch told the BBC that he believes "Google's governance and oversight are not sufficient or meaningful enough to deploy AI safely and responsibly in military and classified settings" or "to develop artificial superintelligence safely in the future." "Google seems to have no right to control or veto how the Pentagon uses its AI and also seems to have limited visibility into how it's being deployed," he added. Supplied Former Google employee Andreas Kirsch does not think current AI models are "robust enough" for military use In the past few years, the US military has deployed multiple AI-enabled technologies to help advance its warfighting abilities. The most prominent example of this is Maven Smart Systems, the Pentagon's main software platform for organising intelligence and data. Developed by US defence company Palantir, it uses AI to help personnel select and identify targets to strike. Palantir has integrated the technology from several leading AI companies into Maven, and it has enabled some processes to be significantly speeded up. Retired Lieutenant General Jack Shanahan, who is the former director of Project Maven, said the "philosophy" seems to be: "Go as fast as possible to deploy [AI technology] as widely as possible, potentially at the expense of the rigour and discipline of test and evaluation." However, the Pentagon has maintained that adopting AI technologies is essential for winning wars. "Speed defines victory in the AI era," said Emil Michael, an under secretary in the US Department of Defense, in a statement earlier this year. Google's contract with the Pentagon, which was signed earlier this year , allows its AI technology to be used for classified military work. The agreement says Google's AI models can be used for "any lawful government purpose" and "should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weapons (including target selection) without appropriate human oversight and control". Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Google's AI Principles include implementing AI with "human oversight" and aligning with "international law and human rights" Similar contracts were signed by OpenAI, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Oracle, Nvidia, and the start-up Reflection, to allow AI technology to be deployed across a range of military settings such as transport, planning and battlefield operations. As the tech quickly evolves, concerns are growing about the use of AI in theatres of war. "AI compresses the time an operator has to make a decision because it works much faster than a person, and that's especially risky in a high-stress environment," said Sarah Shoker, formerly head of OpenAI's Geopolitics team. "When you have hundreds of targets that are selected by AI and a short amount of time, it is almost impossible for a human operator to meaningfully review the AI's outputs for errors." Employees at Google have told the BBC that staff are scared to speak out about AI safety and its uses in warfare because their employment contracts prohibit them from publicly criticising the company. "In principle I'm not allowed to criticise Google for the duration of my life," Sofia Liguori told the BBC. But she decided to do so "because I believe it's important for these things to be known and I also think that talking about facts is not criticising". Liguori added that at Google "people are scared of retaliation and putting their career at risk. You feel you are being watched, you can't speak." A current employee at Google DeepMind, who declined to be named for fear of retaliation, told the BBC that "a lot of motivated employees who signed up for [the company's] original mission could leave – but there's also a pipeline of people at the start of the careers who could fill those positions. It could be a changing of the guard." Another Google DeepMind staff member, who also wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC: "A lot of people have left the company that feel strongly about this [how Google DeepMind has changed its ethics position]." "Some people are putting up a fight, others are thinking: 'it's a big company. What do you expect to change?'", the employee said. Google's agreements with Israel have also caused controversy. In 2024, the company was criticised by staff for a joint contract with Amazon worth $1.2bn (£960m) called Project Nimbus which provides Israel's government and military with AI technology and cloud computing infrastructure. At the time, Google said Project Nimbus "is not directed at highly sensitive, classified, or military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services". Moreover, Israel's AI capabilities in warfare have been the focus of debate after they were featured in a recent documentary, Naza, which examines the role of AI-powered targeting systems to bombard the Gaza Strip, resulting in high civilian casualties. An Israeli government minister has said the claims presented in the film were false and distorted.

title: Texas data center boom could erase decades of progress on air quality
abstract:
Audio recording is automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story. See our AI policy , and give us feedback . Texas’ rapidly growing data center industry could reverse much of the state’s progress on air quality by the end of the decade, according to a new report released Tuesday. The air emissions report published by the Houston Advanced Research Center revealed that the industry’s impact on air quality depends heavily on how data centers are powered. The outlook is far worse if the facilities rely on natural gas plants . “What we are showcasing here is that there is a significant increase in different pollutant emissions that needs to be addressed because otherwise this could have strong implications for the population and environment,” said Carlos Gamarra, vice president for energy, air and IT for HARC, whose team produced the air quality impact scenarios. Between 2002 and 2024, Texas sharply cut its major air pollutants — particularly from transportation, industry and the power generation sectors — even as the state’s population grew by millions and its economy roughly doubled, according to the report, which used federal and state agencies’ data on air emissions. At least 288 data center projects are planned across the state, according to a recent Texas Tribune analysis . The scale of the projected data center build-out means that the sector’s future emissions trajectory now depends heavily on how electricity is supplied. According to the report’s modeling, emissions could plausibly range from a marginal increase to a reversal of two decades of progress in reducing air emissions. By 2031, the report projects that statewide nitrogen oxide emissions could rise 35% — even under a cleaner “net zero” scenario where data centers connect to the grid and deploy wind and solar on site. Under a different scenario where data centers choose traditional on-site natural-gas power sources, those emissions could increase nearly 400%. Such emissions can damage the human respiratory system with long-term exposure, causing chronic lung disease. “We need to treat data centers as the industrial facilities they are … to hold them accountable to the same industrial and power generation emissions standards that produced Texas progress,” Gamarra said. The report’s researchers argue that it’s not too late to stop this outcome. Instead of relying on the cheapest, fastest power options, Gamarra said, Texas lawmakers and industry leaders have the opportunity to shape the state’s air quality by choosing cleaner choices like renewable and wind and implementing regulation that could help reduce the impact. How do data centers impact air quality? Data centers need electricity to keep their servers running. Those servers also need cooling systems to avoid overheating, and some of the most water-efficient technologies use the most electricity to operate. As AI computing chips get more powerful and run at hotter temperatures, the need for cooling increases — and that means more energy. Data centers can get that electricity in a number of ways. Historically, the most common method has been connecting to the Texas power grid. But there’s a wait to get connected. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator, in the last two years received over 500 requests to connect large electricity users, many of which are data centers, compared to two dozen such requests the year before that, according to state records from this summer . Proposed data centers in Texas range from five to 11,000 megawatts in planned capacity, which reflects the maximum power an individual facility could use in any given moment. The estimated electricity that large projects could need from the grid added up to 439 gigawatts — which would equal roughly a third of all the power generation in America. Gov. Greg Abbott has temporarily halted new data centers from connecting to the state’s power grid pending an audit examining each facility’s power demand, water and cooling use, public financial assistance and community impacts. Data center developers and operators that can’t wait for a grid connection look for alternatives. “The challenge right now is for these data centers when they try to connect to the grid, they have long timelines, like three to five years, and they cannot wait,” Gamarra said. “So they start deploying their own on-site energy systems, and they don’t always pick the cleanest version of on-site generation because of timelines.” He also notes that cleaner, more renewable technologies cannot always provide continuous energy to the data centers. Operators that choose cleaner technologies pay a higher price. Going back on Texas air quality progress Researchers modeled how four power supply scenarios could affect air pollutant levels over the next five years, based on projections of data center energy demand. The report studied a number of scenarios, comparing pollution from data centers connected to the grid versus combinations of on-site generation, including natural gas, solar and wind. Gamarra attributed Texas’s declining emissions over the past two decades to changes in the electricity mix, especially the growth of wind and solar, pollution controls across power generation for industry and transportation, and the retirement of coal-fired generation. That progress could be reversed if natural gas plants are the primary power sources for data centers. Levels of nitrogen oxides would increase 136% by 2031 and approach the level they were at in 2004. Volatile organic compounds would exceed their 2002 level by 32%. Levels of particulate matter, microscopic particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, would increase to levels not seen since 2006. Some scientists call particulate matter the deadliest form of air pollution because it can trigger health problems such as asthma attacks, irregular heartbeat and respiratory diseases. The report also found that the power sources of data centers can drive enormous swings in air pollution. On-site natural gas engines emit about four times as much nitrogen oxides as grid power for the same data center, according to Gamarra. At least 32 natural gas-fired power plants are planned in Texas — more than any other state — according to the nonprofit Environmental Integrity Project. “We need to pay attention to it because we don’t want to go back to the emissions levels we had in the early 2000s.” Carlos Gamarra Nitrogen oxide emissions from data center power generation could be two to 10 times higher if all new demand were met with combustion instead of grid supply paired with solar and wind, depending on which demand forecast is used. Major metros like Houston, Dallas-Fort Worth, San Antonio and Austin frequently struggle to meet federal air pollution standards already, mainly due to intense traffic, vehicle exhaust and high summer temperatures. Even under the cleanest power supply scenario, the report found that the sheer volume of data center power demand leads to an increase in emissions. “If the industry grows as is expected to grow, we need to be careful with air quality. We need to pay attention to it because we don’t want to go back to the emissions levels we had in the early 2000s,” Gamarra said. There’s also a role for data center operators to play, Gamarra added. Operators could choose cleaner power when possible and meet existing pollution-control standards. They could also disclose electricity use, power sources and resulting pollution so communities can assess impacts before development decisions are made. Disclosure: Houston Advanced Research Center has been a financial supporter of The Texas Tribune within the past five years. The Texas Tribune is a nonprofit, nonpartisan news organization that is funded in part by donations from members, foundations and corporate sponsors. Financial supporters play no role in our journalism.

title: AI agent fixed the bug, but what else did it change?
abstract:
Page content Today we’re publishing patching-bugs and regression-hunt , two plugins that let engineers delegate patch development and regression checks to agents. Our patching-bugs plugin reproduces reported bugs, develops fixes, and tests them. The regression-hunt plugin checks whether any changes break previously working and supported behavior. Engineers can direct the work and review their results; maintainers can supply their own security assumptions and patching requirements, so the agents work within the project’s rules. We built patching-bugs and regression-hunt through Patch the Planet , our joint initiative with OpenAI, where we’ve co-authored hundreds of security patches for widely used open-source projects. Motivated by our major successes on projects like Scapy , our plugins draw on our analysis of merged patches and thousands of our engineers’ Codex sessions. The plugins provide maintainers with a structured workflow, evidence, independent checks, and best practices to improve their patching hygiene. In our preliminary evaluations, regression-hunt produces 25% fewer false-positive findings than a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Standardizing the patching process Our September post reported regressions introduced by some of our Patch the Planet patches. Since then, we’ve reviewed every patch that a Trail of Bits engineer authored and maintainers merged upstream. The review confirmed 21 regressions from over 130 PRs merged: 16 functional, one performance, and four build/test. None broke a security protection. (“Regression” refers to a new defect introduced by a change that breaks previously correct and supported behavior along a path a real user or attacker can reach.) For each patch, an agent looked for potential regressions, confirmed each one with a proof-of-concept (PoC) run before and after the change, and then passed the results to an engineer for review. The review was noisy: today’s bug disclosures arrive at an unprecedented speed and scale, and for patching to keep pace, the industry needs to increase its signal-to-noise ratio. The 21 confirmed regressions were identified among 58 candidates in a single run (~36% precision). But because agents take many different approaches and reach different results, each run generates more candidates to manually sort through. That led us to two conclusions: To introduce fewer regressions, we needed a standard way to write patches, with the same checks applied every time. To catch the regressions we still introduce, we needed a standard way to check for them, with written rules for what counts as a regression. Standardizing both steps also makes every run repeatable and comparable. No fixed checklist will catch every regression, so we collect agent trajectories from our engineers’ patching sessions, and use the tasks that an earlier version failed to benchmark for the next one (figure 1). Figure 1: Feedback loop for generating and evaluating patches. How we designed the plugins We used two primary sources to guide the design of our plugins: a review of every patch we merged upstream and the thousands of Codex sessions our engineers used to write those patches. This led to four principles that shaped our patching-bugs and regression-hunt plugins: Opinionated guidance in as few words as possible. We give the agent wide latitude and record only Trail of Bits’ judgment of what constitutes a good patch and a real regression. The goal is to direct the agent towards the desired result with the least possible guidance. Modular steps. You don’t have to run either plugin end-to-end, as both provide multiple skills that can be used in tandem or in isolation. Strict input and output schemas. Every step takes and returns a defined schema that includes the claim, the code revision, the required check, the raw evidence, and open questions. Fixed schemas reduce variability across runs and allow each step to verify the previous step’s work rather than trusting its summary. A live proof of concept for every claim. Every conclusion depends on a PoC run against a live deployment: a built, running instance of the project, reached through the interfaces a real user would use. When reproducing a bug, proving a fix, and confirming a regression, if a step can’t produce a live PoC, its result is inconclusive. regression-hunt reduces false positive rates The regression-hunt plugin (Figure 2): Enumerates candidate regressions by tracing the changed code (the diff) through its callers to its real interfaces. Reproduces each candidate regression on a live deployment of the system. Replays the PoC on the live deployment on a fresh-context agent. Judges the results of all the previous steps to validate that the proof meets the requirements of a regression. Figure 2: The regression-hunt workflow. In addition to the four principles above, there are two core aspects that are critical to the plugin: Defining a regression: The plugin has strong opinions about what a regression is and, more importantly, what a regression is NOT. The burden of proof is placed on the agent (specifically during the “adjudication agent” step) to prove that there is sufficient evidence to show that the suspected regression is not a false positive, an incomplete fix, a latent bug, a pre-existing bug, and so on. The plugin only reports a regression if all of these gates are passed. Incorporating a threat model: If a threat model is available, the orchestrator will intentionally pass this document as part of the global context for each individual agentic step. This is an attempt to require each step/agent to refer back to the threat model before reaching its conclusion. Our review of merged PRs yielded a set of 21 confirmed regressions that we could use to evaluate regression-hunt. We used the whole set to compare the plugin with a baseline Codex agent prompted to “review the PR for regressions.” Across those runs, regression-hunt produced 25% fewer false-positive findings than the baseline, with a 95% confidence interval of 14% to 38%. Its strict evidence requirements also left some known regressions classified as borderline: the plugin identified a possible regression but did not gather enough evidence to confirm it. Fewer false positives therefore came with a tradeoff in how many known regressions it could confidently report. Next, we’ll investigate why these cases remained borderline and improve the plugin’s strategies for gathering evidence. Our goal is to confirm more real regressions while giving maintainers clearer information when the evidence remains inconclusive. patching-bugs streamlines best practices from thousands of agent sessions The patching-bugs plugin is a distillation of all the best practices we’ve identified by analyzing thousands of Codex sessions by Trail of Bits engineers (Figure 3). In addition to the more traditional capabilities (such as reproduction on live deployments and independent adversarial review), the plugin emphasizes: The three-arm proof : The proof runs the same reproduction against three specifications: the original code must fail, the patched code must pass, and a complete revert must fail again. Bringing the bug back by removing the patch provides stronger evidence that the patch—rather than an unrelated environment or test change—actually fixed the bug. Invariant-guided repair: The patch attempts to fix the underlying, violated security invariant rather than fix the specific bug. This helps generalize the patch for possible variants of the same bug class. Incorporates regression analysis: The plugin mandates that regression-hunt is run to ensure that any patch goes through the same standard pipeline to check for mistakes. Figure 3: The patching-bugs workflow. What’s next for the plugins Both patching-bugs and regression-hunt will continue to evolve.

title: Several Linux kernel vulnerabilities accidentally posted to public mailing list
abstract:
Several Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities Accidentally Posted To Public Kernel Mailing List Written by Michael Larabel in Linux Security on 22 October 2026 at 06:05 AM EDT. 19 Comments Seemingly as an accident, overnight several new Linux kernel vulnerability reports were posted to the public Linux kernel mailing list rather than the private security mailing list. The vulnerabilities have yet to be patched on mainline but at least in some cases there are patches undergoing testing or queued in "-next" branches. The CVSS scores are as high as 9.0. Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative sent out a number of vulnerability reports to the public Linux kernel mailing list (LKML) rather than the typical private security mailing list. This seemingly was a mistake with Linux's second-in-command Greg Kroah-Hartman responding to each report asking about their submission to the public mailing list. Among these newly-disclosed vulnerabilities include: ZDI-CAN-33549 as a CVSS 9.0 scored vulnerability for SMB Direct remote code execution vulnerability due to integer underflow. For this one there is a patch in a Git branch of code intended for Linux v7.5 but now presumably will be expedited for getting to mainline. ZDI-CAN-33774 as a KSMBD race condition that can lead to remote code execution. Another CVSS 9.0 rated vulnerability. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a vulneravbility for skbuff skb_zerocopy in the network code that can lead to local privilege escalation. For this one Linux kernel developers received a security report from another source last week over the same issue and a patch is expected to be posted soon. ZDI-CAN-34068 as a VMWGFX VMware graphics driver bug with an out-of-bounds write leading to local privilege escalation. ZDI-CAN-34076 an uninitialized resource in the NVMET code leading to information disclosure. ZDI-CAN-32005 was also posted to the mailing list a day prior for a search-domain TCP query stack buffer overflow leading to local privilege escalation. The bug and security reports keep on coming in the AI fueled world. 19 Comments

/ GitLab Critical Patch Release: 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 On October 21, 2026, we released versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13 for GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). These versions contain important bug and security fixes, and we strongly recommend that all self-managed GitLab installations be upgraded to
one of these versions immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include these fixes and do not need to take action. GitLab releases fixes for vulnerabilities in patch releases. There are two types of patch releases:
scheduled releases and ad-hoc critical patches for high-severity vulnerabilities. Scheduled releases are released twice a month on the second and fourth Wednesdays.
For more information, please visit our releases handbook and security FAQ .
You can see all of GitLab release blog posts here . For security fixes, the issues detailing each vulnerability are made public on our issue tracker 90 days after the release in which they were patched. We are committed to ensuring that all aspects of GitLab that are exposed to customers or that host customer data are held to
the highest security standards. To maintain good security hygiene, it is highly recommended that all customers
upgrade to the latest patch release for their supported version. You can read more best practices in securing your GitLab instance in our blog post. Recommended Action We strongly recommend that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible . When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected. title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
abstract:
Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip. In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture: Minimize coordination Decouple storage from compute In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own. How we got here The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly. While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived. Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady. During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process: No repository left behind So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories? In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push. This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently. So, we’re changing the scope of the quorum from the whole repository to individual references. Holding a repository-wide lock for the entire reference update, round trips included, turns the quorum into a single, unordered request queue with one write in flight at a time. Each write in that queue takes as long as the slowest healthy replica. As the write rate grows, so does the queue, and each write waits longer than the one before it. With per-reference serialization, only writes that contend on a shared reference must wait for each other. In practice, most writes to a repository touch different references—for example, agents and developers pushing to their own branches—so they no longer wait on each other. Each write still experiences the cross-region latency but writes to different references can be in flight at the same time. That removes the single bottleneck on the repository. We can visualize how queueing and timeouts build up by comparing the two approaches side by side under similar load: These changes raise a repository’s write throughput ceiling roughly in proportion to how many references are being written at once, and get the last remaining repositories into Azure. In internal testing with realistic traffic, writes to different references consistently saw 3–4x higher throughput at lower latency. Scaling reads on their own Most repositories are heavily read-skewed, with somewhere between 100 and 1,000 reads for every write. Today, reads and writes hit the same replicas, so they compete for the same resources and can’t be scaled independently. Decoupling storage from compute changes that. Once repository data is durably stored in Azure Blob Storage and updated with each incoming write, we can begin to decouple read traffic from the write quorum, and independently scale the compute needed for each. For example, reads would benefit from far more in-memory cache than we give them today, but that memory is also needed for compaction. Once they’re separated, each gets its own configuration. The first step is making object storage a member of the quorum, but a special one that we call a virtual replica. The compute that represents it is our first fully ephemeral node. It serves as a bridge to object storage, streaming incoming writes and serving no reads. Because it’s a member of the quorum, a write isn’t acknowledged until it’s durable in object storage. That adds a little latency to each write, but just like the cross-region round trip, per-reference serialization keeps it from becoming a throughput bottleneck. The virtual write replica also coalesces transactions on disjoint references into a single set of network I/Os to object storage, so a busy repository pays for one round trip across many concurrent writes instead of one per write. For now, the virtual write replica also handles compaction, and read replicas inherit the compacted state. With the virtual write replica in place, we can scale out as many virtual read replicas as a repository needs, on demand. Each read replica warms its cache from Azure Blob Storage and starts taking read traffic without joining the quorum, using object storage as the source of truth and reconciling its local state against it in the background. This step unlocks significant read scale. In internal testing, our distributed load testing harness routinely found ceilings in the current architecture. Against virtual read replicas, the harness hit its own limits first. It also comes with a few challenges that are solved in subsequent steps: Virtual read replicas start out reconciling with object storage in the background, which makes them a good fit for some read workloads but not all of them. Serving every kind of read requires moving that reconciliation in-line, fetching only the reference state and data that changed since the replica last caught up. While we’ve incrementally increased write throughput by shifting to a per-reference model, the quorum remains the bounding factor for increasing further.

title: Show HN: Omnara – Open-source alternative to Claude Managed Agents
abstract: Hey all, Kartik from Omnara ( https://omnara.com ) here. We're building an open-source API for running durable agents. You create an agent with an API call, and Omnara runs the agent loop, gives the agent sandboxes to run commands in, and handles secrets, permissions, and RBAC. Each agent's state is stored in Postgres, so agents survive restarts and cost nothing while idle. You can message them and stream their events over the API. You may remember us from our early days, when we made a remote-control phone app for Claude Code and Codex. Since the harness ran on a laptop back then, we had to build a relay to reach it, it stopped when the laptop closed, and moving it to a cloud sandbox meant syncing code and agent state between machines. We didn't think remote-controlling a local agent was end-game for how people would run agents, so we built a new product where the agent runs in the cloud, any client can talk to it through an API, and it can still use your laptop as one of its machines. Anthropic and OpenAI are building hosted versions of this, like Claude Managed Agents and the OpenAI Agents API. Omnara is an open-source version you can run on your own servers and use your own models. It's basically a harness server like the opencode or codex servers, but durable, scalable, with the usual harness features like file and shell tools, subagents, compaction, permission prompts, MCP, skills, memory, yada yada yada. Here's some interesting architectural decisions we made while building this out: Most harnesses, like Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, Goose, etc, run the agent loop in one long-lived process that keeps its log in a JSONL or SQLite file. In Omnara, the log is an append-only event log in Postgres, with inputs, model outputs and tool calls stored as typed rows in their own tables. The loop runs on stateless workers in the control plane. A worker runs one iteration of the loop, either a model call or the tool calls it produced, then releases the agent and puts the next iteration on a queue in Postgres. Whichever worker is free picks it up, so each iteration of an agent's loop can run in a different process on a different machine. Each iteration's result commits in one transaction, so the model output, its tool calls, usage and the next wakeup are saved together or not at all. If a worker dies mid-iteration, nothing commits, its lease expires, and another worker retries it. Agents waiting on a user, a tool or a retry don't hold a worker, so one worker can multiplex thousands of agents. Also unlike other harnesses, the machines that the workers (our agent loop) run on aren't where the agent runs its commands. Instead, any macOS or Linux machine with an internet connection, like your laptop or any cloud sandbox, can run a small daemon (omnarad) that connects out to Omnara, so it doesn't need any open inbound ports. The agent then gets tools for that machine, like running a command or editing a file. An agent can have any number of machines connected to it. A fun thing I like to do is I have my laptop and a cloud sandbox connected to the same agent, so when my laptop is on, my agent codes there and I can interact with it, and I have it often push to Github. When I close my laptop, my agent sees the laptop went offline, pulls the latest changes to its cloud sandbox, and continues there. The entire codebase is open source at  https://github.com/omnara-ai/omnara , and it’s self hostable, even on a single machine with docker compose. You can also use the hosted version at  https://omnara.com . Let me know what you think!

title: Rust Style Guide
abstract:
This document is a style guide for the usage of the Rust programming language
at Google. In this context, “style” refers to more than just formatting; it
includes guidance on API and implementation design. Rust is used in many places, including google3 ,
Android, ChromeOS, Fuchsia, and Chrome, and we’d like for Rust usage at Google
to be consistent both within and across codebases. In addition to bringing
consistency to our Rust code, style guidance also helps establish a standard of
quality. The current scope of authority of the rules outlined in this guide: By and large, we have this document for the same reasons we have a C++ style guide . Most style rules come from one or more of the goals listed below. We expect our code to be around for long periods of time, and we
consider a little bit of extra effort applied during code writing to be
worth it in the long run if the style rule improves readability. Large-Scale Changes (LSCs)
are common at Google, and consistency helps
make LSCs easier to carry out. The broader Rust ecosystem already has a pretty good amount of consistency
in style, and we should rely on that where possible to reduce surprise and make
it less work to learn Google’s Rust style. Every Rust developer and reviewer at Google has to keep these style rules
in mind: as such, we should be careful to include rules that have a tangible
benefit. There are many cases where reasonable people may disagree about a style, and
we expect that disagreement to show up often on CLs. Having a style rule helps
avoid having to rehash this each time. Rules in this category that do not have other
benefits should be kept to a minimum. Follow the official public Rust style rules to the extent they don’t conflict
with this style guide. A “conflict” would be a case where this style guide suggests a pattern that is
discouraged, or counter to the primary encouraged pattern in the Rust style
guide. Why does the guidance in this style guide deviate from regular Rust style rules? Most style guides have three goals: consistency, readability, and encouraging
good API design. Regardless of the specific choices made, it helps everyone to
have these choices made beforehand to limit bikeshedding. This style guide shares those goals, but it also has an additional goal not seen
as often: smoothing the way for Large-Scale Changes (LSCs). Large codebases like
many of the ones at Google occasionally need to run codebase-spanning
refactorings that are assisted by tooling: for this to work well, the code
should be something tooling has an easy time working with. Consistency helps for
this, but so does having deliberate refactor-friendly patterns. When applying rules that relate to API design, you should distinguish two types
of code: For library code , style guide rules that concern API design are binding. For application code , the rules on API design are a strong recommendation. As
you apply them, keep in mind that since application code is written to solve a
specific problem, it should generally favor simplicity and directness over broad
reusability. Avoid premature generalization and abstraction; focus on what is
required to meet the immediate need. A crate is a unit of compilation. A crate always contains a nameless Rust
module, the “root module”. A Rust module is a unit of code organization within a crate. Rust modules
are used to control visibility of names. Modules can be nested. They can
also be used to split code across files and directories. The following sections convey that in Chromium, it is preferable to not make
use of all possibilities of splitting modules across files. Prefer small crates in Chromium; ideally, but not necessarily, a single file
(focusing on one abstraction). If your code can be split up into small crates,
do so. A crate corresponds to a single rust_static_library (chrome) rule, which may
contain one or more .rs files. The root module is allowed to re-export public APIs from leaf
submodules , making submodules an implementation detail of the crate (as
users don’t need to know about these submodules). This rule about small crates applies equally to crates with and without
submodules. First, evaluate whether the APIs need to be in the same crate,
and only then consider whether submodules could help organize the APIs. If you decide to use submodules, follow the expected file structure . Larger crates are allowed when trait impl coherence rules force multiple types and traits to be included in one library, or if you’re
building a large foundational library. Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size
of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph,
and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching. In Chromium .rs source files belonging to one rust_library (one Rust crate)
must reside in a single directory. Don’t use subdirectories to organize files that belong to a single crate. If
organizing one crate’s files into subdirectories feels necessary, this is a
strong indication that the crate has grown too large and should
be split. This crate layout is intentionally different from the conventional Cargo
directory structure typically used in open-source repositories. Exception: Rust code in //third_party that is also built with Cargo should follow the conventional Cargo
directory structure. The approach in Chromium is driven by the following factors: When a leaf module has a primary user-defined item (e.g., Foo ), the module
should be named after that item (e.g., mod foo and foo.rs ). Leaf modules that are not primarily about any particular abstraction can be
named as desired. This makes it easy to identify the content/purpose of a source file or leaf
module at a glance. The only items in non-leaf modules should be module declarations (not
definitions) and re-exports . Note that the definition of leaf modules allows the following sub-modules: mod test and cross-language binding modules like #[cxx::bridge] . This makes it easier to find things, and avoids mixing structure and contents. Don’t use glob imports, except in the following situations where you may
optionally do so at your own discretion: C++ interop: Since the same namespace (in C++) is a submodule in different
Rust crates (in Rust), you may merge the namespaces into a private copy
using glob imports. For example: In this hypothetical example, you can use absl::Status and absl::StrCat from Rust, the same way you would from C++, instead of spelling them as status::absl::Status and strings::absl::StrCat . This must only be used for merging C++ namespaces, and the resulting merged
module must not be public. If using third-party crates that encourage a prelude, it is up to the reviewer’s
discretion to allow it. This also means that defining preludes should be avoided. Glob imports increase toil for code janitors running LSCs, and make it harder to
know where a type comes from in contexts without xrefs. This rule corresponds to the rustfmt setting imports_granularity = Module . Basically, there should not be any :: ’s inside the {..} block of a use statement. For example: Import traits within function bodies, unless the trait’s methods are used
extensively throughout the file. To use top-level functions defined in other modules or crates, import their
module and call them with modulename::functionname() . For example: In Chromium, when importing functions from small, single-purpose first-party crates . Many Rust codebases consistently keep a style such that unqualified lowercase
names are assumed local, so foo() can be assumed to be from the same module.
This rule largely exists to avoid reviewer disagreements, the benefit is mostly
consistency and a minor edge on reading code without xrefs. By default, types and traits should be referenced in code without using their
module path, e.g.

title: Show HN: Run full iOS 16.5 firmware on Android Devices
abstract:
HackiOS — XNU kernel HackiOS boots Apple's open-source XNU kernel ( xnu-8796.121.2 , the kernel of iOS 16.5) on Android phone
hardware and runs the unmodified iOS 16.5 user space on top of it: launchd → backboardd → SpringBoard →
apps. Our own EFI loader, our own replacements for Apple's closed drivers, a UEFI port, and a Linux Wi-Fi driver
on a compatibility layer make that possible. It runs in two places: POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood, Snapdragon 778G) — nothing is flashed: the UEFI is started with fastboot boot ,
the whole system lives in RAM, and after a reboot the phone is back in Android; QEMU ( virt , aarch64) — the same thing on any Linux computer, no phone needed. This repository is half of the project: Repository What hackios-xnu-kernel (this one) XNU patches, the EFI loader, the UEFI port, Wi-Fi, QEMU scripts, xl , prebuilt kernel/loader/UEFI, common/ scripts hackios-xnu-userland our init, injected libraries, launchd jobs, the APFS image builder, the scripts that take iOS out of Apple's IPSW, Metal/Mesa work No Apple files are in either repository. ios165/fetch.sh downloads the iOS 16.5 IPSW from Apple's own CDN
to your machine and extracts what is needed there. HackiOS is an independent research project by OOSEX GANG and
is not affiliated with, authorised or endorsed by Apple Inc. iOS, iPhone and Apple are trademarks of Apple Inc. Photographed on the phone, the Adreno GPU drawing ( gpu=1 ). More in Screenshots . What works Works Does not work (yet) Lock screen, swipe to unlock, home screen with all icons (two pages), stock iOS 16 wallpapers Cellular, Bluetooth System gestures: swipe up (home, app switcher), edge swipe (back), Control Center Charging under our kernel (the phone only discharges) Apps: Settings, Clock, Calendar, Photos, Notes, Safari and more; widgets (Weather, Calendar) on the phone Metal for apps (in progress: 293 of 456 system shaders already run on the Adreno, see docs/air.md in hackios-xnu-userland) Phone touchscreen (Goodix GT9916), multitouch, wake on touch; real power and volume keys App Store content and Apple ID sign-in (no Secure Enclave; FairPlay daemon exits) Up to 8 CPU cores ( cpus=8 ), big core at 2.4 GHz, ~20 s to the lock screen Video and Live Photo recording Adreno 642L GPU through Mesa/freedreno ( gpu=1 , OpenGL ES for CoreAnimation) Wi-Fi (WCN6750, ath11k): join from Settings, Safari over Wi-Fi, 55–90 Mbit/s Sound (speakers, main microphone), camera in Camera.app (front/rear, preview, focus, HEIC photos) Data that iOS writes survives a reboot ( var_store=1 ufs_write=1 ); iOS root volume on the phone's flash Sileo + Procursus (dpkg, apt), tweaks, SSH It is a research bench, not a ROM: a session lasts a given number of seconds, then the kernel returns to the
loader and hands over its log. Quick start: QEMU, no kernel build prebuilt/ holds the kernel, loader and our programs built from these repositories, so all you need is the system
image, which is made on your machine from Apple's IPSW. Needs: Linux x86-64, ~12 GB free disk, 4 GB free RAM. Packages (Arch): sudo pacman -S --needed git python 7zip lz4 gcc qemu-system-aarch64 qemu-ui-gtk edk2-aarch64 (Debian/Ubuntu: git python3 7zip liblz4-dev gcc qemu-system-arm qemu-efi-aarch64 ; 7-Zip must be 23 or newer — it
reads APFS.) git clone https://github.com/oosexgang/hackios-xnu-kernel.git hackios cd hackios
common/setup.sh # brings hackios-xnu-userland into the same tree, checks the host ios165/fetch.sh # downloads 7.4 GB from Apple's CDN and extracts what is needed (5-15 min) common/build.sh qemu-virt # builds the APFS images (and the kernel, if the toolchain is there) common/run.sh qemu-virt # a 20-minute session in a QEMU window The lock screen appears after 2–3 minutes. Mouse with the left button held = finger. Unlock / leave an app: swipe up from the very bottom edge; back:
swipe from the left edge. Keys: H home, L lock/power, ↑ / ↓ volume, F11 (hold) five fingers. From a script: qemu/touch.py swipe 0.5 0.985 0.5 0.3 250 , qemu/touch.py tap 0.615 0.71 , qemu/touch.py key home ; screenshot: qemu/screendump.sh shot.png . Right after SpringBoard appears the system is still registering apps: give it 30–40 s. Debian/Ubuntu UEFI firmware: QEMU_EFI=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_CODE.fd QEMU_VARS=/usr/share/AAVMF/AAVMF_VARS.fd . On the phone (POCO X5 Pro 5G) You need a POCO X5 Pro 5G (redwood) with an unlocked bootloader, adb and fastboot , and the images from the
section above. Nothing is written to the phone's storage. The phone's own firmware is not in the repository and cannot be: it is the vendor's and is taken from the very
phone it will run on, from its Android: adb pull /vendor/firmware/a660_{gmu.bin,sqe.fw,zap.mdt,zap.b00,zap.b01,zap.b02} fw-gpu/ # GPU (gpu=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/wpss.{mdt,b02,b03,b04,b05,b06,b07} fw-wifi/ # Wi-Fi (wifi=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware_mnt/image/adsp.{mdt,b02,...,b36} fw-audio/ # sound (adsp=1) adb pull /vendor/firmware/aw8697_haptic.bin fw-haptic/ # haptics (Put the fw-* directories next to the workspace. Wi-Fi also needs fw-wifi/mac — the radio's address on one
line — and fw-wifi/network — network name and password. userland/build.sh prints which firmware went in.) common/build.sh redwood GL=1 # images + out/redwood-boot.img common/run.sh redwood 900 # loader into RAM, system image into RAM, a 15-minute session or step by step with xl : ./xl enter # Android -> fastboot -> our loader in RAM (fastboot boot); it brings up its own USB link ./xl ramdisk # upload the system image into the phone's RAM (2.5 GB, ~80 s), once per loader session XL_SECS=900 XL_CMDLINE= " touchscreen=1 cpufreq=1 bootcpu=7 cpus=8 gpu=1 wifi=1 adsp=1 " ./xl run
./xl screenshot shot.png
./xl reboot # back to Android ./xl with no arguments lists every command (logs, screen and sound recording, camera frames, stop, state...). Prebuilt boot image Every release has hackios-redwood-boot.img attached: the redwood UEFI with our loader inside, ready for fastboot boot . It contains no Apple files; the system image is still made on your machine (above). Building from source common/build.sh <device> runs every step that this machine can run and uses prebuilt/ for the rest. Kernel — needs theos in ~/theos (cctools and iPhoneOS16.5.sdk ) and clang lld python perl . Details: xnu/README.md . xnu/apply.sh && xnu-deps/setup.sh && ./xnu-build.sh -j8 -k Loader — xnuloader/build.sh (clang + lld-link, an EFI application without EDK2). Images — REST=1 userland/build.sh (variables documented at the top of that file). UEFI — uefi/README.md (Project Silicium port); not needed to run, prebuilt/uefi has it. After rebuilding: tools/update-prebuilt.sh refreshes prebuilt/ . Porting to another device common/new-device.sh < codename > path/to/device.dtb # profile + loader platform from the phone's device tree Then follow docs/PORTING.md : the UEFI port, the loader's platform description, the kernel's
drivers, the firmware. Device profiles live in common/devices/ ( redwood.conf , qemu-virt.conf , _template.conf ). How it works fastboot boot ──► UEFI (Mu-Silicium) ──► xnuloader (EFI application) │ stays resident: USB link (fastboot protocol), │ watchdog, receives the kernel's log ▼ XNU (BCM2837 config as the base + our platform) ├─ GICv3, timer, video console, return to the loader ├─ APFS (images in RAM, iOS volume on flash), ramfs (/private/var, /tmp) ├─ minicrypto instead of corecrypto, AMFI and Sandbox stand-ins (MAC policies) ├─ driver replacements: IOSurface, IOMobileFramebuffer, AppleKeyStore, network stack ├─ input: /dev/redwood-touch ◄─ Goodix GT9916 (phone) / virtio-input (QEMU) ├─ GPU: Adreno 642L, Wi-Fi: WCN6750 (ath11k via LinuxKPI), sound: ADSP / virtio-sound ▼ iOS 16.5 launchd → logd, notifyd, cfprefsd, runningboardd, backboardd, SpringBoard, apps ├─ our libraries are injected into backboardd, SpringBoard and mediaserverd │ (virtual HID services, a few ObjC method swaps — in memory only) └─ mediaserverd gets our CoreAudio output device (RedwoodAudio.

title: OpenAI CLI
abstract:
OpenAI CLI The official command-line tool for the OpenAI REST API. Install · CLI reference · Guides Call the OpenAI REST API from your terminal or shell scripts. Generate images, upload
files, submit batches, and inspect API results without writing an application. Note OpenAI CLI or Codex CLI? Use openai when you want to call a specific API
or put API operations in a script. Use Codex CLI ( codex ) when you want a coding agent to work on a project: read and edit code,
run commands, and help implement or debug a change. Things to try These examples use an API key; see installation and authentication below. Generate an image and save it locally openai images generate --prompt " A tiny orange robot watering a houseplant " Images are saved to ~/Downloads/gpt-images/ , and the command prints their paths.
Use --output-dir for an existing destination directory or --name for a filename.
Supported terminals can preview the result. See the image guide for editing, model selection, and preview settings. Upload a file and retrieve it later openai files upload report.txt --purpose user_data
openai files get file-example
openai files download file-example --output downloaded-report.txt Use your own local file and replace file-example with the ID returned by the upload.
See working with files for more examples. Run requests in a batch Submit a JSONL request file, then wait for the batch and download its results: openai files upload requests.jsonl --purpose batch
openai batches create --input-file-id file-example \ --endpoint /v1/responses --completion-window 24h
openai batches wait batch_example --output-dir ./results Replace the file and batch IDs with the returned IDs. The batch guide includes a sample requests.jsonl and explains result files and failed requests. Export API data for a script openai models list --format jsonl | jq ' .id ' openai files list --format json > files.json Choose --format json for a JSON document or --format jsonl for records.
The default output is readable text, even in pipes . The first example uses jq . Installation Installing a prebuilt binary Download the archive for your operating system and architecture from GitHub Releases .
Binaries are available for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Extract the archive and
place openai ( openai.exe on Windows) in a directory on your PATH . Installing with Homebrew brew install openai/tools/openai Installing with Go Requires Go 1.26 or later . go install ' github.com/openai/openai-cli/cmd/openai@latest ' Once you have run go install , the binary is placed in your Go bin directory: Default location : $HOME/go/bin (or $GOPATH/bin if GOPATH is set) Check your path : Run go env GOPATH to see the base directory If commands aren't found after installation, add the Go bin directory to your PATH: # Add to your shell profile (.zshrc, .bashrc, etc.) export PATH= " $PATH : $( go env GOPATH ) /bin " The CLI checks for updates on eligible interactive runs; it never installs them
automatically. Set OPENAI_CLI_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 to disable checks and notices.
See update notices for details. Authentication Run the setup guide to enter your API key safely: openai help setup For scripts, supply OPENAI_API_KEY through your environment or secret manager.
Create a key in API settings . Try a request: openai responses create \ --model gpt-5.5 \ --input " Say this is a test " Admin endpoints use OPENAI_ADMIN_KEY , a separate admin API key .
For example, retrieve one day of organization usage: openai admin organization usage completions \ --start-time 1735689600 \ --end-time 1735776000 \ --bucket-width 1d Usage Commands follow the API's resources: openai < resource > [subresource...] < command > [flags...] Browse commands and options with help. Help needs no API key or network connection. openai --help
openai images generate --help
openai admin organization --help openai help COMMAND and openai COMMAND --help show the same page.
Existing colon-separated commands, such as openai admin:organization:usage completions ,
also work. Output and errors Successful JSON responses display readable text by default. Select a data format
explicitly when parsing results. Use --transform to extract fields with GJSON syntax : openai files get file-example --transform filename --raw-output Errors go to stderr as readable summaries. Use --format-error json for API error
details, or --transform-error to extract error fields. Explicit --format json , jsonl , raw , and yaml also apply to errors unless --format-error overrides
them; --format-error text restores summaries. API error details and --debug logs can contain sensitive data: sanitize them before sharing. Check the command's exit status before using redirected results; a failed request
can leave an incomplete output file. See reading command results for list formats, streaming, binary downloads, and error behavior. File input Binary uploads take a plain path. JSON input flags can read a value from a local
file with @path : openai files upload report.txt --purpose user_data
openai responses create --model gpt-5.5 --input @prompt.txt Use OPENAI_UNTRUSTED_STDIN=1 when piping JSON or YAML from an untrusted source
so input cannot cause local file reads. In that mode, provide upload paths
explicitly as flags. See file arguments and encoding for escaping literal @ values, JSON/YAML input, and text or base64 encoding. Shell shortcuts Set up shell completion to complete commands and file
paths. Command insertion lets you search examples
with Ctrl+X, then Tab and insert them without running them. The first eligible interactive run saves image-picker Tab shortcuts for future
Bash, zsh, and fish sessions. Open a new terminal to use them. See setup and removal for requirements and opt-out.
In PowerShell, press Enter after openai images generate to open the picker. Guides Task Guide Generate, edit, save, and preview images Images Upload and download files Files Submit batches and collect results Batches Generate speech and work with audio Audio Inspect and count tokens locally Tokenizer Test webhook handling Webhooks Parse results in scripts Output formats Configure headers, mTLS, and file input CLI reference Tip Managing OpenAI resources with Terraform? Use the official OpenAI Terraform provider to manage projects, service accounts, rate limits, and other supported resources
as infrastructure as code. Development From a clone of this repository, run the CLI with: ./scripts/run --help To test against another OpenAI Go SDK version, use ./scripts/link : ./scripts/link github.com/org/repo@version
./scripts/link ../path/to/openai-go With no arguments, it uses ../openai-go . See CONTRIBUTING.md for setup, checks, and repository structure. Contributing Please share bug reports and feature requests through GitHub issues .
Pull requests are limited to repository collaborators; we do not accept pull requests from non-collaborators.
See CONTRIBUTING.md for the contribution policy and development guide.
For security vulnerabilities, follow SECURITY.md . License Copyright 2026 OpenAI This project is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 .

title: Security Disclosure
abstract:
Jacob Cooper Oct 21, 2026 Earlier this morning, Railway detected anomalous activity involving systems that store customer environment variables. After further investigation, our investigation to date indicates that an unauthorized third party may have accessed encrypted environment variables and, for some of them, obtained the decrypted contents. Environment variables may contain secrets such as API keys or database and registry credentials. We believe this is part of a series of attacks recently targeting platform companies with the aim of compromising AI inference providers. We have notified these upstream providers to revoke all keys proactively, as we take these kinds of events extremely seriously. While our initial analysis suggests the impact may be limited to a subset of users, we are nevertheless recommending that all users take the actions described below as a precaution to protect your systems while we complete our review. What you should do: As such, we strongly recommend that you immediately roll all environment variables, including any API keys, stored in Railway, as well as any private registry credentials, and review logs for those services for unusual activity. All deployments are paused while we investigate. Until builds are restored, you will not be able to roll out new versions. We apologize for this inconvenience. Follow this incident to be notified when builds resume. As we confirm which accounts were affected, we will contact those customers directly by email with additional details. We will provide new updates on this announcement, and on status.railway.com as we narrow the scope of impact.

title: Claude Now Works with Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides
abstract:
Claude for Google Workspace™ is now in public beta on all paid Claude plans. It adds Claude to Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides, so that you can work with Claude directly in your open files. Additionally, we are releasing new Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors (beta) that Claude uses to create and edit Google files directly from Claude. Claude works where you work With the add-on, Claude opens in a sidebar next to your file, so you don’t need to switch between apps or browser tabs when you work. Claude can read the doc, sheet, or deck you have open, see which text, cells, or slides you’ve selected, and make changes directly in the file. In Docs , for example, Claude can fix a sentence or restyle a heading in place without touching the surrounding formatting. For bigger rewrites, it can propose edits as suggestion cards in the sidebar. Each card highlights the passage it would change, and you can apply or dismiss it. You can ask Claude to tighten the executive summary of a product requirements document and turn the next steps into a table, and Claude will do both directly in the doc. In Sheets , Claude can write formulas, build pivot tables and native Sheets charts, and add new tabs. For joins or data cleaning, it can pull a range into Python and write the results back into the sheet. You can start from an empty sheet, attach your source files, ask for a Q3 budget vs. actuals report with a tab for each team and a summary chart, and Claude can flag anything that’s over the budget. In Slides , Claude can build new slides from your deck’s layouts and themes, so they match the rest of the deck. Then it can check its work and flag elements that overlap or run off the slide, or text that’s hard to read. You decide how much Claude does on its own. In the default “Ask before edits” mode, each change appears as an approval card with a summary and Claude waits for your approval to make the edit. In “Accept all edits” mode, Claude works through the task and applies changes without stopping. Your connectors, skills, and enterprise controls come with you When you are signed in with your Claude account, the sidebar has the same models, connectors (opens in new tab) , and skills (opens in new tab) you use in Claude. For example, if you ask for a quarterly business review (QBR) deck for your customer, Claude can pull the account history from Salesforce and recent call notes through your Google Drive connector. If you save the QBR format as a skill, your team can build the next deck following the same format and steps. On Enterprise plans, controls such as the Compliance API, customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK), and OpenTelemetry audit export apply to the add-on too Edit Google files from Claude With the Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors (opens in new tab) , also in beta, you can start in Claude and it will create and edit your Google files from the chat. Paste a Google file link or ask for a Google doc, sheet, or deck, and on supported setups it will open in a pane beside your conversation. Starting from Claude makes most sense when you need a new file or your work spans several files. Claude’s access matches your existing Google sharing permissions. Getting started Claude for Google Workspace (opens in new tab) is in beta on all paid plans. Install it from the Google Workspace Marketplace (opens in new tab) , then open a file and go to Extensions > Claude > Open Claude. Admins can deploy it to their domain or selected groups from the Google Admin console. The Help Center guide covers setup (opens in new tab) . To edit Google files from Claude, turn on the Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides connectors (opens in new tab) . On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner or primary owner needs to enable the connectors first.

title: Development of BASEER: a comprehensive Arabic–English process improvement platform integrating Lean Six Sigma tools with AI-powered waste classification
abstract:
This paper aims to address the limited success of Lean Six Sigma (LSS) initiatives in Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) contexts, where cultural and linguistic misalignment often undermines adoption. It introduces and pilots BASEER, a bilingual Arabic–English digital platform designed to embed LSS tools into public sector and service organizations while accounting for linguistic nuance and organizational culture.
 
 
 
 Using a minimum viable product (MVP) approach, BASEER was iteratively developed and refined through workshops involving Omani Government ministries. Feedback from participants guided system enhancements, while natural language processing (NLP) models were trained and evaluated on a data set of 1,041 Arabic operational statements across eight waste categories to classify Lean wastes. Qualitative feedback, observational notes and system outputs formed the empirical base for analysis.
 
 
 
 Results suggest that BASEER made improvement initiatives more inclusive by enabling broader staff participation, especially among younger and frontline employees. Compared with traditional board-and-sticker approaches, the platform facilitated faster input collection, more systematic waste classification and easier dissemination of visual analysis. Participants perceived BASEER as better aligned with local context than consultant-led interventions, though findings remain perception-based rather than quantitatively validated.
 
 
 
 As an MVP pilot, this study is limited to workshop settings in Oman and relies largely on participant feedback. Broader testing across GCC countries, the private sector and larger data sets is required to confirm generalizability. Dialectal variation in Arabic also presents ongoing challenges for NLP integration.
 
 
 
 BASEER demonstrates that LSS tools can be localized for Arabic-speaking environments. By embedding improvement tools in culturally sensitive, bilingual formats, the platform provides a more sustainable model for government and service-sector organizations pursuing digital transformation.
 
 
 
 By enabling staff at all levels to contribute feedback in their native language, BASEER promotes more inclusive decision-making within government and service organizations. This fosters greater transparency, reduces barriers to participation and supports a shift from individual blame to systemic improvement. In the wider social context, culturally adapted quality platforms can strengthen public trust in services, enhance citizen satisfaction and reduce the dependency on external consultants whose recommendations may not reflect local realities. This study highlights how digital transformation, when culturally grounded, can advance both organizational excellence and social equity.
 
 
 
 To the best of the author’s knowledge, this is among the first studies to integrate Arabic NLP with LSS for public-sector applications. It contributes to the Quality 4.0 literature by suggesting that digital transformation must address not only technological sophistication but also linguistic inclusivity and cultural alignment. The paper offers an early model for adapting global methodologies into locally relevant, user-friendly digital tools.
